it, for every contract, which is unsafe, is entitled after nuptial present according to the <term>Brehon <note>original: "breitheamh"; a member of the professional class of jurists in early Ireland who interpreted and applied the customary law</note></term>, except in case of poverty, or prohibition, or want of power."*

In this passage there are involved the doctrines of <term>consideration <note>the value or benefit given by each party in a contract that makes it legally binding</note></term> as the necessary basis for a contract, of purchase for valuable consideration and part performance, and of the <term>rescission <note>the cancellation or overturning of a contract</note></term> of the contract by an inequality in the condition of the parties which in <term>equity <note>a branch of law focused on fairness and justice, often used to correct situations where strict legal rules would lead to an unfair result</note></term> would now cause an agreement to be set aside, or specific performance to be refused. In the latter portion of this paragraph "poverty" must mean such pressure of poverty upon one of the contracting parties as would prevent his acting as a perfectly free agent; and "prohibition," according to the <gloss>explanatory note</gloss>, the fact of notice affecting the purchaser that the vendor has no equitable title; "want of power" is explained as <term>duress <note>threats or violence used to force someone to do something against their will</note></term>, or influence of a moral or immoral character.

There are other passages in this tract which lay down in a direct manner the ancient theory of society that the individual exists only as a member of some recognised community and therefore that his contracts are always subject to rescission by the head of the community to which he belongs.

> "There are four covenants which are not binding, though they (*the parties*) are proceeded against; *that of a bondman with his chief; of a son with his father; of a monk with his abbot; of an <term>ulach <note>likely referring to a person who is legally incapable or mentally unstable</note></term> person with another if alone. For the chief, and the tribe, and the church may redeem (rescind) every good contract, and every bad contract which are made with their subjects, except what they themselves order them; for these are the three defective covenants mentioned by the <term>Feini <note>the ancient free land-owning class of Ireland whose customs formed the basis of the law</note></term>; the covenant with the subject of a church; the covenant of a servitor of a chief; a covenant with fugitives from a tribe.*"†

### III.

### THE "FAMILY" AND THE "HAND-KIN" SYSTEM.*

In all the <term>Brehon Law <note>the ancient native legal system of Ireland, which operated until the 17th century</note></term> Tracts there are references to an existing organization, generally known as the <term>Geilfine <note>literally "hand-kindred"; the smallest and most immediate circle of family members in the Irish kinship system</note></term> system, and to the four classes designated as the <term>Geilfine <note>the immediate family group</note></term>, <term>Deirbhfine <note>the "true family," usually extending to first cousins</note></term>, <term>Iarfine <note>the "after-family," extending to second cousins</note></term>, and <term>Indfine <note>the "end-family," the most distant recognized circle of kin, reaching to third cousins</note></term>.† No distinct explanation of the system is anywhere given by the writers of these tracts, but it is everywhere assumed as existing, and of so well-known and notorious a character that it did not seem to our authors necessary to state its details or to lay down the rules by which it was governed. That it was familiar, or assumed to be familiar, to the students of these works is proved by the figurative use of the terms primarily indicating the members of this system as indicating certain definite relations of place; remarkable passages of this nature occur in the "Bee-Judgments"‡ <note>a set of laws governing the ownership, theft, and stings of bees, which were highly valued for honey and wax</note> and the "Right to Water."§ <note>laws concerning the shared use of water for mills and irrigation</note> It is obviously impossible to understand the scope or meaning of many of the rules contained in the original text, or of passages in the commentary, without forming some clear conception of this peculiar organization of individuals assumed throughout, as pre-existing, and endeavouring to define the technical terms connected with this system, which so often occurs, used sometimes in a primary, and sometimes in a secondary sense. In the <term>Book of Aicill <note>one of the principal surviving texts of the Brehon Law, traditionally attributed to King Cormac mac Airt and the scholar Cenn Faelad</note></term>, published in the last volume of the <term>Brehon laws</term>, there occurred a very remarkable passage, explanatory of the mode in which property was divisible among the members of a family in

> “The most remarkable custom described in the <term>Book of Aicill</term> is the fourfold distribution of the family into the ‘<term>geilfine</term> <note>the immediate family unit, consisting of the father and his four closest male descendants</note>,’ ‘<term>deirbhfine</term> <note>the "true family," typically extending to first cousins or the next circle of kin</note>,’ ‘<term>iarfine</term> <note>the "after-family," a more distant circle of relatives, often second cousins</note>,’ and ‘<term>indfine</term> <note>the "end-family," the most distant recognized group of relatives, usually third cousins</note>’ divisions. From both the text and the commentary it appears that the object of the institution did not extend further than the regulation of the distribution of their property. Within the family seventeen members were organized in four divisions, of which the junior class, known as the ‘<term>geilfine</term>’-division, consisted of five persons; the ‘<term>deirbhfine</term>’ the second in order, the ‘<term>iarfine</term>’ the third in order, and the ‘<term>indfine</term>’ the senior of all, consisted respectively of four persons. The whole organization consisted, and could only consist of seventeen members. If any person was born into the ‘<term>geilfine</term>’-division its eldest member was promoted into the ‘<term>deirbhfine</term>’; the eldest member of the ‘<term>deirbhfine</term>’ passed into the ‘<term>iarfine</term>’; the eldest member of the ‘<term>iarfine</term>’ moved into the ‘<term>indfine</term>’; and the eldest member of the ‘<term>indfine</term>’ passed out of the organization altogether. It would appear that this transition from a lower to a higher grade took place upon the introduction of a new member into the ‘<term>geil-fine</term>’-division, and therefore depended upon the introduction of new members, not upon the death of the seniors. The property held by any class, or by its members as such, must have been held for the benefit of the survivors or survivor of that class; but, upon the extinction of a class, the property of the class or of its members as such passed to the surviving classes or class according to special and very technical rules.

->### INTRODUCTION.<-

Let it be assumed that each class possesses property represented by the figure 16. The class or classes extinct are denoted in the subsequent columns by a cypher <note>a zero</note>, and the distribution of the property of the extinct class or classes is indicated by the numbers set opposite the names of the surviving classes. Three-fourths of the property of any extinct class pass to the next junior class, and in default of any junior surviving class, to the next senior class. The remaining one-fourth is treated in the same manner. If, exclusive of the class which has received its share, there remains but one class, the residue passes to that class, but if two classes survive, three-fourths of the residue pass to the next junior class, and, in default, of such class, to the next senior class; and the residue, one-fourth of a fourth, or one-sixteenth of the entire, goes to the remaining class. If two classes become extinct, the property of each is distributed according to this rule, in which case, if the two classes which become extinct are next to each other, the distribution of the property of both is identically the same; but if the extinct classes are not next to each other, the property of each is distributed to the remaining classes in varying proportions. It is evident from the commentary that the original principle, however it arose, had been forgotten, so that the distribution contained in column 8 of the above diagram is very awkwardly expressed, and the cases in columns 9 and 10 are altogether omitted. The meaning of this very artificial arrangement appears from the following passage:—

‘If the father is alive and has two sons, and each of those sons has a family of the full number—*i.e.*, four—it is the opinion of *lawyers* that the father would claim a man's share in every family of them, and that in this case they form two 'immediate family <note>original: "geilfine"</note>'-divisions. And if the property has come from another place, from a family outside, though there should be within in the family a son or a brother of the person whose property came into it, he shall not obtain it any more than *any other man* of the family.’

From this it appears that the whole organization existed within the family, and consisted of the actual descendants of a male member of the family, who himself continued in the power of the head of the family. As soon as a son of the house had himself four children, he and his four children formed an ‘immediate family <note>original: "geilfine"</note>’-class, and each succeeding descendant up to the number of seventeen was introduced into the artificial body. The entire property exclusively belonging to this family within a family was confined to the members of the organization until the number exceeded seventeen, when the senior member lost his rights to the separate estate, retaining those which he possessed in the original family.

The majority of the tracts now published have been specially selected, so that it may not be considered an abuse of the restricted duties of an editor to explain the views upon this subject put forward upon such distinguished authority, and to state the objections to the reception of any of them in its integrity, before an attempt is made to propound a theory of the origin and working of the system, wholly deduced from the <term>Brehon Law</term> <note>The indigenous legal system of early medieval Ireland, practiced by professional jurists known as Brehons</note> Tracts themselves. The essential principle of the system seems to me a distribution into fours. The fifth person in the Geilfine division, I take to be the parent from whom the sixteen descendants spring, and it will be seen, from the proviso which I inserted above, that I do not consider his place in the organization to have been ever changed. ->## INTRODUCTION.<-

I have already stated that I consider the fifth person in the group of five to be the parent from whom all the other members of the four divisions spring, or with whom they are connected by adoptive descent. Thus, the whole of the natural or adoptive descendants are distributed into four groups of four persons each, their rank in the Family being in the inverse order of their seniority. The <term>Geilfine</term> <note>The 'hand-family,' the most immediate circle of five relatives in the ancient Irish kinship system</note> group is several times stated in the <term>Brehon Law</term> <note>The indigenous legal system of early medieval Ireland</note> to be at once the highest and the youngest.

> "Now Mr. W. Stokes has conveyed to me his opinion that ‘Geilfine’ means ‘hand-family.’ As I have reason to believe that a different version of the term has been adopted by eminent authority, I will give the reasons for Mr. Stokes’ view. ‘Gil’ means ‘hand’—this was also the rendering of O’Curry—and it is in fact the same as the Greek word for hand <note>original: χείρ (*cheir*)</note>. In several <term>Aryan</term> <note>A term used by 19th-century scholars to refer to the Indo-European language family</note> languages, the term signifying ‘hand’ is an expressive equivalent for power, and especially for Family or Patriarchal Power. Thus in Greek we have terms for the person 'under the hand' <note>original: ὑποχείριος (*hypocheirios*) and χέρης (*cheres*)</note>. In Latin we have *master* <note>original: *herus*</note>, from an old word cognate to the Greek word for hand; we have also one of the earliest cardinal terms of ancient Roman Family Law, *hand* <note>original: *manus*</note>, in the sense of Patriarchal authority. In Roman legal phraseology, the wife who has become in law her husband’s daughter by marriage is *in the hand* <note>original: *in manu*</note>. The son discharged from Parental Power is *emancipated* <note>literally "sent out from the hand"</note>. The free person who has undergone <term>manumission</term> <note>the formal act of freeing a slave</note> is *in hand-taking* <note>original: *in mancipio*</note>. In the Celtic languages we have, with other words, ‘Gilla,’ a servant, a word familiar to sportsmen and travellers in the Highlands, and to readers of Scott in its Anglicized shape ‘Gillie.’
> 
> "My suggestion, then, is that the key to the Irish distribution of the Family, as to so many other things in ancient law, must be sought in the <term>power of the father</term> <note>original: *Patria Potestas*</note>. It seems to me to be founded on the order of emancipation from Parental Power."

\* The use by Sir H. S. Maine of the term “power of the father” <note>original: *patria potestas*</note> is very unfortunate as basing his theory upon a doctrine of the Roman Law, which their own lawyers admitted to be peculiar and exceptional. The more general term “headship of the joint house” may, however, be substituted for it without injury to the argument.

->### INTRODUCTION.<-

Authority. The <term>Geilfine</term> <note>The 'hand-family,' the smallest and most senior unit of the ancient Irish kinship system, typically consisting of five people</note>, or the Hand-family, consists of the parent and the four natural or adoptive sons immediately under his power. The other groups consist of emancipated descendants, whose dignity or status decreases in proportion to their distance from the primary group, which according to archaic notions, constitutes the true or representative family.

> "The remains which we possess of the oldest Roman Law point to a range of ideas very similar to that which appears to have produced the Irish Institution. The family under the <term>paternal power</term> <note>original: *Patria Potestas*</note> was, along with the <term>head of the household</term> <note>original: *Paterfamilias*</note>, the true Roman Family. The children who were emancipated from paternal power may have gained a practical advantage, but they undoubtedly lost in theoretical dignity. They underwent that loss of status which in ancient legal phraseology was called a <term>diminution of rights</term> <note>original: *capitis diminuto*</note>. We know too that according to primitive Roman law they lost all rights of inheritance, and these were only gradually restored to them by a relatively modern institution, the equity of the <term>Roman Prætor</term> <note>A high-ranking magistrate in ancient Rome who could modify laws to ensure fairness</note>. Nevertheless there are hints on all sides, that, as a general rule, sons as they advanced in years were enfranchised from paternal power, and no doubt this practice supplies a partial explanation of the durability of the <term>paternal power</term> as a Roman Institution. The statements therefore which we find concerning the Celtic Family would not be very untrue of the Roman. The youngest children were first in dignity."*

The entire <term>geilfine</term> system rests according to this view upon the <term>paternal power</term> <note>original: *patria potestas*</note> of the original progenitor without any reference to common property; the members are those up to the number of sixteen, who are the subject of the paternal power, whether sons or remoter descendants, either by actual descent or adoption, and irrespective of age or the possession of property. It may be inferred that in Sir Henry Sumner Maine's opinion the existence of the common ancestor is essential for the maintenance of the system, and that he regards all the members as living at the same time.

> "The whole **Ancestral Kinship Group** <note>original: *Fine Duthaig*; the term refers to the entire body of relatives entitled to share in the family's land and heritage</note> included several stages of consanguinity;—(1) the **Head-kin** <note>original: *Cindfine*; the most immediate circle of children</note> or children, the sons having the primary right;—(2) the **Womb-kin** <note>original: *Bruindfine*; derived from *bruind*, the womb</note>, the sons and daughters of heiresses or daughters of the **Noble Grade** <note>original: *Gradh Fine*; the social rank of nobility who inherited property in their own right</note> inheriting property in their own right; (3) the **Hand-family** <note>original: *Gelfine*; the core group of five close relatives who held the most immediate legal rights</note>, which seems to have been sometimes used for all relatives to the fifth degree, and sometimes for the relatives to the fifth degree exclusive of the direct heirs. These constituted the family in the strict sense of the word. From the *Hand-family* branched off, (4) the **True-kin** <note>original: *Derbfine*; relatives from the fifth to the ninth degree</note>, which included relatives from the fifth to the ninth degree; (5) the **After-kin** <note>original: *Iarfine*; relatives from the ninth to the thirteenth degree</note>, or relatives from the ninth to the thirteenth degree; and (6) the **End-kin** <note>original: *Indfine*; relatives from the thirteenth to the seventeenth degree</note>, or relatives from the thirteenth to the seventeenth degree. Beyond the latter degree, the *Kinship* merged into a **National Community** <note>original: *Duthaig Daine*; literally the 'inheritance of people,' referring to the wider nation</note>, that is, the nation at large, who were not entitled to a share of the **Inheritance of the Deceased** <note>original: *Dibad*; property left behind by someone who died without direct heirs</note>, or property of deceased persons, or liable for the payment of fines or <term>legal penalties</term> <note>original: *americaments*; a financial penalty or fine imposed by a court</note> on account of crimes, etc., except those of their own special *Kin*, within the recognised degrees of consanguinity. The *Hand-family* were the representatives of the rights and liabilities of the family or house; they formed a kind of family council styled the **Five-person Family Council** <note>original: *Cuicer na Fine*</note>, or the five **Pledges** <note>original: *Gials*; individuals who acted as a security or guarantee for the family's conduct</note>, or pledges of the family. As they represented the roots of the spreading branches of the family, they were also called the **five fingers of the Kin** <note>original: *cuic mera na Fine*</note>. When property, in default of direct heirs, passed to collateral heirs, the *Hand-family* received the inheritance in the first instance, and assumed all the responsibilities attached to it. In default of relatives of the fifth degree, the property passed to the representatives of the other *Kinship groups*."*

The text continues as follows: “We may observe, I think, a similar case in the difficult instance of the Irish **Kinship Group** <note>original: *Fine*</note>. The ingenuity of the Brehon professors <note>the legal scholars of ancient Ireland</note> multiplied distinctions which are not found in the laws of other countries, and it is not easy to clearly understand their writings on this subject. <meta>This page continues the analysis of the ancient Irish kinship system, specifically critiquing contemporary theories (such as those in Hearn's "The Aryan Household") regarding how the various "Fine" or family divisions were calculated and whether they functioned as real social groups or merely theoretical legal categories.</meta>

->### INTRODUCTION.<-

The theory of Mr. M‘Lennan regarding this subject differs in every respect from those proposed by Sir H. S. Maine and Dr. W. K. Sullivan. The three fundamental assumptions upon which his argument proceeds are: (1) that the terms **Hand-family** <note>original: *geilfine*</note>, **True-family** <note>original: *derbhfine*</note>, **After-family** <note>original: *iarfine*</note>, and **End-family** <note>original: *indfine*</note> are mutually dependent, meaning that all four classes of the system must exist from the very beginning; (2) that the arrangement was based upon the ownership and specifically tied to the distribution of property; and (3) that the members of these groups included only certain specific members of the family rather than the whole kindred.

The **Hand-family** <note>original: *geilfine*</note> system, according to this view, originated from the existence of *four* persons who were related in the same degree to the original **ancestral root** <note>original: *stirps*</note>. Each of these individuals was the primary member of one of the four classes. As a necessary result, the Father or **ancestral root** <note>original: *stirps*</note> was excluded from the formal organization himself, and the subsequent members of each class were the direct descendants of that class's original member.

> “If we imagine one of these organizations—initiated as in the case decided upon by the lawyers—to be completed (1) through the death of the Father, with his two sons leaving a set of four grandsons in their places, each acting as the eldest member of his division; and (2) through the filling up of the divisions by the birth of descendants to the various grandsons, the following table will then represent the organization:—

| **End-family** <note>original: *Indfine*</note> | **After-family** <note>original: *Iarfine*</note> | **True-family** <note>original: *Deirbhfine*</note> | **Hand-family** <note>original: *Geilfine*</note> | |
|----------|----------|------------|-----------|-----------------------------------|
| A¹ | A² | A³ | A⁴ | Fathers and Brothers. |
| B¹ | B² | B³ | B⁴ | Sons and First Cousins. |
| C¹ | C² | C³ | C⁴ | Grandsons and Second Cousins. |
| D¹ | D² | D³ | D⁴ | Great Grandsons and Third Cousins. |
| — | — | — | E⁴ | Great-great Grandsons. |

The family of the German Emperor includes all the descendants of Frederick IV, **Burgrave** <note>original: *Burggraf*; a title for a count of a castle or fortified town</note> of Nuremberg, who died in 1332. As to their probable number when discovered, it is a matter of mathematical increase. If we consult the biblical lineage of David, it appears that, as the seventeenth in descent from Reu, he counted among his relatives within the seventeenth degree the entire nations of the Jews, Edomites, Ishmaelites, Moabites, Ammonites, Midianites, and several others.

> “The seniors of the division are A¹, A², etc., the brothers who constituted the ‘family of the full number, that is, four’; and the other men in the divisions along with them respectively, are their first-born sons, grandsons, etc. A¹ is the eldest of the four brothers, A² the next eldest, and A⁴ is the youngest. The following features of the system now become intelligible:—
>
> “1. It is at once obvious why it is said the <term>geilfine</term> <note>hand-family: the first and youngest circle of kinship in the Irish system, consisting of the father and his four closest descendants</note> division is the youngest, and the <term>indfine</term> <note>end-family: the fourth and most distant circle of kinship, containing the members furthest removed from the current head of the family</note> division is the oldest.
>
> “2. We can see a reason why, as a rule, there should be four men only in a division, and why there should be a fifth man in the <term>geilfine</term> division. The age of marriage among the ancient Irish was seventeen years—the age for finishing fosterage <note>The practice of sending children to be raised by other families to strengthen social and political bonds</note>. Thus A¹ would be at least fifty-four years old before his great grandson D¹ would be born; he would be between eighty and ninety years old before E⁴ could have a son; which would be the signal to A¹ to ‘go out of the community.’ As a rule then, there could be only four generations of men in existence at a time, and represented in the divisions. The fifth man, or rather boy, in the <term>geilfine</term> division must have been added to postpone the going out ‘into the community’ of the senior of the <term>indfine</term>. When he went out, he became, as we shall see, a pensioner on his division, and were he to go out when E⁴ was born, he might be a charge on that division for a term of years. Before E⁴ could have a son, however, A¹ would be a very old man. Indeed, the ‘going out’ must have been rare. The law, however, provided for it, as it did for the divisions not being full, and even for their becoming extinct. Whatever the purposes of the organization were, the existence of the whole number of the seventeen men was not essential to them, and in the eye of the law a division existed so long as there was one man in it (*The Great Tradition* <note>original: *Senchus Mor*, the primary collection of ancient Irish Brehon Laws</note>, Vol. III., p. 333).
>
> “3. So far as the organization was an artificial institution, it may have been a sufficient reason for limiting the number of divisions to four, that there were four men only in a division. More probably the reason was that four was, on the average, the full number of sons in a family.

Henry S. Maine aptly calls it, according to which the oldest member of each division passed into the next, on a new man 'coming up' into the <term>geilfine</term> <note>hand-family: the first and youngest circle of kinship in the Irish system, consisting of the father and his four closest descendants</note> division. Among the Irish, the next brother, or other nearest male-line relative next in seniority to a deceased chief, succeeded to the chieftaincy in preference to a son. We can, therefore, understand how they should provide for the succession of brother to brother, in order of seniority, in the leadership of divisions; and failing brothers, for the succession of cousin to cousin (of the same class) in order of seniority. It accords with this succession law that when A¹ 'went out,' A² should succeed him as head of the <term>indfine</term> <note>end-family: the fourth and most distant circle of kinship, containing the members furthest removed from the current head of the family</note> division, that A³ should succeed A² as head of the <term>iarfine</term> <note>after-family: the third circle of kinship</note>, and A⁴ succeed A³ as head of the <term>derbhfine</term> <note>true-family: the second circle of kinship</note>. But we saw that before A¹ went out he would be very old. Before another 'going out' could occur through the birth of a grandson to E⁴, the brothers would certainly be all dead, and the first cousins, B¹, etc., would be the heads of divisions. It would be next B¹'s turn to go out, and he would be succeeded in the leadership of the <term>indfine</term> division by B² as the cousin next in seniority; and B² being succeeded by B³, and B³ by B⁴, all the seniors would be promoted as before. By the fourth occurrence of such an occasion it would be D¹'s turn to go out; if, indeed, before then the organization had not collapsed through the extinction of divisions and a lack of men to reform them.*

In a subsequent passage Mr. McLennan explains the mode in which this system would work as a <term>near-entail</term> <note>original: "quasi-entail"; a legal arrangement that restricts the inheritance of land to a specific line of heirs to keep it within the family</note> of the family lands. 

> "The most simple way of regarding the rules established for the fourfold organization, in order to see how they operated as a succession law, is to conceive it to be started by four brothers, A¹, A², etc., on the death of their father, leaving to them ancestral lands, which had come to him as next-of-kin, and which, at common law, they were entitled to divide equally between them. Thus regarded, the arrangement operated, in the first instance, as a settlement of the respective shares of the brothers on their heirs of line, the survivors, or survivor of them, as far as great-grandsons. When a son B appeared, A shared the division lands..."

guishes between the actual existing form of any legal organization, and the legal theory by which such form is determined. He does not assert that the Irish <term>fine</term> <note>the basic unit of Irish society, often translated as 'family' or 'kinship group'</note>, as a rule, was organized as a complete <term>geilfine</term> <note>the 'hand-family,' representing the closest and most immediate circle of kin</note> system, but proposes his theory as the abstract system of the <term>Brehon</term> <note>ancient Irish lawyers and judges who maintained the legal system through oral tradition and later written tracts</note> lawyers, upon which, under certain circumstances, the <term>fine</term> would be organized so far as it went, and which it should assume if fully developed. The English lawyer knows that the abstract and complete form of the English manor is as purely ideal as any Platonic archetype <note>an ideal or perfect model of something that exists more in theory than in reality</note>, but that the existing manors do, as far as circumstances admit, present more or less resemblance, and approach more or less nearly, to the theoretical manor described in our Real Property text books. Why should the ordinary rules for the succession to land be suddenly arrested upon the birth of a fourth son, and the shares of the several sons thereupon pass in strict entail <note>a legal limit on the inheritance of property to a specific line of descendants</note> for three generations according to the law of **primogeniture** <note>the right of the firstborn son to inherit the entire estate</note>? Mr. M'Lennan simply says that in this case the geilfine division drops the fifth man, but we must confess that such exclusion appears to us as inexplicable as his original inclusion.

In dealing with a question such as the present, there is nothing more misleading than analogies and assumed resemblances. Each of the three above-mentioned authors, who have treated of this subject, has supported his theory by reference to rules existing in other archaic systems of law, which are more or less confidently stated as arguments for the acceptance of the proposed theory as correct. But a profitable comparison can only be instituted between two known objects. An attempt to define the qualities of any thing unknown by reference to the qualities of a known quantity rests upon antecedent proof (more frequently the suppressed assumption) of their identity. This argument from tacitly assumed resemblances has been often in the present day too far pressed, frequently with very unfortunate results; in dealing with an inquiry like the present, it would seem to us that the first step is to discover, as far as possible, what the actual texts with which we are dealing say upon the subject, and to draw our conclusions from them free, as far as may be, from those **preconceived** <note>original: *a priori*; refers to knowledge or ideas that exist independently of experience or observation</note> ideas of law, which, as incident to the form of society in which we live, naturally influence our judgment; and that when we have arrived at some definite conclusions in this manner, then, but not until then, the analogies and resemblances of other system are useful for the purpose of testing the probability of the correctness of the results to which we have attained, and as explaining or illustrating many points of detail which at first failed to attract the attention which they deserved.

The earliest date of the original text, or rather of the customary rules laid down in the original text, is not, and probably cannot be, ascertained; the latest commentaries and glosses are probably not earlier than the 16th century; they certainly cover a period extending from the Danish invasion to the reign of Elizabeth, during which the country was exposed to continued war and confusion, and subjected to all the political and social causes which would naturally lead to the breaking up of the ancient tribe and family system, and the substitution of the arbitrary power of chiefs commanding bands of armed retainers for the regular action of ancient and established custom. The analogy of other nations in a similar condition would naturally lead us to anticipate that during this period the chiefs were constantly gaining ground as against the rights of the individual members of the tribe, and such would appear to have been the case from the days of **Conn Cetcorach** <note>Conn Cétchathach, known as 'Conn of the Hundred Battles,' a legendary High King of Ireland</note> to that of the chiefs, who, in the 16th century, obtained from the English Government grants of the tribe lands in fee or fee-tail with the object of defeating the custom of <term>Tanistry</term> <note>The Gaelic custom where a successor or 'Tanist' was elected from the ruling family during the lifetime of the current chief</note>, or of destroying the rights of the customary holders. The original constitution of the tribe or family during such a period gradually ceases to be an existing *social fact*, and tends to become merely a rule for the distribution of property upon death, after a fashion which would be strange and inexplicable, if we did not understand it to represent a social system which had for all practical purposes disappeared. The most important document upon the subject of the tribe and family organization is the tract entitled "Of the Divisions of the Tribe of a Territory" published in this volume, and we desire particular attention both to the text of this tract, and the obvious deductions to be drawn therefrom.

The word translated tribe in the title of this tract is "kindred" <note>original: "cinel"</note>, which is generally understood to mean a tribe in the full extension of the term, and containing a greater or less number of "families."

The word translated "territory" means not a mere extent of land, but primarily the tribe or people themselves, and thence a tract inhabited by a definite body, and regarded with reference to the rights of the occupants.

The word "family group" <note>original: "fine"</note>, translated variously "tribe" or "family," (a circumstance which has been noticed as an error by some critics of the present translation of the <term>Brehon Laws</term> <note>The native legal system of Ireland, practiced from the Iron Age until the 17th century</note>,) appears on the face of this document as not having any very precise or technical meaning, implying any number of persons conceived as forming a class whether from identity of descent, or similarity of rights.

This document must not be considered as a description of the ordinarily existing tribe, but rather as an explanation of the form which a tribe would assume if fully developed in every direction. It is remarkable that this tract would appear to consider the tribe and family as commensurate, if not identical. It would be, however, an error to consider that we must, from the tract in question, infer such to be the case, a result contradictory of many other passages in the <term>Brehon Law</term> tracts and opposed to all analogy.* The number of families in the Celtic tribe was never theo-

A permanent division of murderers is indeed an anomaly in a tribe organization, and there is a much simpler and more obvious explanation; in the present volume there is contained a tract entitled "The Land is forfeited for Crime," in which it is laid down that the land of one who had committed a crime was "given for his crime;" that his land was the primary fund for the payment of the "<term>honor-price fine</term> <note>original: "dire-fine"</note>" and compensation in exoneration of those who by reason of their kinship, or family relation, to the criminal, were bound to make good his default. ### INTRODUCTION.

From this tract the following deductions may be safely made: (1) the organization of the "<term>family group</term> <note>original: "fine"</note>" was based upon the exclusive possession of land by the "<term>family group</term>" as a distinct community, and had direct reference to the mode in which the land was divided among them.

(2) The four classes of the <term>close family</term> <note>original: "geilfine"</note>, <term>true family</term> <note>original: "deirbhfine"</note>, <term>after family</term> <note>original: "iarfine"</note>, and <term>end family</term> <note>original: "innfine"</note> consisted of seventeen members of the "<term>family group</term>" of pure descent, and full rights.

(3) Each of these four classes was complete in itself and possessed distinct joint rights both as against the other three classes as well as against the general members of the "<term>family group</term>."

(4) The four classes of full members do not comprise all the members of the family group. The "<term>black family</term> <note>original: "dubhfine"</note>" man, who had succeeded in establishing his position in the "<term>family group</term>" by ordeal or lot did not enter into the "<term>close family</term>" classification, but received a share of a fixed amount.

With reference to the "<term>true family</term>" division there is stated a rule that their property was not divided according to the number of kindred heads; it is possible that this may be introduced to point out that as between the "<term>close family</term>" and "<term>true family</term>" divisions, the two classes were to be considered as different and equal stocks, and the "<term>close family</term>" had no advantage in the division of property by reason of the greater number of its members; it would seem more probable that this is a general rule to the effect that property which passed to the "<term>true family</term>" class was to be divided "**by the branch**" <note>original: "per stirpes"; meaning inheritance is divided by family line rather than by the number of individuals.</note> and not "**by the head**" <note>original: "per capita"; meaning an equal share for every individual regardless of their branch of the family.</note>. This fact is put beyond doubt by the passage in page 259 describing the mode of the division of the "<term>atonement fine</term> <note>original: "dire-fine"; a compensatory payment for a crime or injury.</note>" payable to the family (and "<term>family group</term>") of a slain man: "Three <term>units of value</term> <note>original: "cumhals"; a standard unit of value in ancient Ireland, typically equivalent to three cows.</note> of "<term>atonement fine</term>" go to the son and to the father; there are three <term>units of value</term> of "<term>atonement fine</term>" remaining after that; a <term>unit of value</term> of "<term>atonement fine</term>" of them goes to a brother collaterally.—There is one '<term>unit of value</term>' of '<term>atonement fine</term>' then after that—that is to be divided from the lowest man of the '<term>close family</term>' division until it reaches the uppermost man; and from the uppermost man until it reaches the lowest, etc."

The movement of individual members through the different classes was not caused by the vacancies in the three latter classes but by a superfluity of members in the first class; and that the social position and rights of the classes among themselves was in the inverse order of the seniority. That there were some connexion of kinship between the members of the four classes is everywhere assumed, but the relationship which may have existed at any time between the members may not have been that upon which the system was originally constituted. The passage to which we refer lays down as a general principle that "the natural bondman does not bear the crimes of his relatives," but that if there were five houses of <term>outsider tenants</term> <note>original: "fuidhir"; these were often refugees or men from other tribes who settled on a lord's land with lower status</note>, each householder having a stock of one hundred cattle, and all under one chief, they formed an association recognized as a portion of the tribe; for each thereupon shared in the <term>common tribe land</term> <note>original: "dibadh"; property that reverts to the kin-group when a family line becomes extinct</note> and paid for the crimes of the other members of their separate organization. The phrase "They share the tribe property," translated as in the last sentence by an earlier <term>commentator</term> <note>original: "glossist"; a scholar who added explanatory notes to the legal manuscripts</note>, is translated by a subsequent commentator as, "Each of them shall share the tribe property of each other." According to this view, the reciprocal liability for crimes drew with it common rights and joint ownerships in the aggregate stock of the five houses.* But whatever rights the five head men of these <term>outsider tenant</term> houses acquired in the common stock, it must have been subject to the succession of lineal heirs, as in a subsequent passage we read (in respect of the case of <term>outsider tenants</term>), "the father does not sell anything to the prejudice of his sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, or great-great-grandsons."† To constitute such a community there must have been a certain number of persons belonging to different households, and also possessing an adequate amount of property. The sons, brothers, etc., of a household were liable for each other's deeds without such organization, and the addition of impecunious persons into such an association would create a liability without any reciprocal guarantee.

lxxv
->INTRODUCTION.<-

There must have existed distinct and early laws of hereditary succession to lands of inheritance (<term>orba</term> <note>Irish: land inherited from ancestors</note>) among the Irish Celtic tribes, but these rules have in fact been amalgamated in the "<term>geilfine</term>" <note>the smallest and most central unit of the Irish kin-group system, typically consisting of five close male relatives</note> system, and cannot be now understood apart from it; the Welsh rules which may be assumed to have some general resemblance to those of the Irish, throw, in our opinion, considerable light upon this subject. The relation of the father and son in the Welsh law in respect of the family inheritance resembled rather the <term>civil law substitution</term> <note>a concept from Roman law where one person is named to inherit if the primary heir cannot</note>, than the English <term>joint-tenancy</term> <note>a form of ownership where individuals hold equal shares of a property with rights of survivorship</note>; "neither is the son to deprive his father, during his life, of land and soil; in like manner the father is not to deprive the son of land."\* Such a rule, if strictly carried out, would have created a perpetual succession, and the right of the heir could be barred only in one way, namely, by an agreement between "father, brothers, cousins, second cousins, and the lord;" a proceeding the same as the present mode of barring a <term>Scotch tailzie</term> <note>a Scottish legal term for an "entail," which prevents an owner from selling or gifting land away from the lawful heir</note>.

Upon the death of the father, the daughters took nothing, unless there was a failure of male heirs; upon the death of the father the sons divided the lands between them in the following manner: "When brothers share the patrimony between them, the youngest is to have the principal <term>tyddyn</term> <note>Welsh: a homestead or farmstead</note>, and all the buildings of his father, and eight <term>erws</term> <note>Welsh: units of land roughly equivalent to acres</note> of land, his boiler, his fuel hatchet, and his coulter <note>the sharp blade of a plow</note>; because a father cannot give these three to any but to the youngest son; and though they should be pledged, they never become forfeited. Then let every brother take an homestead with eight erws of land; and the youngest son is to share, and they are to choose in succession from the eldest to the youngest."†

The inheritance having been thus divided among the first generation of descendants, was again divided among the grandsons, and again among the great grandsons, after which there was no further apportionment. By this we must understand that the three first generations of descendants took "<term>by the head</term>" <note>original: "per capita"; meaning the estate was divided equally among all eligible individuals regardless of which branch of the family they belonged to</note>, and that the fourth generation retained

The “family” came into being under certain circumstances, and again was dissolved upon the existence of a certain state of facts; the “tribe” existed before the “family” came into being and continued to exist after the latter had been dissolved; the “tribe” consisted of an aggregate of individuals connected by a real or assumed relationship, and occupying in separate households a district of which they in some manner were the common owners.

Let us consider the circumstances under which a “family” organized upon the *<term>geilfine</term>* <note>The 'geilfine' (meaning 'hand-kin') was the primary and smallest unit of the ancient Irish kinship system, originally consisting of five persons.</note> system came into existence; the mere fact that a member of the tribe had a certain number of children would be insufficient, for it rested upon the basis of the possession of a distinct and separate property; nor again would the bare fact of the possession of land enable a member even of the “family” to found a new *geilfine* group, for there was only one such organization in each family.

The property upon which a family was formed was not a right to a share greater or less in the general tribe land to be allotted from time to time, or a right to depasture the waste <note>Common land used for grazing.</note> of the tribe, but the exclusive possession of a definite portion of the tribe land, granted out the general mass, and appropriated as the exclusive and hereditary property of the descendants of some definite individual, an estate corresponding to the <term>Anglo-Saxon book-land</term> <note>original: "A.S. bocland"; land held by a written charter or "book," as opposed to customary folk-land.</note>, and described in the <term>Brehon Law</term> <note>The body of native Irish law that governed Ireland until the 17th century.</note> as “<term>patrimony</term>” <note>original Irish: "orba".</note>.

lxxix

->INTRODUCTION.<-

If land has thus been dedicated to the use of a separate family, the claims of its members to enjoy their several proportions by hereditary right must be traced from the original acquirer, or in the old English law term "from the conqueror" <note>In historical law, "conquest" or "the conqueror" refers to the first person to acquire land by means other than inheritance, such as by gift or purchase.</note>. This is very clearly shown by the Welsh rule that heirship is traced back in the first instance to the ancestor, and not to the deceased. As the family increased, the additional further accommodation is provided for, not by the enlargement of the original dwelling, but by the erection of new buildings with several allotments. The brothers under the Welsh law did not upon the father's death take equal undivided or divided shares, but to each was allotted his homestead with his eight *erws* <note>A Welsh unit of land measurement.</note> of land in severalty. The existence of the thickly scattered "*raths*" <note>Ancient circular earthen banks that served as the enclosures for Irish farmsteads.</note> in Ireland would of itself prove that the "family" occupied its district in this manner, and in the tract of the "*Crith Gabhlach*" <note>Literally "The Branched Purchase," a famous 8th-century Irish legal text that defines the social status, rights, and property of various classes of people.</note> (also published in this volume) the several members of the tribe are assumed to occupy separate houses, classified as to size, etc., in accordance with the rank of the occupiers; the Celtic family never seems to have clung together in the peculiar form of the Slavic <note>Original: "Sclavonic."</note> household.

In considering how a *geilfine system* <note>An ancient Irish kinship structure based on groups of five or seventeen relatives.</note> might have been formed, the question why the number of *seventeen* formed an element in the organization may be *postponed for subsequent consideration*. Nothing can be more embarrassing than an attempt to reconstruct a system founded both upon hereditary descent, and certain *assumed arithmetical proportions*. A family arranged upon *some rules of inheritance* can be easily understood, if once the principle of *hereditary succession* which underlies it, be ascertained; a political institution resting upon the selection of a *fixed number* from the indefinite mass of the population, can be supposed to have been an actually working institution. But when we read of assemblies formed of members *selected in certain proportions, or in fixed numbers, out of different stocks, or of property divided among the descendants of some ancestor, in a fixed number of shares*, it is clear that we are no longer

-># INTRODUCTION.<-
lxxx

dealing with actual facts, but with theoretical descriptions of what the institution was supposed in the abstract to have been. The numbers in each family must be uncertain; some men have many, some few or no descendants. The actual condition of the population must soon have rendered its arithmetical classification impossible, if such classification ever existed in fact. No one pretends to believe in the actual existence of the early Roman constitution, with a permanently fixed number of tribes, <term>curiæ</term> <note>original: "curiæ"; the political and religious divisions of the early Roman people.</note>, <term>gentes</term> <note>original: "gentes"; clans or lineages sharing a common name.</note>, and <term>familiæ</term> <note>original: "familiæ"; individual family units.</note>; and yet upon the assumption of the existence of an almost impossible state of facts rest the number of the members of the <term>senate</term> and the organization of the <term>legion</term>. Institutions, as all else, must accommodate themselves to existing facts, and in such cases as those to which we have referred the principle of hereditary right must shake off the incumbrance of arithmetical arrangement, or the numerical arrangement be carried out in disregard of the strict rules of descent.

The original acquirer of <term>orba</term> <note>original: "orba"; likely from the Old Irish "orb," meaning inheritance or patrimony. The author refers here to land set aside to be passed down through a family.</note> land establishes upon it his household, and as the number of his sons increases beyond the capacity of one common dwelling, they successively go out, take separate allotments, and establish themselves in distinct homesteads. The members of the <term>geilfine</term> stood in definite relation to each other; they had certain rights in each others property, but what was more important, they were jointly liable for the wrongs committed by any of the "family," and were guarantors among themselves for the payments to be made in respect of any such. That a man's four infant sons, who resided in his house, and possessed no independent property, were joined with him as security for his debts, would be of no advantage to external creditors, and the father could not expect any benefit from having joined with himself as co-securities, his sons, who had no property except a contingent interest in what he himself possessed. The nature of the relation between the members of a "<term>geilfine</term>" system implies that they all are <term>of their own legal right</term> <note>original: "sui juris"; a Latin term for individuals who are not under the legal control of another, such as a father or guardian.</note>, and all owners of property efficient to answer their joint and reciprocal obligations. This was, as stated in the passage before referred to, effected by combining into one, five distinct households, not individuals, each possessing a fixed minimum of property. the respective classes were not tied down by any fixed rules as to numbers, although at the date of the commentary on the <term>Book of Aicill</term> <note>original: "Book of Aicill"; one of the two most important manuscripts of the Brehon Laws (early Irish law), traditionally attributed to King Cormac mac Airt and the scholar Cenn Faelad.</note> the number of seventeen was considered as of the essence of the system. The numerical form of early institutions arises from the desire of half-educated men for an unattainable arithmetical completeness in their arrangements, and from the wholly unwarranted assumption, with the view to enable them to construct theoretical systems, that all the families would be of some fixed amount, and that the members would be born or die off in the required order. The lawyers who reduced to writing the customs of the "*<term>fine</term>*," <note>original: "fine"; the general term for a joint-family or kin-group in Gaelic society.</note> assumed that the number of children in each family would be five, that is, four who go out, and one who remains in the original home, and that, therefore, the system in its complete development must consist of seventeen persons, although probably as a fact it frequently fell short of that amount. The perfect form of seventeen persons, divisible in the four classes, each representing four brothers, with the addition of the head of the household occupying the original home, became the accepted theoretic form of the institution. As upon the failure of any class the property is to be divided among classes and not individually <note>original: "per capita"</note>, their shares are in the first instance determined by the assumed natural relationship of these divisions, and if this does not differentiate the classes, then by their representative relationship; the nearest class taking three fourths, the next three sixteenths, and the most remote taking one sixteenth. On the extinction of the *geilfine*, three fourths would pass to their first cousins the *deirbfine*, three sixteenths to their second cousins the *iarfine*, and one sixteenth to their third cousins the *innfine*. The distribution of the property of any two extinct classes follows precisely the same rules; if the property of each class be separately divided in the proportion of twelve to four between the surviving classes in accordance with their nearness of kinship. Thus upon the failure of both the <term>hand-family</term> and <term>true-family</term> division, the property of both is divisable between the remaining classes, their second and third cousins, three fourths to the <term>after-family</term>, and one fourth to the <term>end-family</term> division; but upon the extinction of the <term>after-family</term> and <term>end-family</term> divisions, the two surviving classes standing in the same degree of actual kinship to both, the principle of representation is introduced and three fourths pass to the <term>true-family</term> and one fourth to the <term>hand-family</term> division.

The four generations of the male issue of the settler seem to have been regarded as forming four classes equivalent to the classes of the <term>hand-family</term> <note>original: "geilfine"</note> system, and having similar rights of property and succession <term>among themselves</term> <note>original: "inter sese"</note>.\*

Upon the completion of the <term>hand-family</term> <note>original: "geilfine"</note> system, the “family” does not appear to have dissolved beyond the extinction of hereditary rights in the land of the family; the organization still continued upon the basis of mutual guarantee and liability. -># INTRODUCTION.<-

->xciii<-

The distinction of the "tribe" and "family" must have been clearly marked: the family rested on the lands of inheritance booked to the original acquirer, and as a *family* had no property external to that; the tribe possessed the general undivided tribe lands and the waste pasturage lands. It is to be observed that these latter cannot have been included in the lands of the "family" which were finally divided upon the completion of the <term>hand-family</term> <note>original: "geilfine"; the most intimate circle of kin, whose internal structure determined how land was partitioned</note> system. The claim of an individual to share in the pasturage was founded upon his being a member of the tribe, and had no connection with his membership of a family; and when we proceed to consider the <term>Branched Purchase</term> <note>original: "Crith Gabhlach"; an important law tract detailing the social status, rights, and property of various classes in early Ireland</note>, it will be clear that, in the organization of the tribe, the family was wholly disregarded. As in a military legion, the individual citizens were equal in the face of the law, and the paternal authority was disregarded.

The conclusions to which we arrive may be briefly stated as follows:—

(1) The <term>hand-family</term> <note>original: "geilfine"</note> system was an ingeniously contrived organization of the "family" with the object of keeping it together upon the basis of mutual guarantee, founded upon the antecedent rules of succession to <term>inheritance lands</term> <note>original: "orba"</note>; and of retaining the lands of inheritance in the descendants of the original acquirer, as far as the existing rules as to "remoteness of limitations" <note>a legal concept referring to how far back or forward a claim to property can reach before it becomes invalid</note> permitted. 

(2) It was contrived in the interest of the noble classes, who possessed sufficient influence to procure portions of the public tribe lands to be granted to them and their families to the exclusion of the rights of the general body of the "tribe."

(3) As the general tribe lands were appropriated by the noble class, the system in its earlier stages gradually became obsolete, and merely a subject of antiquarian inquiry; and the later commentators <note>medieval legal scholars who wrote explanations and glosses on the older laws</note>, especially once the idea of seniority as the basis of succession had been established, were unable clearly to explain its origin and probably found more difficulty in understanding it than does the modern student.

(4) The system, when existing in its latest state of survival, was adopted as the basis for a system of rules relative to the distribution of the property of a household, to which in its origin it had really no analogy.

<summary>This page concludes the analysis of the geilfine system, arguing it was a noble-class innovation designed to consolidate land ownership that eventually became obscure even to medieval legal scholars.</summary>

# IV.
## ON THE RESPONSIBILITY FOR FINES AND COMPENSATION FOR CRIMES.

It is a fundamental principle of <term>Brehon Law</term> <note>The ancient native legal system of Ireland, administered by professional jurists known as Brehons</note> that the duty to pay fines and compensation for crimes committed by a member of a tribe or family should fall upon the individuals who would be entitled to inherit that person's property upon their death, and in the exact same proportions.

In this volume, there are two legal tracts regarding the specific people responsible for these payments and the proportions they must pay: the tract titled “Of the Judgment of every Crime which any Criminal Commits, etc.,” and the one titled “The Land is forfeited for Crime.” If we can successfully determine how these fines and compensations were assessed against people other than the criminal themselves—and how the compensation paid for the death of a tribe or family member was divided—we will inevitably gain a better understanding of how property was distributed after an owner's death. This will allow us to grasp the otherwise confusing rules regarding land succession found in the first tract of this volume.

The first of these two tracts appears to be of a much later date and seems to be influenced by the principles of <term>English Law</term> <note>The Common Law system introduced by the Anglo-Normans, which eventually replaced native Irish law</note>. The reasons for this conclusion are as follows:

(1) It clearly identifies acts of violence as "crimes" <note>An offense against the public or state</note> rather than treating them merely as <term>torts</term> <note>Civil wrongs or private disputes between individuals that are settled with a payment to the victim</note>, viewing the consequences of these acts as punishments for illegal behavior.

(2) The payments made by the criminal or his guarantors are viewed as legal "settlements" through which he might escape the actual punishment for his crimes, rather than as a private arrangement to end a feud between two parties.

(3) It seems to acknowledge that the Judge possessed a "coercive jurisdiction"—meaning the parties were legally forced to accept the judge's authority.

(4) It mentions the execution of the criminal, his imprisonment, or his forced servitude as possible outcomes.

<summary>This section explains that under ancient Irish law, a family’s liability for a relative's crime was directly tied to their right to inherit that relative's property. The author notes that later legal tracts show significant influence from English law, shifting the focus from private compensation to state-sanctioned punishment.</summary>

All these ideas are clearly different from <term>archaic law</term> <note>The original, ancient customs of the Irish people before they were influenced by outside legal systems like the English Common Law</note>.

The extreme vagueness and uncertainty in the use of the terms “<term>deirbfine</term>” <note>The 'true family' group, traditionally consisting of four generations of male descendants</note> and “<term>geilfine</term>” <note>The 'hand-family,' the smallest and most immediate kinship circle in Irish law</note> in this tract are very remarkable; this uncertainty was very puzzling to the authors of the <gloss>glosses</gloss> <note>brief explanations written between the lines or in margins</note> and <gloss>commentary</gloss> <note>longer explanatory notes on the legal principles</note>, who frequently have to correct and explain the way these words are used.

It appears that the former term <note>deirbfine</note> is used without distinction in three different senses: (1) as a description for all the members of the <term>geilfine</term> organization, (2) as the specific <term>deirbfine</term> class as distinct from the <term>geilfine</term>, and (3) as a general term for certain relationships.

The glosses and commentary are especially important when dealing with this tract, because without a very careful reference to them, a reader might reach wrong conclusions by looking at the original text by itself.

The tract begins with a statement of the property and people liable for the payment of fines and compensation. The rules of priority laid down here may be summarized as follows:—(1) The criminal himself was primarily liable; this is inferred from the words, “If he absconds <note>runs away to avoid trial or punishment</note>,” which begins the paragraph and states the condition under which other people become responsible; (2) The property—both moveable <note>such as cattle or goods</note> and immoveable <note>land</note>—of the criminal was liable in the second degree; when we move to the second tract on this subject, it will appear that this liability was considered a specific charge against the property in question. It should be noted that this rule implies that the injured party had a *legal right* to the payment of the fine and compensation, a theory that is anything but ancient. (3) His father was liable in the third degree, whose responsibility is obviously based not so much on being a relative, as on his position as the head of the household to which the criminal belonged; this passage is explained by a <gloss>gloss</gloss> stating, “when he has no son, for it is upon the <insert>son</insert> it <note>the responsibility for the crime</note> should fall before it falls upon the father;” we may conclude therefore that the author

A mere sojourning stranger, from whom the chief had not and could not have taken pledges, if guilty of a crime, and not possessed of property, did not render any of the family or tribe liable to contribute to the fine or compensation payable in respect of his crime; he was simply "put upon the road," declared "outside the law" <note>original: "exlex"</note>, and abandoned to his fate.

(The principle that the liability to pay should be commensurate with right to receive is remarkably laid down in the following rules contained in the Commentary:)

In the case of any unintentional* crime except "killing," the *body-fine* <note>original: "eric fine"; a payment made to the victim or their family to compensate for injury or death</note> is primarily payable by the criminal; the compensation ("*what he owes beside the body-fine*," i.e. the <term>honour price</term> <note>a value assigned to an individual based on their social rank, used to calculate legal damages</note>) is payable by his family "in the proportions in which they divide his property."

In the case of unintentional "killing" (with certain exceptions) both the family and criminal contribute to pay the entire, whether he has means of payment or not, the criminal paying one "unit of value" <note>original: "cumhal"; literally a female slave, but used as a standard unit of currency worth three cows</note> of the compensation, and the same share as his father or son in the six *units* of the *legal fine* <note>original: "dire fine"</note>, the family contributing the residue in the shares in which would divide his property. The reason for this rule is stated to be that if he himself were killed the entire family would participate in the compensation.

As to intentional crimes, the rule was different. In such cases the criminal, his son, and his father were successively liable to the full extent of their property in exoneration of the family.

The second tract entitled "The Land is forfeited for Crimes," is of a very miscellaneous nature, and of a palpably late date. The idea of the forfeiture of the lands of a criminal, irrespective of their value and amount, arose in the English and other feudal systems from the nature of the <term>tenure of land</term> <note>The legal regime under which land is owned or held.</note>. The lord possessed the absolute ownership, the tenant only the <term>usufruct</term> <note>The right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property without destroying it.</note> upon the condition of the performance of the incidents of his tenure; the commission of a <term>felony</term> <note>In this context, a serious crime that breached the bond between lord and tenant.</note>, in its nature a <term>quasi-treasonable</term> <note>original: "quasi-treasonable" — an act that is treated as if it were treason because it violates a duty of loyalty.</note> act, terminated the right of the tenant to the usufruct, and the land <term>escheated</term> <note>Reverted back to the original owner or lord.</note> to the lord of whom it was held; the escheat of the land in such a case rested upon an entirely different basis from that of the forfeiture of the felons' goods; but when the land was held in absolute ownership, and the possession of the owner was that of the head or member of a family, although his goods might be forfeited, the land could not; the law as to the <term>gavelkind</term> <note>A system of inheritance where land is divided equally among sons, common in Kent and resistant to feudal forfeiture.</note> lands of Kent was a survival and illustration of this principle. In the preceding tract the wrongdoer either lost the possession of his land temporarily until its profits paid off the amount to which he was liable, or absolutely as the result of his loss of status, not as a punishment in the correct use of that term. Although evidently drawn up for some practical purpose, the tone and manner of this tract closely resemble portions of the introduction to the *Book of Aicill* <note>A major collection of Irish civil law traditionally attributed to King Cormac mac Airt.</note>, which the author manifestly had before him, and it is probably of the same and as late a date.

At the date of its composition the Irish lawyers were perplexed by the conflicting ideas of the old law on the one hand, and Christianity and the Roman Law on the other, the state of mind so curiously exemplified by the introduction to the laws of Alfred <note>Referring to Alfred the Great, whose legal code blended Mosaic law with Saxon custom.</note>.

In the preceding section we have endeavoured to ascertain the proportions in which fines and compensations were payable by the parties secondarily liable, as affording some reliable information as the rules of succession to property, and enabling us thus to explain the passages in the first tract in this volume dealing with the subject, and as also explaining the practical effect of the *geilfine* <term>geilfine: the smallest and closest unit of the Irish family organization, typically consisting of five people, used to determine inheritance and liability</term> system upon the succession to land.

The rules for the incidence of these payments must have been drawn up to meet ordinary cases; and the more complicated and unusual must have been decided according to the principle involved in these rules—involved, not expressed—because the <term>Brehon lawyer</term> <note>A practitioner of the indigenous Gaelic legal system of Ireland, which operated until the 17th century.</note> is always dealing with specific concrete cases, and however elaborate in his arithmetic calculations, never attempts any abstract rule or definition. Before discussing the rules as to the succession of land, it may be observed that to a large proportion of the tribe land the legal idea of a succession must have been inapplicable. It is now an admitted fact that the Irish tribe was not in its organization an anomalous institution, but was simply one example of those village communities which existed among all the early <term>Aryan nations</term> <note>A 19th-century linguistic and historical term used here to describe the Indo-European peoples.</note>, and that the forms of all these communities resembled each other in their general features. In all the numerous books published lately upon the subject, this principle has been laid down; and the difficulty in dealing with the subject at present is not to discover analogous cases, but to escape being entangled in or misled by the countless examples of institutions more or less similar, with which we are now so abundantly furnished. The district of the tribe was at first as a matter of fact, and was always in theory considered to be, the property of the tribe; from this are first to be subtracted the dwellings of the members of the tribe, with their <term>curtilages</term> <note>The enclosed land or yard immediately surrounding a dwelling house.</note>; next the chief's share; and lastly, those portions of the general tribe land which had been in some manner (it is immaterial how) allotted to individuals or families in exclusive ownership. The residue of the lands, unappropriated to individuals, consisted of the common tillage and meadow land, and the common pasture or waste. The common tillage and meadow lands were divided out from time to time in separate proportions, and according to some customary law among all the members of the tribe who also enjoyed the right to <term>depasture</term> <note>To put cattle or other livestock out to graze.</note> the waste according to certain fixed rules. The ownership of these lands was vested in the collective tribe, but the rights of each member were personal, temporary, and incorporeal <note>In legal terms, "incorporeal" refers to rights over property—like an easement or a right to graze—rather than ownership of the physical soil itself.</note>. But the nature of the interest of the owners in land cut out of the general tribe land, and allotted in exclusive ownership was entirely different. They claimed under a grant made to one or more persons, and made their title through the grantee or grantees; this title to land is usually spoken of as being hereditary, and the land in question described as inheritable land, or land of inheritance; but it does not follow that although the title must be made under a particular grant, and through the original grantee, that the actual owners stand in the relation of “heirs” to the person through whom they claim. Our modern ideas of inheritance and heirship are involved with those of the transmission of property by descent and primogeniture <note>Primogeniture is the legal preference for the eldest son to inherit the entire estate, a concept the author argues is not universal.</note>; and much of the confusion which exists upon this subject, has arisen from the inquiry proceeding upon the assumption that purely local and arbitrary rules of our own municipal law <note>The internal laws of a specific nation or city-state.</note> are universal and eternal principles.

Land might be allotted in separate ownership for a limited period (*for example*, for a life), or in perpetuity <note>original: "in perpetuum"</note>; but although the former class of grants are found among the Anglo-Saxon <note>original: "A. S."</note> charters, in the case of the Irish tribes we have no reason to believe that the grants were limited in duration.

When land was alienated in perpetuity <note>original: "in perpetuum"</note>, it passed upon the death of the original grantee to the person or persons entitled, according to the custom, to the succession to his property; such persons might, or might not, be identical with his nearest agnates <note>Agnates are relatives whose kinship is traced exclusively through the male line.</note>; but even if they were, it did not follow that their title to the succession was founded on descent or even blood relationship. The origin of all successions appears to be not descent, but co-ownership.

# INTRODUCTION.

The legal unit is not the individual but the household; the head of a house acquires property for his household, and possesses it as the manager of an implied partnership, not as an absolute owner. The household need not include all his descendants, or consist exclusively of them. The emancipated sons <note>In Roman law, "emancipation" was the legal act of releasing a son from the father's absolute authority (patria potestas), which often severed his legal ties to the family estate.</note>, under the old Roman law, would not have shared in their father's property, which would have passed to an adopted son. Our ideas as to the transmission of property in ancient times are, perhaps, embarrassed by too exclusive a reference to the Roman law, in which the <term>hæres<note>Latin: "heir." In Roman law, the heir was a universal successor who stepped into the deceased's legal shoes, inheriting both assets and debts.</note></term> presents a misleading resemblance to the feudal heir; but in countries in which the technical unity of the family, exhibited in the existence of the Roman *heir*, was not continued, the succession was manifestly equivalent to survivorship among joint tenants; and this principle of survivorship applies not merely to the property of the head of the household, but to that of every member of it. 

Let us observe how a perfectly simple process is obscured by the use of words. If a household consists of A, the father, and B and C, the sons, they are co-tenants or co-partners in the property of the household, with the father, A, as the manager; if the father, A, dies, the property survives to B and C, the sons; in this case the sons would be commonly spoken of as taking in the character of their father's heirs. On the other hand, if B, one of the sons, dies, the property survives to A, the father, and C, the surviving son; we should in this case think that no rights to property had passed, and speak of the possibility of B succeeding to his father as having ceased. Again, if a third son, D, is born no visible change has taken place, but, in fact, a new member has been introduced into the joint tenancy or partnership, and the rights of the three original joint tenants, diminished <term>pro tanto<note>Latin: "to that extent" or "only for so much."</note></term>. The extent to which heirship is traced in the collateral line <note>The "collateral line" refers to relatives who share a common ancestor but do not descend directly from one another, such as brothers, cousins, or uncles.</note> in any ancient law depends upon the greater or less magnitude of the original joint family. If, for any reason, families have hung together for several generations, continuing to form one household, the death of each member increasing the shares of all the
