it was offered for sale. Thus at the present day we deal in so many head of cattle, barrels of potatoes, or sacks of corn. Here the difficulty arises how to express the ratio which the value of any number of cattle bears to any given number of sacks of corn. For this purpose an abstract measure of value is invented, which is roughly estimated to be represented by a certain amount of each of the articles ordinarily brought to sale, and a given quantity of each article having been fixed as representing this value in exchange, the several quantities of the different articles are supposed to be equal in value to each other in the normal condition of the market. As in the present day, in remote country districts, a man who pays for the grazing of so many cows may take it out in the grazing of sheep or geese, each cow being represented by a customary number of the smaller animals, so in ancient times the value of a cow would be considered as equivalent, for the purpose of exchange under ordinary circumstances, to so many sheep, geese, &c. <note>The author uses the cow as a historical "unit of account" before the widespread use of standardized currency.</note>

It has been frequently remarked that in primitive societies the rule of supply and demand has almost no existence, and that the same price will continue to be paid for the same article during very long periods of time, and without regard to what are called <term>mercantile considerations</term> <note>Refers to profit-driven market fluctuations typical of modern capitalism.</note>. As long as this mode of dealing is applied to articles which can be sold by measure and weight, and are of the same average quality, there is no difficulty in working the system; but as soon as an attempt is made to apply it to land, the difficulties involved become apparent. Land can only be sold by reference to its superficial extent, but the qualities of any two pieces of land of the same acreage are very different, and therefore their value in exchange cannot be the same. How, therefore, can the value of any piece of land be expressed with reference to the imaginary standard of value to which all other articles are referred? This is the question which the author of this tract attempts to solve, viz. :—What is the <term>par of exchange</term> <note>The equivalent value between two different types of assets.</note> of land in the market with reference to the other subjects of exchange? That he should fail in doing so in any practical manner was inevi-

He assumes as the base of his calculation a fixed measure of land, which he defines as the <term>land-cumhal</term> <note>A "cumhal" originally meant a female slave, but became a standard unit of value equivalent to three cows; here it refers to a specific extent of land worth that value.</note>; he then divides land with reference to fertility or fitness for pasturage, and brings out the result in cattle; he then considers the accidental qualities of any particular land, and treats them as raising the value in a certain ratio; the value of any land in exchange would thus be represented by a certain number of cumhals in cattle, irrespective of the actual acreage of the land.

The basis of the whole calculation rests upon the superficial extent of a <term>cumhal of land</term> <note>Original: "tir-cumaile"</note>; and the commentator naturally appends a table of the superficial measurements upon which his calculation is founded. "How is a land-cumhal measured?" By grains; three grains in a proper inch; six inches in the hand; and two hands in a foot; six feet in a pace; six paces in an "intritt" measure; six "intritts" in a "lait" measure; six "laits" in a "forach" measure.

### XI.
## THE BRANCHED PURCHASE. <note>original: "CRITH GABHLACH." This is a fundamental law tract concerning social status and the grades of nobility.</note>

This tract has received especial attention from Irish Antiquarians, inasmuch as it professes to give a detailed description of the several social ranks and organization of the Irish tribe. Mr. O'Curry has, in his Lectures on the Manners and Customs of the Ancient Irish, adopted this treatise as an authentic and ancient work, and without hesitation accepted its statements as a sufficient authority for his detailed account of the earliest form of the Celtic tribe system. Dr. W. K. Sullivan, adopting the views of Mr. O'Curry upon this subject, attributes the date of its composition to the middle or end of the seventh century. The most important passage, as indicating the probable date of the composition, is the statement relative to the four rights to which it was proper that a king should pledge his people, the first of which is stated to be "a right to help him to drive out foreign races, i.e. against the Saxons."* Assuming that these latter words are not a gloss which has crept into the text (and there is no reason to believe that they are), the date of the work must coincide with a period at which the Saxons <note>The Germanic tribes that settled in Great Britain; here used to refer to the English.</note> were regarded as the enemies *par excellence* <note>original: "par excellence"; meaning the supreme or definitive example.</note> of the Irish people, and not merely as a hostile, but as an invading race. It is obvious that no Irish writer would have singled out the Saxons as the special enemies of the Irish during the period covered by the Danish invasions, nor after that date until the Saxon had, in the mind of the people, been substituted for the Dane as their natural enemy. The date of the work must therefore be either before the end of the eighth century, or after the English invasion, the period covered by the Danish invasions being absolutely excluded. The early relations of the Irish and Saxons were of the most friendly character, and naturally so as the Irish were then busily employed in plundering, and perhaps to some extent, conquering, their christian and Celtic neighbours across the channel. The date of the work must be brought down to some time after the English invasion <note>The Anglo-Norman invasion of Ireland, which began in 1169.</note>, unless there be internal evidence which would render such a conclusion improbable; and, if the date be so far postponed, it must be referred to a period considerably subsequent to the first invasion, to that at which all the Irish tribes stood in a hostile position to the English king, and the invasion was at length successfully checked, or at the earliest date, to the first quarter of the fourteenth century.

There is also internal evidence which, independently of the passage referred to, would lead to the same conclusion.

The most remarkable change in the organization of the early Irish Church was the substitution of an episcopal <note>A system governed by bishops.</note> for the monastic system. In the earlier form of church government the abbot, not the bishop, was the ruling ecclesiastic; the "coarb" <note>original: "comarba" — meaning a successor to the founding saint of a monastery.</note> of the original saint was the head of the ecclesiastical tribe; the pre-eminence and territorial jurisdiction of bishops arose at a date long subsequent to the commencement of the Danish invasion <note>The Viking Age in Ireland, beginning roughly in 795 AD.</note>. Is it probable that a treatise descriptive of the ranks of society, if written during the life of Adamnan <note>Abbot of Iona (679–704) and biographer of St. Columba.</note>, and the vigorous existence of the Columban monasteries, would omit any allusion to an abbot, and speak of the bishop as travelling "for the good of the church and the territory," and as of rank equal, if not superior, to the king of the tribe? There is further no allusion whatsoever to the *geilfine* system <note>A complex Irish legal structure for family land inheritance involving four groups of five persons.</note>, nor to the *geilfine* lord <note>original: "geilfine flaith"</note> as representing his "family group" <note>original: "fine"</note>, and therefore an important item in the social system.

# INTRODUCTION.

—a very remarkable omission in a treatise of the character of the present. The condition of society exhibited in this work is that of the tribe system in state of decay and decadence, and rapidly tending to assume a feudal form. The simple freeman has sunk to the condition of the Saxon <term>ceorl</term> <note>A freeman of the lowest rank in Anglo-Saxon society, often a small-scale farmer</note>; the tribe lands have, to a great extent, if not altogether, been monopolized by the noble classes; the political power has passed into the hands of the chiefs and greater nobles; all classes, from the highest to the lowest, are bound together by the semi-feudal bond, founded upon the system of lending out cattle; all classes are rated for the payment of tribute to their superiors; and the basis of society seems rather to be personal service than the common rights of the members of the tribe. Except for the survival of ancient terms, and some archaic rules and peculiarities arising from the absence of a circulating medium <note>A standardized form of money or currency</note> and the material conditions of the people, the condition of the country, as thus described, was not very different from that it exhibited in the last century. This is the opinion of Mr. O'Curry, as expressed in the following passage:—

> “It is not very easy to translate into modern language the technical terms of the ancient law of Landlord and Tenant; but a very well matured system existed at a very early period indeed, under which, although there was no such thing as absolute property in land in any individual, still, within the tribe, individuals held exclusive property in land, and entered into relations with tenants for the use of the land, and these again with undertenants, and so on, much as we see in our own days. Now these relations constitute the first test of rank and condition. The <term>Flaith</term> <note>original: "Flaith"; an Irish term for a lord, ruler, or member of the aristocratic class</note>—a word in some sense may be translated the Lord or Nobleman—was distinguished by being the absolute owner (within his tribe) of land for which he paid no rent, so that, if a man possessed but a single acre in this way, he was a <term>Flaith</term>. All other persons holding land held it either from a <term>Flaith</term> or from some tenant of his; and the rank and precedency of these persons depended upon the amount of their possessions.”*

The same causes were at work in Ireland as elsewhere, and with the same results. The chiefs and nobles had succeeded in crushing the lower orders, and had converted into their own separate property the land originally the common property of the tribe. The *Crith Gabhlach* might fairly be described as a compendium of the rights and emoluments of the higher classes, of their house tributes, rents, <term>cuttings</term> <note>Arbitrary levies or taxes exacted by a lord from his tenants.</note>, and <term>cosherings</term> <note>From the Irish 'cósair'; the right of a lord to be entertained and lodged at the expense of his tenantry.</note>, and is not dissimilar from the old law book of the <term>Brehon</term> <note>An ancient Irish judge or legal expert who interpreted the customary laws.</note> whereby the English commissioners "perceived how many vessels of butter, and how many measures of meal, and how many porks, and other such gross duties did arise unto M'Guire out of his <term>mensal lands</term> <note>Lands set aside specifically to provide food and provisions for the table of a chief or bishop.</note>."*

It is not to be concluded that any Irish tribe or province was ever actually organized in strict conformity with the rules laid down in this tract. It is impossible to believe that a nation so mobile and turbulent as the Irish Celts lived under a system so rigid in its laws and pedantic in its minutiæ; that the different classes possessed so much and no more than the amount of property herein set down against them; inhabited houses of precisely the prescribed size, furnished in the manner described, and supplied with the farming instruments directed; that the occupiers of them paid so much and no more than their customary rents; and that the whole society, from the provincial King downwards, were bound, and acquiesced in, a complete system of semi-feudal service. The work must be considered as a description of society fully organized according to the current legal theory at the date of its composition; but it can no more be assumed that the existing community accurately corresponded to the legal theory, than that the condition of England in the

The <term>Crith Gabhlach</term> <note>literally "The Branched Purchase," an 8th-century Irish law text concerning social status</note> treats of the various ranks of the freemen of the tribe, their mutual rights and duties, and the power and privileges of the King; the unfree classes of the community are only referred to in connexion with the rights and qualifications of the free.

<margin>}</margin>The author lays down as the cardinal principle that the proper grade of the layman among the people is determined by the amount of his property. The number of classes of men is stated to be seven. That this number was selected as the sacred number, and was not in accordance with the actual state of facts, appears from the statement of the author himself, and the mode in which the division in classes is varied in different passages. The grades of a people are stated to be as follows:—(1) the “<term>fer mbidboth</term>” <note>man of the hut; a young man who has not yet inherited property</note> man, (2) the “<term>bo-aire</term>” <note>cow-lord; a wealthy farmer</note> chief, (3) the “<term>aire-desa</term>” <note>noble of vassal-property</note> chief, (4) the “<term>aire-ard</term>” <note>high noble</note> chief, (5) the “<term>aire-tuisc</term>” <note>noble of precedence</note> chief, (6) the “<term>aire-forgaill</term>” <note>noble of superior testimony</note> chief, and (7) the king. This sevenfold division is stated to be derived from the similitude of the ecclesiastical orders, “for it is proper that for every order which is in the Church, there should be a corresponding one among the people.”*

The two first classes represent the free but not noble, the latter five the free and noble.

The divisions of the noble class are then specified, and the number of them is again seven, viz.:—(1) the “<term>aire-desa</term>,” (2) the “<term>aire-echta</term>” <note>noble of vengeance; a specific military/legal role</note>, (3) the “<term>aire-ard</term>,” (4) the “<term>aire-tuisc</term>,” (5) the “<term>aire-forgaill</term>,” (6) the “<term>tanaise</term>” <note>original: "tamaise"; likely a typo for "tanaise," the heir apparent</note> of a king, and (7) the king. To complete the number seven in this, two further classes are introduced, the “<term>aire-echta</term>” and the <term>tanist</term> <note>the successor-designate to a kingship</note>; the latter of these was an official person and not a class of individuals, and the same observation is applicable to the “<term>aire-echta</term>.” The non-noble classes are classed as follows:—(1) the two grades of “<term>fer-mbidba</term>” <note>original: "fer-mbidba"; likely referring to the "fer mbidboth" or man of the hut</note> men, (2) the “<term>og-aire</term>” <note>young or junior noble/freeman</note>, (3) an “<term>aithech</term>” <note>tenant or commoner</note> person, (4) the “<term>bo-aire febhsa</term>” <note>cow-lord of excellence</note>, (5) the “<term>mbruigh-fher</term>” <note>land-man or wealthy farmer</note> man, (6) the “<term>fer-fothla</term>” <note>man of withdrawal; a wealthy commoner moving toward nobility</note> man, and (7) the “<term>aire-coisring</term>” <note>noble of binding; the representative of a kin-group</note>.

# INTRODUCTION.

The seven classes are here again completed, first by the introduction of the <term>commoner tenant<note>original: "aithech"; a member of the rent-paying class, often a tenant farmer.</note></term>, a very anomalous class, as subsequently explained in the text, and by the addition of the last three, viz., the <term>land-man<note>original: "mbruigh-fer"; a wealthy farmer who possessed specific amounts of land and livestock.</note></term>, the <term>man of withdrawal<note>original: "fer-fothla"; a wealthy commoner who has begun to acquire the status of a lord by lending out surplus cattle.</note></term>, and the <term>representative lord<note>original: "aire-coisring"; a leader who acts as a legal representative for his kin-group.</note></term>, two of which are the names of officers, and not of classes.

The scheme of classification used by the author of the tract on <term>Precincts<note>original: "Maighne"; referring to the sacred or legal area of protection surrounding a person's dwelling.</note></term>, must have been different from that of the author of this tract; for he also, dividing the society into seven classes, states the two lowest to be the <term>cow-lord<note>original: "bo-aire"; the typical wealthy free farmer.</note></term> and the <term>lord of vassalage<note>original: "aire-desa"; the lowest rank of true nobility, defined by the number of tenants he possessed.</note></term>, and the highest to be the king, omitting to give the names of the four intermediate divisions, and, with reference to the extent of their precincts, he fixes their rank upon the basis of a geometric progression, a gradation inconsistent with the ratio of their properties and <term>honor-price<note>original: "lóg n-enech"; the legal value of a person's status, used to determine fines and compensation.</note></term> as fixed in this treatise.

The several ranks are divided with reference to the amount of property requisite to qualify for each respectively, and from and in the proportion to the requisite amount of property follow their rights and privileges (some of which we should now class as duties) : (1) the legal value attributed to their oath, contract, guarantee, and evidence; (2) the honor-price; (3) <term>refections<note>original: "biathad"; the right to be fed and housed by others according to one's rank.</note></term>, or the nature and amount of food they should receive from a host; (4) <term>sick maintenance<note>original: "folog n-othrusa"; the legal requirement to provide nursing and medical care for an injured person.</note></term>; (5) the extent to which they could give protection to a third party who claimed it; (6) the <term>fore-purchase<note>original: "taurcreic"; the advance payment or grant of livestock given by a lord to a subordinate to seal their relationship.</note></term>, or the amount of stock to be delivered to them by the superior to whom they commended themselves (the commendation to a lord in consideration of the "fore-purchase" might be oppressive or advantageous to the inferior, according to the circumstances of the time); and (7) the <term>house-custom<note>original: "bes tigi"; the annual food-rent or tribute paid by a tenant to his lord.</note></term> or house tribute, payable in kind by the inferior to the superior to whom he had commended himself.

The following analysis of the necessary qualifications and rights of the several classes will render the relative positions of the respective ranks clear.

### A.—THE NON-NOBLE CLASSES.

1. The "midboth" man <note>original: "mbidboth"; likely referring to a youth or "man of middle huts" who has not yet established a full independent household</note>. This class is sub-divided into two sub-classes, namely, the "midboth" man who had attained the age of fourteen years, but not yet that of seventeen years, "unless he has taken possession or succession before that, or a man of the commoner grade <note>original: "Feini grade"; the class of free farmers who owned land</note> be a co-occupant with him," *i.e.*, unless he is himself in possession of a house, or be the joint occupant of one with a free man of full age (?), and the "midboth" man who had attained the age of seventeen years. The oath, contract, or guarantee of the former extended to the value of a young heifer <note>original: "dairt"; a yearling heifer</note>; his refection <note>The formal meal provided to a guest or superior</note> was milk and porridge; his protection <note>The legal right to extend safety to others within a certain area</note> extended to one of his own grade over the territory; his honor-price <note>The monetary value assigned to a person's status, used to calculate fines for injuries against them</note> was a young heifer. The value of the oath, etc., of the latter was a two-year-old heifer <note>original: "colpach"</note>; his protection extends to one of his own rank until he has given him double food (two meals?); his refection was milk and porridge; his honor-price a two-year-old heifer; his proportionate stock <note>original: "taurcreic"; the cattle given by a lord to a tenant to establish a formal relationship</note> was four "seds" <note>A unit of value, often equated to a young cow</note> in value; his food rent <note>original: "bes tigi"; the annual tribute of food paid to a lord</note> a castrated ram <note>original: "wether"</note>; his sick maintenance <note>The legal requirement for an injurer to provide nursing and food for the victim</note> for himself and his mother new unskimmed milk every third, fifth, ninth, and tenth day, and also on Sunday.

It appears from this that the very lowest class of freemen were not, as has been stated, wholly devoid of property; they are presumed to possess a house, in respect of which they may be required to pay food rent to a superior, and they had a share, however small, in the common pasture, otherwise they could not have availed themselves of the proportionate stock (advancement of cattle) they might receive.

2. The Cow-Lord <note>original: "Bo-aire"</note> or enriched commoner. The "midboth"-man, upon acquiring the necessary amount of property, became *by that very fact* a "cow-lord" chief, because, in this case, there was no change of status, as in the transaction afterwards mentioned from the non-noble to the noble class. This increase is attributed to the profits made by stock received from a lord in the first instance; for he is assumed to have commended himself to a lord; such would seem to be implied by the rule:—"In three days after notice half a portion

Not so the '<term>bo-aire</term>' <note>Literally a 'cow-lord'; a wealthy free farmer who attained status through cattle ownership rather than hereditary nobility.</note> chief; it is in right of his cows he is paid '<term>dire</term>'-fine."†

Upon this subject Mr. Hearn makes the following observations: —

> "Among the members of the clan itself, within the '<term>cinel</term>' <note>A kindred group or lineage tracing descent from a common ancestor.</note>, in the strict sense of the term, and apart from the exceptional privileges of the royal house, there was a well-marked difference. That difference was between the noble and the free, or, as it may otherwise be expressed, between the gentle and simple. Both classes were equally members of the clan, and, to a certain extent had equal rights. But both by public opinion, and by the custom which supplied the place of law, certain sections of the community possessed, in comparison with other sections thereof, an acknowledged superiority. Their descent was purer; their wealth was greater; their <term>wer-geld</term> <note>A Germanic term used here by the author to describe 'blood-money' or the value placed on a person's life, similar to the Irish 'dire'.</note> was higher; their share in the public lands, or in the distribution of booty, was larger; they were the natural leaders of the community in war, and its natural councillors in peace. Accordingly, we observe in the early history of all <term>Aryan nations</term> <note>A 19th-century linguistic and historical term used here to refer to Indo-European peoples.</note>, the presence of what may be called a natural aristocracy, as the leaders and kinsmen of a natural democracy. It is not difficult to understand that some households should be more prosperous, more numerous, and more wealthy than the others. Yet these advantages are rather the effects than the causes of such a difference as that which we are considering. Even if there were no evidence, that in at least certain societies, land was distributed according to the rank of its holders, they are inadequate to explain all the facts of the case. They may account for the difference in modern society, where individuals rise and fall with a rapidity unknown to <term>archaic nations</term> <note>Ancient or traditional societies governed by custom rather than modern statutory law.</note>; but they do not explain the strongly marked lines, which intersect the society of the ancient world. The preceding inquiries point, for the cause of the difference, to some sentiment connected

# INTRODUCTION.

Mr. Hearn refers to a passage in the Introduction of the preceding volume relative to the claims of his original church upon the property of a former member.\* Upon the practical working of this rule Mr. Hearn further remarks:
> —"These considerations indicate the triple distinction of the ancient free population. It consisted of freedmen, of freemen, and of nobles. The distinction rested exclusively upon blood, and could not, therefore, be removed by grant either of people or of King. By the operation of time, if there were no disturbing influences, each lower class naturally passed into the one next above it. Each step of the promotion brought with it increased consideration, additional strength and influence, by reason of a more numerous kindred, and more extended alliances, and no small material advantage, both direct and indirect. At a later period, when the dependent portion of the household became developed, and the *domestic retinue* <note>original: "Gesindschaft"; a German term for the body of servants or dependents belonging to a household</note> was established, other varieties of rank arose. Nobility was then derived, not from birth, but from official position, and attendance upon the throne."†

The idea of "limitation" <note>In a legal sense, the period of time after which a right or status becomes fixed</note> in the Irish law was connected with three successive lives, either of three persons in lineal descent, grandfather, father, and son; or of three successive over lords, as in the case of <term>Base-tenant of a stranger</term> <note>original: "Daer Fuidhir"; a class of tenant with limited rights, often outsiders or refugees under the protection of a lord</note> tenants,‡ or of three successive owners, as in the case of rights of water. The same idea of three, or its multiples, being the basis of such calculations, also appears in the passage in this tract, stating that cottiers and "<term>stranger-tenants</term>" <note>original: "fuidhir"</note> become "<term>old-adherents</term>" <note>original: "sencleithe"; a class of unfree tenants who became permanently attached to the land after several generations</note> tenants, and irremovable after serving for nine times nine years.

We may now proceed with the analysis of the remaining ranks in the tribe.

## B.—THE NOBLE CLASSES.

1. The “<term>aire-desa</term><note>A noble of the lowest rank whose status was based on his ownership of land and his number of tenants.</note>.”—The property with reference to which this and the subsequent class are arranged, is manifestly land, as the number of the tenants of each is respectively stated, as in the non-noble classes the number of their cattle. The tenants of the “*aire-desa*” were ten, five “<term>giallna</term><note>Base tenants who provided labor and food-rents in exchange for livestock.</note>,” and five “<term>saer</term><note>Free tenants who held a higher status and provided more limited service.</note>”-tenants. The amount of food to be furnished by the tenants is stated in detail. An incident to the right of feasting at the houses of his tenants (“*coshering*” <note>A traditional Gaelic custom where a lord and his retinue were entitled to food and lodging from their tenants.</note>) was the number of persons whom he might take to their houses from the “Calends” <note>The first day of the month; here likely referring to the Christmas season.</note> to Shrovetide; ten couples are the number specified in this case; in return he was expected “to protect his tenants in all just suits of ‘<term>cain</term>’ law <note>Statutory law applying to all of Ireland.</note> and ‘<term>cairde</term>’-law <note>Inter-territorial law or treaties between different tribes.</note>, standing towards them in the relation of a patron to his clients. The legal value of his oath, &c., and honor-price was ten ‘<term>seds</term>’ <note>A unit of value, often equated to a young heifer.</note>; the length of his house twenty-seven feet; his proportionate stock was six ‘<term>cumhals</term>’ <note>A high-value unit of account, originally meaning a female slave, but later valued at three cows.</note>, and his food-rent two cows.”*

2. The “<term>aire-echta</term><note>Literally a 'noble of feats' or 'noble of vengeance.'</note>” was an officer of the tribe, and does not represent a class; this is obvious because no property, qualification, rights, or liabilities, are specified in his case.† The duty of the “*aire-echta*” was “to avenge the insult offered to a territory in which a person was lately killed;” he was an appointed avenger of wrongs. This is illustrated by the case of the blinding of Cormac Mac Airt <note>A legendary High King of Ireland.</note>, “Aengus Gabhuaidech” was an “*aire-echta*” (translated “champion”), who was avenging a family quarrel in the territories of Luighne, and he went into a woman’s house there and drank milk in it by force; and the woman said, “It were better for thee to avenge the daughter of thy kinsman upon Cellach, son of Cormac, than to consume my food by force.”‡ Aengus thereupon at once proceeded to Temhair <note>Tara, the seat of the High Kings.</note> and slew Cellach; the point of the story seems to be that the woman reproached the “*aire-echta*” for plundering her under colour of avenging a family quarrel, while he left unperformed the more important and dangerous duty of slaying the king’s son for the abduction of one of the women of the tribe.

# INTRODUCTION.

3. The "high-lord" <note>original: "aire-ard"</note>. He had twenty tenants, ten base-tenants <note>original: "giallna"; these tenants provided labor and food-rents in exchange for cattle</note>, and ten "free"-tenants <note>original: "saer"; these tenants held a higher status and provided more specialized service</note>; twenty couples were "his right at a feasting;" his honor-price <note>the legal value assigned to a person's status, used to determine fines for injuries against them</note> and the value of his oath, etc., was fixed at fifteen units of value <note>original: "seds"; a 'sed' was a standard unit of wealth, often equal to half a cow</note>; his proportionate stock <note>the amount of cattle he provided to his tenants</note> was seven "female-slave units" <note>original: "cumhals"; a 'cumhal' was a high-value unit of account originally equal to one female slave, later valued at three cows</note>, and his food rent was three cows. There is no statement as to the size of his house.*

4. The "leader-lord" <note>original: "aire-tuisi"</note>, who had twenty-seven tenants, fifteen "base" tenants, and twelve "free" tenants; he had thirty couples at the feasting. The value of his oath, etc., and his honor-price was fixed at twenty "units of value"; his house was twenty-nine feet in length; his proportionate stock was eight "female-slave units," and four cows his food rent. The leader-lord in the third generation participated in the government of the tribe. "He makes <insert>assists in making?</insert> 'legal-custom' arrangements <note>original: "corus"</note> in the 'fort' <note>original: "raith"</note> right of his father and grandfather."†

5. The "lord of testimony" <note>original: "aire-forgaill"</note> stood in rank at the head of the nobles, and next to the king and heir-apparent <note>original: "tanist"</note>; his position is marked by the words "he testifies to the *character* of the grades we have enumerated, in every case in which a denial of a charge is sought, because his quality is superior to that of his companions." This passage might lead to the conclusion that the "lord of testimony" was an official who had the power of deciding the status of the individual members of the tribe, but inasmuch as the "lord of testimony" chief is introduced into the list of titles of dignities in the subsequent tract, although the "lord of vengeance" <note>original: "aire-echta"</note> is omitted, it is probable that the name indicates a class, not an office, and that the right to give evidence as to the status of a member of a tribe was incident to the position of the first class of the nobles. He had forty tenants, twenty "base" and twenty "free"-tenants; the value of his oath, etc., and honor-price was fixed at fifteen seds <note>Note: The text here says fifteen, though usually this rank is higher than the previous; this may be a transcription error in the original source</note>; his house was thirty feet in length; his proportionate stock nine "female-slave units," and his food rent five cows.‡

6. The "heir-apparent" <note>original: "tanist"</note> of the king or his elected successor. He had five "adscript" tenants <note>original: "sencleithe"; laborers permanently bound to the land</note> more than a "lord of testimony"-chief.

His honor-price <note>The monetary value assigned to a person's status, used to determine fines for injuries against them</note> and the value of his oath was fixed at thirty "valuables" <note>original: "seds"; a unit of value often equated to a young heifer</note>; ten "bondmaid-units" <note>original: "cumhals"; a standard unit of value originally equal to the price of a female slave, later used as a currency measurement</note> were his proportionate stock, and six cows his food rent. There is no reference as to the size of his house, or his receipts from his tenants, which may be assumed to have been considered the same as those of the "chief of superior testimony," and it is probable that the additional five "old-adherent" tenants <note>original: "sencleithe"; unfree tenants whose families had served the same lord for generations</note>, which he is stated to have, were not in addition to the number of the tenants required for the rank of a chief of superior testimony, but are introduced to indicate that his tenants had acquired the position of "old-adherent" tenants under his family, as a proof of the status of the heir-apparent <note>original: "tanist"; the elected successor to a chieftaincy or kingship</note> himself.*

7. The king. This rank is sub-divided into three classes:—

    A. A king of hills or of horns; the term is not easy of explanation; it, however, is used to designate the position of the head of a fully organized tribe. Naturally no property qualification is annexed to this rank. His honor-price and the value of his oath, etc., were fixed at seven "bondmaid-units"; his proportionate stock was twelve "bondmaid-units," and his food rent six cows.* The size of his house is not stated.

    B. A king of companies, the head king of three or four petty kings <note>original: "reguli"; Latin for minor kings or local chieftains</note>. His honor-price and the value of his oath, etc., were fixed at eight "bondmaid-units," for which amount his "sick maintenance" <note>The legal obligation to provide medical care, food, and housing for an injured person</note> was to be commuted; his proportionate stock was fifteen "bondmaid-units," and his food rent eight cows.†

    C. The head king, whose supreme position is indicated by the passage, "under his control every chief is who cannot be corrected by his lord." His honor-price and the value of his oath, etc., were fixed at fourteen "bondmaid-units"; as the supreme head he could give, but not receive, cattle, and therefore there is no reference in this case to proportionate stock or food rent.† His residence is described with much particularity as a fortified "fortress" <note>original: "dun"; a protected royal residence or earthwork</note> fort, but the length of his house does not much exceed that of the higher noble classes, being only thirty feet.

# INTRODUCTION. CXCV

and dependents, and entitled them to proportionate compensation. “Half the sick maintenance <note>The legal obligation to provide food, nursing, and medical care to an injured person.</note> of a man of every grade is due for his lawful son, *and his wife;* for it is half which is due for every lawful person, one-fourth for every unlawful one. The wives of mercenary soldiers have sick maintenance in right of their sons and husbands. Stewards and couriers are sustained with half the maintenance of their chief. They arrange that their share in the maintenance corresponds with their sustenance by their chief. Every artizan who makes the manufactures of a chief, or a church, is sustained with half maintenance, according to the rank of each person whose manufacture he makes.”*

<margin>* Page 333.</margin>

The object of the author in fixing the number seven as the basis of his classification appears in the passage:—“The maintenance of every grade in the church is the same as that of its co-grade in the laity.”* He desired to treat the seven grades of the church as correlative to the seven grades of the laity, the *doorkeeper* <note>original: "ostiarius"</note> corresponding to the “man of humble cottage-holding” <note>original: "mbidboth"-man; the lowest grade of freeman</note>, and the bishop to the King; or rather, finding the number of grades in the church fixed at seven, he attempts to classify the laity in seven grades, and either omits or interpolates ranks to produce the required result. This fact is conclusive of the extremely unreliable nature of the classification contained in this tract, and the impossibility of treating it as historical evidence of the organization of an Irish tribe at any period.

The analysis of this classification is shown in the annexed table. None of the incidents of any rank are introduced except such as are more or less common to all, and capable of being numerically expressed.

In these tables the names of the classes printed in Italics are those which are rejected upon the ultimate analysis. The introduction of the “noble of vengeance” <note>original: "aire-echta"; a specific rank of nobleman responsible for avenging blood-feuds</note> to make up the number is manifest in this table. The series of numbers in all the columns seem to have been fixed before he was introduced, and any numerical qualifications attributed to him would have destroyed the regularity of the numerical sequence.

# INTRODUCTION.

If we turn to the scheme of the ranks of a tribe contained in the next tract, we find the arrangement wholly different. The titles of rank (or of discredit) given here amount to twenty-six. The arrangement is in the inverse order of that in the present tract, commencing with the King and proceeding downwards. The nine last of these classes may be disregarded as representing the unfree class. They are described as not possessing the right to go into the assembly <note>The "assembly" refers to the *oenach*, a local gathering for legal and social business.</note> who had no <term>honor-price</term> <note>original: "dire fine"; the payment due to a person for an offense against them, determined by their social status.</note>, and were not worthy to enter into bonds or securities.

There remain therefore seventeen distinct terms, representing, according to the author, so many classes of the free members of the community. Their respective grades are marked solely by the amount of their honor-price, and the number of persons to free feeding they were entitled. A reference to the case of the class No. 9 (the <term>henchman</term> <note>original: "seirthuid"; literally a "heel-man" or attendant.</note>), and class 21, the <term>Chief of Precedence</term> <note>original: "aire-tuisi"</note>, will show that the phrase "free feeding" means the supply of food to a certain number of individuals, not a right to pasture so many head of cattle. The sequence of the ranks of the free persons in the tribe, according to the sequel, would be represented as follows:—

# INTRODUCTION.

A conclusion may be arrived at by a comparison of the legal tests:—The freeman who possesses no property is called in the <term>Crith Gabhlach</term> <note>A famous Old Irish law tract dating to the 8th century; the title translates to "The Branched Purchase," referring to the various ways status was acquired.</note> a "<term>mbidboth</term>" <note>original: *fer midbad*; literally a "man of the middle-house," referring to a young man or someone of entry-level social standing</note>, and in the later text an "<term>uaitne</term>"-man <note>original: *uaitne*; literally meaning a "pillar" or "support," used here for a basic freeman</note>; these two terms representing the lowest class must be identical.

The "<term>og-aire</term>" <note>Literally "young noble," the lowest grade of freeman possessing enough property to be independent.</note> of the first list corresponds partly with the 'second' rank of a "<term>bo-aire</term>," and partly with the "<term>bo-aire</term>" <note>Literally "cow-lord," a prosperous free farmer whose status was measured by his livestock.</note> of the second list.

The "<term>aire-desa</term>" <note>Literally "noble of the property," the first rank of true nobility who had tenants under him.</note> is common to both, and it appears from the amount of their <term>honor-price</term> <note>original: *eneclann*; the legal value assigned to a person based on their rank, which determined compensation for injuries or the weight of their testimony.</note> that the "full <term>flaithem</term>" <note>A lord or ruler.</note> and the "<term>aire-desa</term>" of the second list are identical.

The titles of the "<term>aire-ard</term>" <note>High-noble.</note>, "<term>aire-tuisi</term>" <note>Chief of precedence.</note>, and "<term>aire-forgail</term>" <note>Noble of testimony; the highest grade of nobility below a king.</note> are common to both lists, but the latter tract treats the "high-noble" as identical with the "noble of testimony." The later text treats the "high-noble" (or "noble of testimony") and the "chief of precedence" as officials simply, and they should, according to this authority, be struck off the list of the actual classes of society.

The result will be to reduce the number of the actual ranks of society to four:—(1) the "entry-level man" or "pillar" man, the freeman without property; (2) the "young-noble" or "cow-lord," the freeman possessing a property qualification; (3) the "noble of property," the noble with property qualification; and (4) three grades of Kingship. It is to be remarked that at these points the valuation as to honor-price exactly coincides.

If we refer to the scale of compensation for the death of any person killed, as set out in the <term>Book of Aicill</term> <note>One of the primary texts of the Brehon Laws, traditionally attributed to King Cormac mac Airt.</note>, the result is as follows:—

1. A king, bishop, professor, chief poet, and every noble person <note>original: *airitech*; referring to those of high legal standing</note>, or the best "noble of testimony" chief, . . . . . . 14 <term>cumhals</term> <note>A unit of value in early Ireland, originally meaning a female slave, but later standardized to the value of three milk-cows.</note>.
2. A middle or lower "noble of testimony" chief, or "high-noble" chief, . . . . 7 do.
3. A "chief of precedence," or "noble of property" chief, . 4 do.
4. A "cow-lord," or "young-noble" chief, . . 3 do.
5. An "intermediate" person <note>original: *fer-midbaidh*.</note>, . . . 2 do.
6. A "stripling" person <note>original: *flescach*; a youth not yet of age.</note>, or "skilled" workman <note>original: *dair*; likely referring to a carpenter or worker in oak.</note>, . 1 do.*

# INTRODUCTION.

Upon comparing these three lists, the following conclusions emerge: the essential distinctions regarding rank were only five in total, namely:—**(a)** the Kings of three orders, and those individuals who, because of their official standing, were placed in the same category; **(b)** the nobles, who were subdivided into four classes:—the **<term>aire-forgaill</term>** <note>Literally "noble of superior testimony"; the highest grade of nobility below a king, whose word carried the greatest legal weight.</note>, the **<term>aire-ard</term>** <note>Literally "high noble."</note>, the **<term>aire-tuisi</term>** <note>Literally "noble of leadership" or "precedence."</note>, and the **<term>aire-desa</term>** <note>Literally "noble of the property"; the first rank of true nobility who had tenants under him.</note>; and that the highest-ranking **<term>aire-forgaill</term>** held an official position that placed him in the same category as a king; **(c)** the freeman who possessed property, the **<term>bo-aire</term>** <note>Literally "cow-lord"; a prosperous free farmer whose status was measured by his livestock.</note>; **(d)** the freeman without property; and **(e)** the non-free classes.

It is evident from the text itself that a large proportion of the classes introduced in the sections that follow are purely imaginary. When comparing this tract and the <term>Crith Gabhlach</term> <note>A famous Old Irish law tract dating to the 8th century; the title translates to "The Branched Purchase."</note>, to which it is supposed to be a sequel, the list in the former appears to be more ancient and trustworthy. If the author of this sequel had the <term>Crith Gabhlach</term> before him, he never would have abandoned the principle of organizing the ranks into groups of seven, nor would he have omitted as many as seven of the grades. He also ignores the precise instructions regarding the sizes of their respective houses and the amount of their furniture, which take up such a large portion of the <term>Crith Gabhlach</term>. Furthermore, he does not mention the amount of proportionate livestock and "food rent" (provisions paid to a lord), which in the <term>Crith Gabhlach</term> is stated as an essential mark of rank, based on the assumption that all classes were bound in a feudal-like tie to some superior. The statements in the <term>Book of Aicill</term> <note>One of the primary manuscripts of the Brehon Laws, focusing on criminal law and social compensation.</note> are clear and practical, and are far more valuable as an authority than these later tracts. It naturally follows that we regard the <term>Crith Gabhlach</term> as, to a great extent, an imaginary work—the *Utopia* <note>original: "Utopia"; a reference to Thomas More’s fictional island, used here to mean an idealized, non-existent social system.</note> of a <term>Brehon Lawyer</term> <note>A professional jurist in ancient Ireland who interpreted the complex system of customary laws.</note>. Although it contains many fragments of archaic law, it does not provide a distinct historical basis. Any description of the condition of the ancient <term>Irish nation</term> founded on a belief that the <term>Crith Gabhlach</term> describes an existing social order must be considered merely imaginary.

Although there is difficulty in explaining many of the details, a definite picture is given of the mutual relations of the king and his people, and the mode of life at the date of the work. The duties and rights of the king are conceived as resting upon his representative character; as the **<term>flaith</term>** <note>original: "flaith"; A lord or ruler who held authority over a territory and provided protection to his followers.</note>, as the patron of his **<term>clientèle</term>** <note>The group of free followers or dependents who provided service and tribute to a lord in exchange for protection and a grant of cattle.</note>, or the head of the house on behalf of his family, represents in the assembly or before the judge all those technically "in his hand" <note>A legal phrase meaning those under his immediate protection and legal responsibility.</note>, so the king stands as the agent of his tribe; "he swears for them to the king (that is, to the superior king) on behalf of the territory. He denies (or makes oath) on their behalf; he proves for them to the extent of seven **<term>cumhals</term>** <note>original: "cumhals"; A standard unit of value in early Irish law. Originally the value of a female slave, it became a general measure for land or compensation.</note>. He goes into co-judgment, into co-evidence, with the king for his people."* The relation of the king to the tribe implied reciprocal rights and duties, as that of head of the household to its members:—"They are entitled to righteous judgments. They are entitled to a pledge on their part. They are entitled to sustenance as they sustain."* <note>This refers to the "right of refection," where the people provided food and lodging for the king, and in return, he provided for the social and legal welfare of the tribe.</note> In three cases the king is authorized to bind the people by his promise made on their behalf; namely, a pledge for **hosting** <note>A formal summons to military service or a gathering of an armed force.</note>, which means a levy of the armed force for a definite purpose, three of which are stated in the text; a pledge for right; and a pledge for international regulations. For three purposes the king was entitled to call the people together; for a fair, for a meeting for correction, or making a contract, or for the purpose of accompanying himself to the boundary.* The paragraph commencing in page 335 states:—"There are now four rights which a king pledges his people to observe." # INTRODUCTION.

other three rights, and it is the king that enforces them." The enactment of rules to bind the people rested with the people themselves; the king had no legislative power; he enforced obedience to the law, but could not himself enact one. As the idea of the enactment of a new law, in the correct use of the term, was quite foreign to the state of society with which we are dealing, this perhaps might be more correctly expressed by the statement that the people declared the custom, and made the regulations incident thereto, and that the king carried them out into execution; having reference to the second right attributed to the king, the <term>Fenechus-law</term> <note>original: "Fenechus"; the traditional common law of the free Irish classes (the Féne), dealing largely with land and social status.</note> proclaimed by the people dealt with the division and management of the tribe land, which at the present day is the all-engrossing business of the Swiss Communes.

The second right of the king is defined as "a right after they have been defeated in battle, and he consolidates his people afterwards so that they are not broken up; and a right after a mortality."\* Both of the circumstances under which this right of the king arose, are cases in which the tribe had suffered the loss of many of its members, and the relative proportions of the several households had been materially altered, and for the stability of the tribe, and to ensure cultivation, it would be requisite to redistribute the tribe land among the surviving members. The extreme case of a tribe having been driven out of its original territory, and establishing itself in a new district, would be an instance of the circumstances under which the exercise of this unusual authority on the part of the king would be necessary; so also if, by any casualty, a large proportion of the tribe perished (we frequently read in history of the destruction or banishment of an entire <term>clan</term> <note>original: "gens"; a Latin term used here to describe a kin-group or tribe.</note>), the result must have been, to a greater or less extent, a recasting of a mode in which the tribe land was distributed.

However, Saint Benignus, wishing to soothe this offense with a welcome favor, began and composed that famous chronicle called the Psalter of Cashel, in which were written the deeds, laws, privileges, and successions not only of the Monarchs of all Ireland, but specifically those of Munster.” <note>original: "Cognati Sancti Benegni, ut populus Eoganiæ Casselensis, Olildiana progenies, et alii Momonienses, audito prædicto ejus facto, non parum offensi et contra virum Dei indignati dicuntur. The Book of Rights is singularly devoid of any legal information or value whatsoever. If the author of this treatise was acquainted with the Psalter of Cashel, or the Book of Rights, it is difficult to understand how he has placed the feudal relation of the kings and their chiefs upon the taking of cattle and food rent, and not upon the receipt by the chiefs of the extravagant and fabulous gifts stated in the Book of Rights. The gifts represented in the Book of Rights, as presented by the King of Cashel to his feudatories, are, of course, imaginary; but that a “king of companies” should take from the head king fifteen <term>cumhals</term> <note>An ancient Irish unit of value, often equated to three cows or the value of a female slave.</note> of cattle as his proportionate stock, and pay eight cows as the food rent of his house, is equally incredible. It would seem that both authors, each after his own fashion, were desirous of stating the relative positions of the King of Cashel and his under-kings. The relation was created by the receipt by the inferior from the superior of some benefit, and a subsequent render of service in consideration of it. The actual transaction may have taken a merely symbolical shape, which the author of the Book of Rights has exaggerated in a poetic (?) form, and the author of this tract described in accordance with the usage prevalent among the lower classes. As there may be some who believe that St. Benean wrote the Psalter of Cashel, I do not rely upon the reference to that work as a conclusive evidence of the date of this tract.

If the over-lords had exercised this right it would have been very fortunate for the general body of the people, and the greater part of the annals would never have been written. The simplest explanation appears to be that the king could enforce the cultivation of the tribe-land in the ordinary course of customary husbandry. The third right is that "of lighting up religion, such as is found in the right (or law) of Adamnan."\* The historical celebrity of the <term>Cain-Adamnan</term> <note>The 'Law of Adomnán' (also called the Law of the Innocents), enacted in 697 AD to protect women, children, and clerics during war.</note> arose from the rule exempting women from liability to military service; but this rule was only one of the clauses, and the reference here made seems to be to those enacting the performance of specified religious duties.

The rank of the king was regarded as official, not personal; if, therefore, he engaged in the labour fit only for a plebeian <note>A commoner or person of lower social status.</note>, he was for the time being reduced to the plebeian grade, and his <term>dire-fine</term> <note>original: "díre"; an 'honor-price' or compensation payment based on social rank. If a king performed common labor, his legal value dropped to that of a commoner.</note> assessed accordingly. The four occasions when he thus lost his status were when he used a clod-mallet <note>A wooden tool used to break up soil after plowing.</note>, or a shovel, or a spade, or when he travelled alone. The reason for this latter rule is remarkable: "This might be the day upon which a woman alone (without witnesses) might swear her child upon a king—a day upon which no one could give testimony but *herself* alone,"\* a rule not devised for the protection of the moral character of the king, but to prevent the danger of the introduction into the family of the king of spurious bastards, and to guard against such mischief as was caused by the facility with which Shane O'Niel <note>Seán 'the Proud' Ó Néill (c. 1530–1567), a powerful Gaelic chieftain whose many children led to various succession disputes and political instability.</note> acknowledged all children attributed to him. In one other case the king lost his status, and was entitled to the "dire"-fine of a non-noble person: when in retreating from battle he was wounded in the back. Upon this point the author remarks, with characteristically trivial accuracy, that the rule did not apply when the weapon had passed through the body and came out at the back.\*

Such a work as the present can be relied upon in its general results only; as to the numerical details we have no means of distinguishing which are imaginary and which are exact.

The king was responsible, both to his own people and to outsiders <note>original: "externs"; those residing outside the king's immediate tribal territory.</note>, for illegal or irregular seizures or requisitions; this appears in a negative form from the exceptions to his assumed liability. In the two latter cases the cattle were to be restored, which proves that what the author was treating was not the return of (or payment for) the goods, but the consequences of their illegal seizure.

The bishop," he replies, "is higher, because the king stands up (*to salute him*), by reason of religion. A bishop, however, raises his knee to a king."*

The impression produced by the <term>Branched Purchase</term> <note>original: "Crith Gabhlach"; an 8th-century law tract that details the grades of society, their property, and their rights</note> as to the condition of the Irish people at the date of its composition, is very unfavorable. Their houses must have been small and ill-furnished; the length of the house of a <term>junior-freeman</term> <note>original: "og-aire"; the lowest grade of independent farmer who owned some cattle and land</note> is set down as seventeen feet—about the size of the cottage of poorer class of farmers of the present day—and the house of the head king is stated to measure only thirty-seven feet in length; from this we must conclude that the habits and mode of life of the upper and lower classes were very similar; the houses would seem to have consisted each of one room only; the description of a house, as having so many "beds," not rooms, in it, shows that they all slept in one chamber; the houses were wood, or wattle-work, of a very unsubstantial character; the back house so often alluded to was probably a detached kitchen; the furniture described is of the simplest nature, and in insignificant quantity; although some golden and silver articles are mentioned, there is scarcely an allusion to rich dresses, jewels, personal ornaments, or works of art; the ordinary diet seems to have been of the coarsest description; and it is remarkable that there is no allusion to wine throughout; the description of the king's court must be very much exaggerated, or the size of his house under-estimated, for it would be impossible to crowd into a room of thirty-seven feet in length, the number of persons detailed as forming his court and retinue; the

# INTRODUCTION.

want of refinement in manners is marked by the fact of the champion and man of deeds at the palace retaining their spears "against the confusion of the ale-house."

The old tribal organization continued to be the supposed form of their social system. We read of the king calling his people together for various purposes, and of the people themselves declaring the <term>customary law</term> <note>original: "Fenechus"; the body of traditional laws belonging to the free Irish people</note>, but the universal system of commendation extending from the low <term>junior youth</term> <note>original: "mbidboth"; the lowest rank of freeman who was still under the authority of his father or a lord</note> man to the king of companies (every one of whom received cows from a superior, and paid his food-rent), and the masses of non-free tenants who swelled the retainers of the <term>noble lord</term> <note>original: "flaith"; the ruling class of land-owning nobles</note>, prove that the new system of personal relation was being rapidly substituted for the bond of tribal union; the tribe lands had been monopolized by the noble class; whether by grant or force, fairly or unfairly, is unimportant. The double process is summed in the Latin sentence—"These pastures were generally given to be grazed, but in common; which many have seized through their power." <note>original: "*Hæc ferè pascua data sunt depascenda sed in communi; quæ multi per potentiam invaserunt.*"</note> As a natural consequence, landless men and <term>unfree tenants</term> <note>original: "fuidhirs"; individuals who lacked tribal land rights and lived in dependency on a lord, often fleeing from other territories</note> abounded; the general instability is proved by the custom of hostages, and the presence of the foreign retainers who surround the king; and the rules, as to the maintenance of the wife of the mercenary soldier, show that the hired <term>foreign soldier</term> <note>original: "gallowglass"; from the Irish "gallóglaigh," elite mercenary warriors who became a fixture of Irish warfare</note>, the curse of Ireland, was not unknown.

The *<term>Branched Purchase</term>* <note>original: "Crith Gabhlach"; an 8th-century law tract that attempts to categorize every rank of society and their specific property requirements</note> may be fairly characterized as the fantastic production of an antiquarian lawyer of a strong ecclesiastical <note>church-related</note> bias, composed at a date at which the tribe system was breaking up, and the condition of the people, both moral and material, had much deteriorated. The work is of the highest value as an antiquarian treatise, rather on account of the general principles which it assumes, and the incidental statements which it contains, than from the accuracy of its classification, or the truth of its minute details; and any deductions founded upon a belief in its historical value must lead to conclusions involving the too common error of substituting an imaginary, for the actual, condition of a people.

-># INTRODUCTION.<-

### XII.
#### SEQUEL TO THE *BRANCHED PURCHASE* <note>original: "Crith Gabhlach"; this title translates literally to "Branched Purchase," referring to the various "branches" or divisions of the social classes and the "purchase" of their legal status.</note>

This tract deals with the same subject as the preceding, and can be advantageously considered in connexion with it. In the original manuscript no special title has been prefixed to the treatise, and for the purpose of the present volume it has been named the sequel to the *Branched Purchase*, implying that the subject dealt with in the preceding tract is further discussed in the present, but not that it was a work by the same author, or composed by another author as an appendix or continuation of the *Branched Purchase*; in the last section of the introduction it has been sufficiently shown that two different schemes for the sub-division of the rank of society are adopted by the respective authors, and that, so far from being complimentary, the latter tract is contradictory to the former.

<margin>Feastings</margin>
The legal rights with reference to which the several ranks are classified by this author are specified by him as nine in number. As stated by the author, these appear to have been as follows:—(1) the greatest and least number of attendants brought by them to their <term>cosherings</term> <note>original: "coisir"; a customary right of a lord to receive food and lodging from his tenants, often involving a large retinue of guests.</note> upon their tenants, or accompanying them as their “company in the tribe”; (2) their feeding, probably the amount and nature of the food to be provided for them; and the amount of compensation to be paid to them under the following heads:—(3) for <term>driving</term> <note>original: "esain"; a legal term referring to the right of escort or the fines related to the driving of cattle or property.</note>; (4) for wounding; (5) for insulting; (6) for the violation of their protection; and as (7) their <term>honor-price</term> <note>original: "lóg n-enech"; the monetary value assigned to a person's status, which determined the amount of fines paid to them for various offenses.</note>; (8) also the obscure fines described as <term>“blush”-fines</term> and <term>“blister”-fines</term> <note>In Irish law, these poetic terms refer to fines paid for insults that "brought a blush to the cheek" or caused "the blister of shame."</note>; (9) and their exemptions before and after <term>refections</term> <note>original: "biad"; formal meals or food-rents provided to a superior.</note>.* Although the classification may have been originally made with reference to these several heads, the detailed rights and duties of each class are very imperfectly stated, and all reference to some is wholly omitted. The twenty-six classes stated in this tract are enumerated downwards—that is, commencing with the high king and proceeding downward to the lowest grade—but it is perhaps more convenient in considering them to adopt the inverse order, and to proceed from the unfree classes as the natural basis. 

The nine last classes are intended to comprise individuals who are not members of the tribe, either because they were originally unfree, or because they have lost their original status. They are described as not possessing a holding of land, or special talents, or followers, and therefore they are not worthy to form part of the tribal assemblies or the groups gathered for formal meals <note>original: "companies of refection"; the right of a lord and his retinue to be fed by those of lower status.</note>, nor are they entitled to a <term>honor-price fine</term> <note>original: "dire"; a legal fine paid to a person based on their social rank. If you had no rank, you had no "dire."</note>, or to enter into legal securities or give evidence. They are evidently regarded not as slaves in the modern sense, but as "unfree"—having no legal standing and possessing no legal rights in their own persons. It would follow by logic that their persons could be protected and their property secured to them only by the intervention of some member of the tribe, in whose "hand" <note>This refers to the legal concept of being under the protection or guardianship of a superior.</note> they would be technically considered to be.

When the definitions of these nine classes are considered, it appears that they are not arranged with reference to their respective rights—for they are all described as possessing none—but rather with reference to the causes by which they had lost, or did not possess, any recognised status. These nine classes are sub-divisions of one single class, distinguished from each other by purely accidental circumstances. The ranks thus enumerated are as follows:

If a writer of our own day undertook to describe the various ranks of English society, and having commenced with the following:—"Tramps, housebreakers, acrobats, idiots, henpecked husbands, dismissed officers, insolvents, etc.," finally concluded with the "bishops, earls, marquises, dukes, the Lord Chancellor, and the Queen," we should understand that he had confused the ideas of legal rank and social respectability in a hopeless manner; and yet any such work, if preserved to a date at which a wholly different form of society had been substituted for that now existing, would be valuable to the antiquarian of the future as an illustration of the layers of our society; but we may hope that enough of our literature will remain to prevent the mistake of thinking that insolvents and acrobats were ranks in society in the same manner as dukes, or that insolvents and housebreakers were permanent castes. <note>The author uses this modern analogy to explain that ancient Irish law tracts sometimes listed people by their reputation or behavior alongside their formal legal standing, which can be confusing for historians.</note>

Bearing in mind the way the classification of the unfree persons has been constructed, let us turn our attention to the seventeen classes into which the free members of the tribe are divided. If we refer to the table on page 197 <note>original: "cxcvii"</note> it will be observed that the ranks not common to both the systems of classification in this tract, and in the <term>Branched Purchase</term> <note>original: "Crith-Gablach"; an 8th-century Irish law tract that details the status, rights, and property requirements of different social classes.</note>, are marked in italics. On examination, all these will appear to be grades of social respectability—not legal ranks—grades of respectability which gave those who possessed them substantial claims against the members of their families or third persons, or affected their compensation for wrong, but did not elevate them in the assembly above the other freemen, or entitle them to political privileges or grades in society arising from official position or public services.

(b)* The "pure" person <note>original: "idhna"</note>, who has a number of sons who are born to him, and of male relatives (or brethren) to the number of thirty champions. He is entitled to free living of five from his "family" <note>original: "fine"</note>. The key to the interpretation of this lies in his right to free living from the family. He must belong to a family, and there must be other households in the family, in which he should have his free feeding for four. His qualification was the possession of sons and brothers, warriors—thirty in all. He appears to have been the head of a household (or joint family) within the family group, so numerous that the household allotment being insufficient to support them, a certain number were supported by the remaining houses of the family. A person, the head of a numerous household, would manifestly be one of much power and influence in the early stages of society.

(c.) The "noble stream" person <note>original: "ansruth"; this term usually refers to a high-ranking poet or noble</note> is described as one "who protects his mansion and his land. He is allowed (lit. *For him is*) the wounding a person in each term of the year. He has no fewer than twenty (attendants) in an extern territory. He has free feeding for four on every side, and from every chief in his 'territory' <note>original: "tuaith"</note>. He is entitled to a trusty sword for his honor-price." As the "pure" person <note>original: "idhma," likely a variant of "idhna"</note> was entitled to support from the "family," the "noble stream" was entitled to it from the tribe. His position involves the wounding or slaying of others, and his absence from the tribe-land with the accompaniment of a strong escort. His peculiar honor-price, the sword, indicated his office. He may be easily identified with the "lord of vengeance" <note>original: "aire-echta"</note> of the *Branching Purchase* <note>original: "Crith Gabhlach," a famous 8th-century legal tract on social status</note>.†

Such bodies of men were called "<term>Lucht Tighe</term>" <note>literally, "people of the house"; Household Troops</note>. The <term>Household Troops</term> <note>original: "Lucht Tighe"</note> of Tadhy O'Kelly, King of <term>Hy-Many</term> <note>original: "Hi Mainé"; a kingdom in Connacht</note>, in Connacht, and of Ferghal O'Ruaire, King of <term>Breifne</term> <note>original: "Breefney"</note>, were conspicuous at the battle of Clontarf, <term>A.D. 1014</term>. The regular organization of these household troops, or bodyguards of the chieftain, appears from the names of divers places; for example, we know that there was anciently a district in Monaghan called <term>MacMahon's Household</term> <note>original: "Lucht Tighe mhic Mathghamhna"</note>, that is, MacMahon's Household, because it was exclusively devoted to the maintenance of the chief's household troops, who thus "were entitled to free feeding on all sides."—*O'Curry, "Manners and Customs of the Ancient Irish," vol. ii., p. 391-2.*

# INTRODUCTION. ccxv

The three classes of the (e) "<term>young lord</term>," <note>original: "ogflaithem"; the most junior grade of nobility, literally "young-lord"</note> (f) "<term>half-lord</term>," <note>original: "lethflaithem"; a lord whose status or income was deemed partial</note> and (g) "<term>lord of one tenant</term>,"* <note>original: "flaithem of one vassal"; the lowest level of noble income</note> are merely sub-divisions of the poorer "<term>lords</term>," <note>original: "flaiths"; the noble, land-owning class</note> with reference to their income, the amount of which naturally depended upon the number of their tenants; but there is no reason to believe that the rights of a <term>lord</term> <note>original: "flaith"</note> were measured in accordance exactly with the number of his tenants. Undoubtedly the "<term>lord</term>," who had a large number of tenants who swelled the train of his retainers, and paid him food rent, which enabled him to support others, was a much more important person than the "<term>lord</term>" with few tenants, and that poor broken-down "<term>lords</term>" with one, two, or three old tenants were very little, if at all, above, in public consideration, the <term>wealthy free farmer</term> <note>original: "bo-aire," or "cow-owning churl"; a commoner who achieved high status through cattle ownership</note>, who was rising into the noble class.

It appears from a passage in the last tract published in this volume that the descendant of "<term>lords</term>" might fall back, under certain circumstances, probably the want of qualifying wealth, into the non-noble class;† but there are no grounds for considering that the "<term>lords</term>" below the <term>lord of precedence</term> <note>original: "aire-tuisi"; a high-ranking noble who leads his kindred</note> were legally divided into ranks in the exact ratio of their fortune. The differences as to this point between this list and that contained in the <term>Branched Purchase</term> <note>original: "Crith Gabhlach"; a famous 8th-century law tract detailing social status and honor-prices</note> are very instructive as to the mode in which these detailed enumerations were composed, and the reliance to be placed upon their numerical statements. It is important to submit the schemes of rank contained in these two tracts to close examination, as the apparently anomalous character of the Irish tribe has been chiefly produced by the assumption that the <term>*Branched Purchase*</term> <note>original: "Crith Gabhlach"</note> should be admitted as an exact and historical document, and its numerical statements received without reserve as truthful representations of existing facts; so long as this mode of treating the <term>*Brehon Law*</term> <note>The ancient native legal system of Ireland, practiced by professional jurists known as Brehons</note> tracts holds its ground, the ancient Irish tribe system must continue to be considered, as it has unfortunately too long been imagined, as an exception and an anomaly, a maze of technicalities incapable of disentanglement.

The scheme upon which the clergy are arranged is a double gradation, partly connected with their holy orders in the church, and partly in connection with the religious condition of the individual. It is needless to observe that the moral and religious merit of the individual is referable solely to the one virtue of <term>continence</term> <note>the practice of self-restraint, specifically refraining from sexual relationships, which was a primary measure of holiness in this legal system</note>; but it is certainly surprising that the author arranges all classes of the church, inclusive of the recluses, into the three classes of virgins, married, and repentant. Every fine must, therefore, be the result of three quantities:—the official position, the moral state of the injured cleric, and the nature of the injury inflicted. It is impossible to construct in a tabular form the amount of compensation payable in each case, as the results stated in the text do not all coincide with the theory on which they are professed to be calculated. The general principle, however, is clear, namely:—that the full amount calculated upon the rank of the injured cleric and the nature of the injury is payable in the case only of the cleric being a virgin; this amount is reduced by one-third if the cleric be married, and again by another third if he be repentant;† and that between

### ccxxi

> “Another <term>lay recluse</term> <note>a person living a life of religious devotion and isolation without being a member of the formal clergy</note> is he who puts bounds to his passions, and who goes to the clergy this day, upon whom a <term>soul-friend</term> <note>original: *anmchara*; a spiritual guide or confessor</note> does not pronounce his character, or recommendation. The author manifestly regards St. Peter as having been a married man, and, with reference to Paul, puts a well-known construction upon the twelfth verse of the ninth chapter of the First Epistle to the Corinthians <note>The author likely refers to the passage where Paul discusses the rights of apostles to be accompanied by a wife, though modern bibles usually locate this in 1 Corinthians 9:5</note>.

The peculiar views put forward in this tract as to the position and duties of the clerics are remarkable, and are of importance in fixing an approximate date for the composition of this tract. The bishop, not the abbot, is the highest known ecclesiastic; indeed, of the abbot there is no mention whatsoever. The marriage of the clerics is assumed as permissible, although discountenanced, inasmuch as the married cleric thereby to a certain extent lost caste, as proved by the proportionate diminution of his <term>dire-fine</term>; the recluse is treated as an acknowledged order in the Church, and he is intimately connected, for the purpose of the amount of his <term>dire-fine</term>, with his <term>soul-friend</term> (*anmchara*); the Pope was recognized as the highest bishop of the Church, and as ruling over Rome; and in the reference to the imaginary work of St. Augustine, there is an allusion to “the emperor of the whole world.” These indications point to the transitional and obscure state of the Celtic Church after the breaking up of the <term>Columban monastic system</term> <note>the network of monasteries following the traditions of St. Columba of Iona</note>, and before its complete reorganization under continental influence—to the latest period of the existence of the <term>Culdees</term> <note>original: *Céili Dé*; "companions of God," a reform movement of ascetic monks</note>, a remarkable era in Celtic ecclesiastical history, which has been lately—
