# INTRODUCTION.

### ccxxii

fully dealt with, so far as the scanty existing materials permit, by Mr. Skene.* <note>William Forbes Skene (1809–1892) was a prominent historian of Celtic Scotland</note> The allusion to "the emperor of the whole world" may help in some degree in fixing the date of the work. A Celtic pilgrim returning from Rome would state the impressions which the existing state of facts produced upon him; he certainly would not be influenced by the legal theories of the civil lawyers; the abstract idea of the all-ruling emperor would not occur to him unless the power of an existing emperor were brought home to his mind by what he saw with his eyes and heard with his ears among the public of the city. A pilgrim to Rome during the interval between the disappearance of the influence of the Eastern emperors and the date at which the <term>Culdees</term> <note>original: *Céli Dé*, meaning "Companions of God"; an ascetic monastic movement in medieval Ireland and Scotland</note> finally ceased to exist, could have his attention drawn to the imperial power, as a universal dominion, only at two distinct periods—either during the reigns of Karl the Great <note>Charlemagne, crowned Emperor of the Romans in 800</note> and his son Ludwig <note>Louis the Pious</note>, that is, between A.D. 800 and A.D. 840, or after the resuscitation of the imperial power by the Emperor Otto in A.D. 951. The expression of the Bishop of Peter's Church "having under his subjection the chiefs of Rome" (unless this be merely a Celtic phrase expressing sovereignty), would exactly describe the position of the Popes after the later date. This would point to the end of the tenth or beginning of the eleventh century as the probable date of the composition of this tract.

From these, and the various remarkable points of difference between this tract and the <term>Crith Gabhlach</term> <note>meaning "The Branched Purchase," a famous 8th-century Irish law text detailing social ranks and their legal rights</note>, already alluded to, it may be inferred that the present treatise is the more ancient of the two, and represents an older condition of Irish society. A considerable portion of it, so much as deals with <term>ollamhs</term> <note>the highest rank of professional poets and scholars in ancient Ireland</note> and poets, is purely fantastic, full of the false discussions and quibbling classification so much in vogue with <term>Brehon lawyers</term> <note>judges and legal scholars who applied the native "Brehon Law" system</note>, and valueless except as a monument of misspent time and ingenuity; another portion, so much as deals with the clerics, although most valuable from an historical point of view, cannot be considered as a practical statement of existing law, but rather as a covert

### XIII.
## SUCCESSION.

The last tract contained in the present has no heading or title in the original; it has been named, for the purpose of reference, as a treatise on “Succession,” inasmuch as that is the subject which the author proposed to discuss. This work is of the fragmentary character, being nothing more than a collection of unconnected extracts or references, thrown together in a note-book as the materials for an intended work.

To this tract there is prefixed the following extraordinary head-note:—“By this book, if I can, in the name of God, I will bring the senior before the junior in every case, as these laws down here state. Beyond this I will make an intermixture of their law altogether.”* <margin>* Page 375.</margin>

The object of the work was not to state what were the <term>customary law</term> <note>the traditional, unwritten laws based on long-established community practices</note> upon the subject dealt with, but to collect authorities in support of an argument in favour of succession by descent and seniority, and, it may be gathered, in opposition to the rules regulating it by personal merit, property qualifications, or election. The author must, for the purpose of extract and reference, have had before him a considerable number of works, which it would be now difficult to ascertain or identify. As to the passage near the commencement of the tract, concerning the succession of an abbot,* <note>The head of a monastery; in the Irish context, this position often stayed within specific powerful families</note> it appears that the authority referred to is the concluding paragraphs of the <term>Senchus Mor</term> <note>original: *Senchas Már*; meaning the "Great Tradition," this is the most significant collection of ancient Irish legal texts</note> with the present annexed commentary.† <margin>† Vol. 3, page 79.</margin>

Although from its form, and the obvious intention of its

### ccxxvi

The most important extracts here contained have reference to the rule of three descents, before referred to, which determined the status of an individual with reference to that of his father and grandfather, namely:—

> “He is a disease of evils after three persons.”*
> “He is a hill of chieftainship in the third person.”*
> “For it gives a prescription of acknowledgment; three heirs have succeeded one another.”*

> generations the name of abbot. The territory termed the <term>Abthania</term> <note>original: *Abthania*; an abthanery, or the lands and jurisdiction belonging to an abbey</note> of Dull, which was of great extent, and included the modern parishes of Dull and Fortingall, seems to have been in the hands of Crinan, the lay abbot of Dunkeld, and, along with the possessions of the latter abbacy, must have placed him on a par as to power and position with the great <term>Mormaers</term> <note>the high stewards or great regional earls of early Scotland</note> of Alban.”—Skene: Celtic Scotland, Vol. II., p. 341.

The causes and the results of the marriage of clerics in Ireland and Scotland is thus stated by Mr. Skene:—

> “In the early Monastic Church of Ireland celibacy was enforced upon at least one class of the monks, for the saints of the second order refused the services of women, separating them from the monasteries; but still there was a succession to the abbacy, the tribe or family in whom it was vested providing a fit person in Orders to fill the office ; but when the stringency of the monastic rule was broken in upon, under the influence of the secular clergy, marriage was gradually permitted and connived at, and at length became general, the rebound toward a secular state being great in proportion to the enforced strictness of the previous system. The natural consequence was that a direct descent from the ecclesiastical persons themselves came in place of the older system of succession, and the Church offices became hereditary in their family. The next step in the downward process was that the Abbots and Superiors did not take Orders, and became virtually laymen, providing a fit person to perform the ecclesiastical functions, but retaining the name, and all the secular privileges and emoluments of the abbacy. The performance of the Church service was either entrusted to a secular priest, who was called the priest <note>original: *sacerdos*</note>, or *priest* <note>original: *sagart*; the Gaelic word for priest</note>, or it fell to the <term>Cele De</term> <note>original: *Cele De*; often called Culdees, meaning 'clients of God' or 'companions of God'—a group of monastic reformers</note>, when there was such a body connected with the monastery, or to both combined. The great ecclesiastical offices thus became hereditary in the persons of laymen in two ways—either by the usurpation of the benefice by the lay chieftains from whose family it had been supplied, or in the family of the abbot by whose direct descendants the office was filled. It must be borne in mind that prior to 1139, though celibacy was enforced upon the monks by the monastic rule, and upon the clergy generally as a matter of discipline, marriage, when it did take place, was not unlawful. It was not until the second great Council of Lateran, held in that year, declared all such marriages by the fact itself <note>original: *ipso facto*</note> null and void that they became so ; and the effect of this, where the benefice had become hereditary in a particular family, was, instead of restoring the former clerical character of its possessor, to stereotype their condition of laymen, and to convert them into a purely lay family.”—“Celtic Scotland,” vol. ii., p. 338.

# INTRODUCTION.

### ccxxvii

> "They were once noble, *that is to say*, unless his father and grand-father were chiefs, though he may be of the same race; as to his origin, his chieftainship is lost to him."*

> "'In which it is stated, that a chieftainship is lost,' *that is to say*, during the lifetimes of three persons."*

> "'A commoner chief,' *that is to say*, one of commoner race, whose father or grandfather was not a chief."*

> "Question.—What is the '<term>poet of the noble stream</term>' <note>original: *ansruth*; the second-highest grade of poet in the Irish system</note>? His father and his grandfather were '<term>poets of the noble stream</term>'; for every grade whatsoever, whether chief or poet, if he parts with his qualifications during the lifetimes of three persons, his lot is not equal to those who are found in possession of their qualifications during the lifetimes of three persons, until they double their qualification or their service."†

These extracts clearly prove the rule before referred to, that the possession of the necessary property, through three generations, was requisite to give the complete status of the rank to which the qualification was annexed; and that, taking a negative form, the rule was applied to the case of those who lost the qualifying property necessary for their rank, and that the third in descent in such a case lost his status absolutely, and fell into a lower grade.

But if a person acquired double the amount necessary to qualify him for a higher grade, he became a fully recognised member of that grade irrespective of descent. This explains the rule in page 317, which fixes the amount of stock <note>livestock, which was the primary form of wealth and currency in early Ireland</note> requisite in the case of a "<term>cow-nobleman</term>" <note>original: *bo-aire*; a wealthy free farmer whose status was based on cattle ownership</note>, adjoining the rank of a "<term>noble of the land</term>" <note>original: *aire-desa*; the lowest rank of true aristocracy</note>, as double the qualification of the latter rank. The amount specified in this passage was that requisite to make the "<term>cow-nobleman</term>" a complete "<term>noble of the land</term>," and it may be inferred that if he acquired the amount of a "<term>noble of the land</term>'s" qualification, he became a "<term>noble of the land</term>" *in a certain manner* <note>original: *sub modo*; implying a conditional or partial status</note>. And in the same way if a "<term>noble of the land</term>" lost his qualification, the status of that rank was not absolutely lost until after the death of himself and his son, when his grandson absolutely passed into the lower grade. This partial acquisition of status in the first generation, and its completion in the third—

ccxxviii INTRODUCTION.

generation constantly appears in ancient laws. Thus among the Scandinavians there were the three gradations of the <term>Frigiven man</term> <note>a freedman</note>, his son, and his grandson, the <term>Bondr</term> <note>a free-born farmer or householder</note>.* In the <term>Sachsen Spiegel</term> <note>The "Saxon Mirror," one of the most important law books of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, the rule is thus expressly laid down:— "If anyone is of unblemished law in his four generations—that is, from two grandfathers and two grandmothers, and father and mother—no one can defame him in law." <note>original Latin: "Si qui in quatuor suis generationibus, hoc est ex duobus avis et duobus aviis, ac patre et matre indiffamati juris est, illum in jure nemo infamare potest."</note> The same principle is marked in Roman law by the specific names for each step in the progression toward complete citizenship, namely:—<term>Libertus</term> <note>a freed slave</note>, <term>Libertinus</term> <note>the son of a freed slave</note>, and <term>Liber</term> <note>a free-born citizen</note>; and explains the passage in the speech of Appius Claudius Crassus, contrasting the full patrician with the ordinary <term>Quirite</term> <note>a Roman citizen</note>:— "If I were not of the Claudian family, nor born of patrician blood, but only one of any of the citizens, who only knew myself to be born of two free parents and to live in a free state, could I keep silent about this?"† <note>original Latin: "An hoc, si Claudiæ familiæ non sim nec ex patricio sanguine ortus sed unus Quiritium quilibet, qui modo me duobus ingenuus ortum et vivere in libera civitate sciam, reticere possim."</note>

The first phrase quoted from this tract is remarkably expressive, "He is a disease of evils after three persons," meaning that when the father and the grandfather have been evil, the fulness of the sins are developed in the grandson; this is precisely the expression of Demosthenes, <term>evil from the third generation</term> <note>original Greek: πονηρὸς ἐκ τριγονίας</note>,‡ and gives the full point to the line in Sophocles:—

->Courage; for even if I should be shown to be a<-
->thrice-slave, born from a third mother, you will not be shown to be base.§<-

To acquire the full rights of an "<term>aire-desa</term>" <note>a 'lord of property,' the lowest rank of the noble grades in Irish law</note>, the "<term>bo-aire</term>" <note>a 'cow-lord' or wealthy freeholder</note> must have qualified himself by the possession of land held by his tenants, although he could acquire a qualified nobility founded upon the possession of cattle simply.

ccxxix INTRODUCTION.

The qualification, therefore, of the chief, as founded upon the possession of land, had no reference, apparently, to the value of the land, or what would be now called his annual income, but was based upon the number of tenants upon his land, and the amount of their food rents <note>A traditional form of tribute paid in agricultural produce (cattle, pigs, grain) rather than money</note>; that is the number of his retainers made up of his tenants and the other followers, whom the food rents of his tenants enabled him to maintain.

The right of acquiring rank in the tribe founded upon the acquisition of property must, of course, be understood as applicable only to free members of the tribe themselves; as in all early communities the freedom of the tribe and the right to acquire or enjoy a portion of the tribe lands may be taken to have been practically identical.

# OF TAKING POSSESSION. <note>original Irish: "DIN TECHTUGAD"</note>

<margin>OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.</margin>
To the powers of free-entry possession belong; the grooms of the horses of the hospitallers; boundaries of equal joining are protected; more quickly is possession taken by the middle entry; it is not the true entry of possession.

---

"To the powers of possession," <note>original: "Tocombachtaib sealb"</note> that is, it is right or it is quick that the claimants recover the land through this legal entry described below so as to be in possession of it. "The grooms of the horses of the hospitallers," <note>original: "Modaig mairc mbruġraite"</note> that is, it is through the actions of the one who justifies the land for them. "Boundaries of equal joining are protected," <note>original: "Bactair cricha coma comol"</note> that is, equal-friendships, that is, the boundaries were always manifest, that is, I follow or I approach so that the land is joined to them in that manner. "More quickly is possession taken," <note>original: "Aitheam gaibear tuiniġe"</note> that is, it is indeed more rapid, it is more quickly that one takes possession of the land from the middle entry than from the first entry. "In the middle entry," <note>original: "Madon teallach medonach"</note> that is, it is not the man who carries out the entry into the land at the first entry who gains legal possession of the land by virtue of his first entry; but only a right <note>a legal claim rather than full ownership</note> to it. If it be his, it is well; if it be not, he waits for it, and possession is his thereafter. "It is not the true entry of possession," <note>original: "Ni fir-teallach tuiniġe"</note> that is, the man who carries out the entry into the land over the boundary-ditch of the land for his entry does not have possession of the land by virtue of the first entry, unless he makes the subsequent legal entries.

---

1. If it be a man who takes possession, it is thus he should take it; a notice of three <term>decmadh</term> <note>A "decmadh" is a ten-day period used in ancient Irish law to pace legal proceedings and provide the defendant time to respond.</note> is to be given regarding the land; notice is to be given every day during the period of the first ten days, or it may be at the first day, the last day, and the middle day; and if he <note>the current occupant</note> does not respond within that time, he <note>the claimant</note> is to go over to the boundary of the land with two horses in his hand, and witnesses with him, at the end of the first ten days; and it would be right for him to have the law at the end of the first ten days, and at the beginning of the middle ten days, and to stay there for a day and a night; and if he is not responded to then, he is to go out during the period of the middle ten days, and it would be right for him to have the law at its end in the middle ten-day period; and notice is to be given by him every day to the defendant during the period of the—

---

# OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION. ¹
VOL. IV. B 2

<margin>ON THE PROCESS OF LAWFUL POSSESSION</margin>
Noble tribes quickly obtain possession of land; it is secured to them by the work of their horses; lands are not taken possession of until proof is given; he shall sooner get possession if from the middle entry; it is not yet true possession.

<margin>ᵃ Irish: *Those things mentioned below*</margin>
**Quickly obtain**, that is, it is soon or quickly that the men of standing <note>noble tribes or those of high social grade</note> obtain actual possession of the land by bringing the<gloss>ᵃ necessary requirements for taking possession</gloss> into it. **The work of their horses**, that is, it is through the labor of their horses that the claim is justified to them. **Lands are not taken possession of, etc.**, that is, through equal <term>cairde</term> <note>original: "cairde" — a legal treaty or "friendship" agreement between different territories</note>; that is, he held the territories before; that is, I hold or I maintain that their land is not retained by them in that specific manner. **He shall sooner get possession**, that is, one obtains possession of the land more quickly or sooner from the date of the *middle* entry <note>the second formal stage of land-claiming</note> than from the *first* entry. **If from the middle entry**, that is, legal possession does not belong to the man who brings the means of possession onto the land for the first time by virtue of that first act; he has only the beginning of a legal right <note>a "right of inception"</note> concerning it. If the claim is valid, it is well; if not, there is a stay of ten days, and the possession is his at that point. **It is not true possession**, that is, possession does not belong to the man who simply brings the means of taking possession over the fence and onto the land for the first time, unless he follows through by making the second [middle] entry.

<margin>ᵇ Irish: *A notice served by him.*</margin>
Whatever man brings the means of taking possession, he shall do it in this way: he shall give notice for the space of thirty days upon the land; he shall serve notice every day regarding it during the first ten days, or *according to other legal experts*, on the first, the middle, and the last day of that period. Unless he has been answered <note>legally responded to by the occupant</note> during that time, he is to cross the border of the land at the end of the first ten days, leading two horses by their bridles and accompanied by a witness. Legal redress is due to him at the end of five days within the first ten-day period, and at the beginning of the middle ten-day period, and he shall remain inside the land for a day and a night. If he is not responded to then, he is to go out during the period of the middle ten days, and legal redress is due to him at the end of five days of that middle ten-day period; and he shall serve a notice<gloss>ᵇ</gloss> upon the defendant during the period of the middle ten days.

<vocab>Noble tribes, possession of land, Brehon Law, cairde, requisites, middle entry, notice, stay of ten days</vocab>

It emphasizes that a first entry only establishes a preliminary right, while the second entry is necessary for legal possession.</summary>

# 4 OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.

<margin>OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.</margin> **The** middle ten-day period <note>original: "dechmaide medonaige" — a ten-day interval in the legal process</note>; or, it may be on the first day, the middle day, and the last day. If the claim is not responded to, he goes in at the end of the middle ten-day period and at the beginning of the last ten-day period, to a third of the land, bringing four horses and two witnesses with him. Notice is given every day during the duration of the middle ten-day period; or it may be on the first day, the middle day, and the last day. If it is not responded to, he goes out, and notice is given to the defendant every day while he is outside during the duration of the last ten-day period. If it is still not responded to, he goes in at the end of the last ten-day period until he reaches half the land, with eight horses and three witnesses with him; and half of these are to be of the noble grades and half of the commoner grades. If law is not granted to him before going in, he is not acting illegally even though he does not come out until he finds out whether the land is his or not his. And if he is certain that law would not be granted to him before going in, he is not acting illegally even if he does not give notice, but simply carries out the taking of possession.

---

->**E**ntry over a boundary, the first entry; the legality of lawful<-
->possession; entry of two long, thick ten-days; the legality of<-
->the clearing of possession.<-

**Entry over a boundary**, that is, over a ditch; or a chariot in the entry of land without notice. **The legality of lawful possession**, that is, the law of the occupancy of the land belongs to him for that act. **Entry of two long, thick ten-days**, that is, the taking of possession that is carried out after the two "long, thick" <note>likely referring to the cumulative or heavy nature of the legal requirements</note> ten-day periods, namely the middle ten-day period and the last ten-day period. **Long thick**, that is, it is a long time they are occupied with it. **Legality of the clearing of possession**, that is, it is the law of the established occupancy of the land for him.

---

<margin>O'D. 409.</margin> **Ninne** son of Matech with a group went north into the territory of Ulster; three horsemen seeking a friend, and they unyoked <note>original: "scoirset" — to unyoke or release horses, a formal act of claiming rights to land</note> their horses in land that had been their kin's territory previously, so that there should be no narrowing of their portion <note>meaning they were asserting their full ancestral right</note> therein. Then the person who was on the land said: "Take your horses off the land." One of the two who were with Ninne said: "No man is greater than another when unyoking horses here; let there be no narrowing of the portion here." It is not easy... it was always free... there would not be one person there. They did not know... land...

*Entry over a wall, i.e. over a fence; or, according to others, to bring a chariot in an entry upon land without forewarning. This concerns a man whose cattle were taken by force from his land. <term>Conchobar Mac Nessa<gloss>A legendary King of Ulster celebrated in Irish lore as a wise judge</gloss></term> subsequently passed judgment on it, and he gave a decision of "un-neighborliness" <note>original: "ecaireteċta," meaning a breach of the legal duties neighbors owed one another</note> against the person who took the cattle from the land; he ordered the restitution of what was taken and an equivalent compensation, and that they should both hold the land in common because of that entry.

> There are seven holdings in <term>Feini law<gloss>the customary law of the free Irish farmers</gloss></term> where <term>distraint<gloss>the legal seizure of property to settle a debt</gloss></term> is not taken, and where one does not bring cattle for an entry; it is a "truth of concluding." <note>original: "is fir in do loingaḋ," a technical term for a final legal determination</note> It is right to recover its seizure and its entry; a fort without property; a church without a precinct; land upon which there was division; a place of cattle disease; a sea-island where one does not bring cattle; a security for the rent of a <term>Nemidh<gloss>a person of privileged status, such as a cleric or high noble</gloss></term>; land which a lord divides after the death of a tenant, where a hole is dug and a stone is placed.

**There are seven holdings**—that is, there are seven types of land of which the laws of the <term>Feine</term> speak, in which distraint is not required, and it is more difficult to bring a claim of possession into them. **One does not bring cattle**—that is, cattle are not brought for the purpose of taking possession. **It is a truth**—that is, it is a truth that is adjudicated or concluded in them, regarding the taking of possession. **Rightfully levied**—that is, it is rightfully or quickly recovered. **Its seizure**—that is, distraint. **Its entry**—that is, the act of taking legal possession. **A fort without property**—that is, without land belonging to it, such as "Dun Araill." **A church without a precinct**—that is, like the church of "Gabhrin." **Land upon which there was division**—that is, where the cattle were not killed <note>original: "ar nar marba na hinḃille," possibly referring to land where animals were not allowed to stay due to specific legal partitions</note>. **A place of cattle disease**—that is, a location of a "bar" <note>original: "bairleac," explained here as "bar-loc" or a place of disease</note> where there are cattle; a place where they are "barred" or die because of a plague. **A sea-island**—that is, a lasting island out at sea, or where the sea is dangerous, such as <term>Inis Cathaigh<gloss>Scattery Island in the Shannon</gloss></term>; <note>original: "oṁun a mḃataḋ," fear of drowning going to or from it</note> because of the difficulty of bringing cattle into it. **Where one does not bring cattle**—that is, cattle are not brought there for entry without a boat. **Security**—that is, the thing by which the rent of a privileged person is truly secured, such as the land of <term>Maghain<gloss>Tir-Maghain</gloss></term> or the Road of Adamair; that is, land which a person holds for which rent is due, and...

There are seven types of land among the <term>Feini<gloss>the free classes of ancient Ireland</gloss></term> into which <term>distraint<gloss>the legal seizure of property to satisfy a debt</gloss></term> is not taken, and where cattle are not brought for the purpose of legal entry; in these cases, it is men who are required to enter. The seizure and the entry are executed quickly; these lands include: a <term>dun-fort<gloss>a fortified residence</gloss></term> without land; a church without a green; land occupied by plunderers; a place of deadly cattle plague; an island in the sea to which cattle are brought; *land which secures the rent of a <term>Nemidh-person<gloss>a person of high status, such as a cleric, poet, or noble</gloss></term>*; and land which the chief divides after the death of the tenant, where a hole is dug and a stone is placed.

**There are seven lands**, that is, there are seven types of land mentioned in the <term>Feinechus<gloss>the body of traditional Irish law</gloss></term> into which it is not lawful to bring cattle to perform <term>distraint</term> or to take lawful possession. **Cattle are not brought**, meaning livestock are not used to signify the taking of lawful possession of those specific lands. **It is men**, meaning that it is men who are permitted or required to be brought into them to take lawful possession. **Quickly are seized upon**, meaning the legal seizure is performed swiftly. **Exaction**, that is, the act of distraint or lawful seizure. **Entry**, that is, the legalized taking of possession. **A ‘dun’-fort without land**, meaning a fortification lacking an attached estate, such as <note>original: "Dun Araill"</note> Fort Araill. **A church without a green**, such as <note>original: "Cell Gabhrin," likely Kilgauren</note> Gabhrin’s Church. **A land on which there are plunderers**, meaning a place where the cattle have already been killed. **A deadly place**, that is, a place of death where there is a murrain (disease) of cows, referred to as a "death-place" <note>original: "bas-loc"</note>; a place where livestock are carried off by death through a plague or a place where disease is prevalent. **An island in the sea**, meaning a dangerous island located in the ocean, or where the sea is treacherous, such as <note>original: "Inis Cathaigh"</note> Scattery Island; there is a fear of the cattle being drowned while traveling to or from it because of the difficulty of the passage. **To which cattle are brought**, meaning cattle are not used for entry there without a boat. **Secures the rent**, meaning the specific property that guarantees the rent due to a <term>Nemidh-person</term>, such as <note>original: "Tir-Maghain"</note> Maghain’s Land or <note>original: "Rot-Adamairi"</note> Adamair’s Road. This refers to land where rent is due, for the cattle brought to it are 

forfeited to the King of <term>Caisel<gloss>Cashel, the seat of the Kings of Munster</gloss></term> on the day he assumes the kingship, because they had previously killed a king of Cashel. Regarding Adamair’s Road, there was once a serpent there, and <term>Mochuta<gloss>St. Carthage of Lismore</gloss></term> expelled it. The reward given to him for driving it out was that everything which the <term>Coarb<gloss>the successor or heir to the founding saint of a monastery</gloss></term> of Mochuta of <term>Lis-mor<gloss>Lismore, a major ecclesiastical center</gloss></term> could find on that land on the day he assumed the abbacy would become his property, for it is considered forfeit.

# ON TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.

<margin>
OF TAKING
**LAWFUL**
**POSSESSION.**
</margin>

The cattle of the entry <term>tellaċ<gloss>the formal legal act of entering land to claim ownership</gloss></term> are let in according to the right of a <term>Nemidh-person<gloss>a person of privileged status, such as a cleric, poet, or high noble</gloss></term>. <note>original: "Liċer ceiṫra in teallaiċ la cir a neiṁid"</note>. Cattle do not perform the entry where the chiefs are in their houses <note>meaning the land is already occupied or under direct supervision</note>. This refers to land of two chiefs, specifically land that the chief divides, known as "land of descendants" <term>tir uibad<gloss>land inherited by a family group</gloss></term>; or it is the "recovery of the kinsman-surety" <term>inbleoġain<gloss>a relative who is legally responsible for another's debts</gloss></term>, where the chief has his share within it, and since he is there with his retinue in his possession, once the land of inheritance is divided, it is not necessary to bring cattle in to take possession of it. A hole is dug—that is, a trench—where the hole is dug at the shared boundary of the land. A stone is placed there—that is, a <term>pillar-stone<gloss>a standing stone used as a boundary marker</gloss></term>—after it has been dug. This boundary stone, the hole, and the "witness-chiefs" are present so that each person’s share is found there.

If <term>distraint<gloss>the legal seizure of property</gloss></term> is taken upon these lands, there are fines of five <term>seods<gloss>units of value, often equal to half a dairy cow</gloss></term> whether it be for the fault of the guilty party or the kinsman-surety. Or, alternatively, there is a fine of five seods for the kinsman-surety, and nothing for the guilty party until they have committed a trespass; once a trespass is committed, there are five seods due from the guilty party. If cattle were brought here for the purpose of taking possession, the fine for taking possession of the land is paid according to whether the land is held with or without legal "sense" and "kinship" <note>referring to the legal status and mental capacity of the claimant</note>. The same number of cattle brought to take possession of other lands should be the number of oxen brought to take possession of these lands.

Cianacht took possession of distant lands; two <term>vats<gloss>units of measurement or perhaps ritual offerings</gloss></term> were then provided; she passed over the mound of her first entry; she asserted her claim over the family; she then drove the cattle according to the <term>Feinechus<gloss>traditional Irish law</gloss></term> for eight days with the evidence of the witnesses of her first entry, so that her first claim should not be sold. On the fourth day thereafter, she performed the legal entry of every woman's entry. She went afterwards to her head-land with double the vats of the change, with "extinguishing," with "protection," and with "western-property" <note>these terms likely refer to specific ritual or legal steps in claiming land</note>; she made a circuit with a man of superior testimony. Afterwards, a change of response was given, for there is a right to a fourth of the first, a different right for the middle, and a final decision for the last.

**Cianacht took possession:** that is, it is fittingly or quickly that <term>Cianacht<gloss>daughter of Fergus Forcraid, a legendary figure in this legal precedent</gloss></term> recovered the lands that were far from her—

# OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.

**LAWFUL**
**POSSESSION.**

Whosoever shall make entry <term>tellach<gloss>the formal legal ritual of entering land to claim ownership</gloss></term> shall be <term>distrained<gloss>legally seized of property to compel payment or performance of a duty</gloss></term> for the rent of the <term>Nemed-person<gloss>a person of privileged or sacred status, such as a noble or cleric</gloss></term>. It is not considered right that an entry by cattle be made there, out of respect for the dignity of the chief who owns the land. This applies to land which the chief divides—that is, the land which the chief distributes, known as <term>dibadh-land<gloss>land left behind by a deceased person without immediate heirs, which reverts to the kin-group or chief for redistribution</gloss></term>. Or, it may be in response to the legal obligations of a kinsman; in this case, the chief retains his share in it—meaning he does not give it up during his reign—and when he divides this inherited land, he is not required to bring the usual ritual means of taking possession into it. In places where a hole is made—that is, a mound or trench where a hole is sunk during the division of the land—and where a stone is placed—that is, a <term>pillar-stone<gloss>a standing stone used as a permanent boundary marker</gloss></term>—after the area is enclosed. There, a hole, a stone, and the chief’s own standing stone are present so that his specific share may be recognized.

If <term>distress<gloss>the legal seizure of property to settle a debt</gloss></term> is brought into *either* of these seven types of land, there are five <term>seods<gloss>units of value, often equal to the value of half a dairy cow</gloss></term> *due*, payable either by the guilty party or their kinsman-surety. Indeed, according to *other* authorities, the kinsman pays the five "seods," and nothing is due from the guilty party until actual damage occurs; once damage arises, then the guilty party must pay the five "seods." If cattle were brought in to take possession in this specific instance, the fine is for "lawful actual-possession of land" with a chief and tribe, or land without a chief or tribe. The same number of cattle required to take possession of other lands is the same number of men that must be brought to take possession of these specific lands.

<margin>a Irish: In.</margin>
Ciannacht took possession <note>original: "Ciannacht gabail"</note> of a distant farm. To do so, she arranged two ewes there; she passed over the mound-fence as her first entry. She challenged the tribe to come to a legal agreement with *her regarding her land*. Afterward, according to the <term>Feinechus<gloss>the ancient body of Irish customary law</gloss></term>, she remained for eight days with women acting as witnesses for the occasion of her first entry, to prove that she did not "sell her first modesty" <note>meaning she acted with legal integrity and followed proper social protocol to protect her reputation</note>. It is only four days after this that every woman’s entry onto land is considered lawful. She later returned to the edge of her land with double the amount of livestock, a kneading trough, a sieve, and a baking implement <note>these domestic items were legal symbols of permanent settlement and "keeping house"</note>. In due order, she claimed her rights with a man acting as a witness. If her claim is responded to afterward, she is entitled to four days for her first *suit*, two days for her middle suit, *and* for her final suit, she is entitled to a speedy judgment.

**Sencha delivered a judgment** <note>Original: "Beartaid Sencha"</note>; that is, Sencha, in his capacity as the first of the judges, had judged the legal entry of women to be exactly the same as the legal entry of men. **So that the blotches**; that is, so that blisters broke out upon his cheeks after delivering the crooked judgments; that is, after [his] false rulings.

**Brig restored** <note>Original: "Hicrai Brig"</note>; that is, Brig, daughter of Sencha, corrected the matter according to justice and her own true judgment. **It is she who decided**; that is, it is she who determined the specific rules for the legal entry of women. **So that the blotches**; that is, so that they subsided; that is, the swellings of the blisters on his cheeks vanished after she delivered the true judgments; and it is for this reason that it is observed, that if any man should be mocked or disgraced for a false judgment, or any other dispute, once it is known that a relative has delivered the true and lawful praise afterward, or if he himself accepts that rightful ruling, it is the same for him as if he had delivered it correctly himself.<sup>1</sup> **Removed**; that is, they were made to sink away.

And the judgment she gave was that women should have their own specific form of legal entry <note>Brig argued that women's entry should be faster or have different requirements than men's to be fair.</note>. And from this it is clear that whatever dispute or arrogance a person may commit, if a friend or relative of theirs should take up the matter on their behalf [and fix it], it is as if they had done it themselves.

<margin>

**Brig**, through her commitment to justice and her accurate rulings, healed him; it was she who established the specific rules for **women taking possession of land** <note>Original: "banteallach," a ritualized legal process where a woman enters land to claim ownership</note>, so that the **blotches** <note>Original: "fearba," supernatural blisters believed to appear on the face of a judge who delivers a false or biased ruling</note> on his <note>Sencha's</note> cheeks were hidden and healed after the rightful judgments were delivered.

**Sencha delivered a judgment**; that is, Sencha ruled in his first decision that the procedure for a woman taking possession of land should be exactly the same as the procedure for a man. **So that there were blotches**; that is, so that blisters erupted on his cheeks after he had passed a biased judgment; that is, after delivering partial or unfair rulings.

**Brig cured him**; that is, Brig, daughter of Sencha, healed him through the integrity of her own true judgment. **It is she that established**; that is, she formulated the specific legal requirements for a woman’s claim to land. **So that the blotches**; that is, they subsided; that is, the swelling of the blisters vanished once the true judgment was passed. From this case, a general rule is derived: even if a person composes a **satire** <note>In ancient Irish law, a satire was not just a poem but a legal injury that could cause physical harm or loss of status</note> or causes other harm to another, if a relative of the offender later composes a **eulogium** <note>A poem of praise or a formal legal restoration of honor</note>, the praise nullifies the previous insult. Similarly, if a relative makes amends for an injury, it is legally treated as if the offender had repaired the damage himself.<sup>1</sup> **Concealed**; that is, they were made invisible or removed.

In essence, the judgment Sencha passed was that a woman’s method of taking possession should be identical to a man’s, and as a result, blisters rose on his face as a sign of his error. The wisdom of Brig healed him. The ruling she gave was that women should have their own distinct ritual for taking possession. This demonstrates that whenever someone attempts to cause legal damage, if a friend or relative undoes that harm, the law views it as if the person had corrected it themselves.

**Seither**<sup>2</sup> claimed the lands which the leaders of her tribe had occupied. She was a **woman of two races** <note>This likely refers to her having parents from different legal classes or different tribes, affecting her inheritance status</note> who was entitled to the land, and she demanded that her claim not be treated according to the customs applied to slaves or those who have been dispossessed. She was released from certain obligations by her tribe because the rights of female possession eventually revert back to the tribe.

<margin>
a Irish: Chariot.
</margin>

**Claimed**; that is, she challenged the status quo. Specifically, **Sithir**<sup>3</sup>, the daughter of Menn and Gabhair—the noble <note>The margin note "a" suggests the original text used a word for chariot ("fén"), perhaps implying "chariot-daughter" or a high-ranking woman</note> daughter of Menn—claimed the lands which the chiefs of her tribe had taken.

She had a son by him named Nia MacAnluain. Sithir claimed her share of land from her brothers, namely Ailill 'Red-Half' and Aengus Aigle. # ON TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION
## VOLUME IV. C

<margin>
OF TAKING
LAWFUL
POSSESSION.
</margin>

**Of the kindred** <note>Original: "ceneoil"</note>. **Possession is established** <note>Original: "Teċtair"</note>; that is, the way is prepared, or the boundary stones are set in place. **She was of double-taking**; that is, I see or I observe that she is a woman who is descended from two branches, for her father was of the **Ulstermen** <note>The people of the Ulaid, a major tribal group in ancient Ireland</note> and her mother was of the **Féni of Tara** <note>The Féni were the free, land-owning class governed by the common laws of Ireland</note>. **Woman-entry of the territory**; that is, she was an honorable woman in the territory that is being entered, or she was a friend to it; that is, she was entitled to enter the territory that is being claimed. 

**She shall not be under the customs of labor**; that is, she shall not be subject to the typical or pleasant duties <note>Footnote 1: The manuscript uses a contraction "biaṫṛ" which likely means "shall not feed," referring to the legal obligation of biathadh or providing hospitality to others</note> of **warding off and attacking** <note>Original: "oc ḟuḃa ocus oc ruḃa," a standard legal phrase for the military and defensive duties of a landowner</note> for the whole tribe; that is, she shall not be the **head of the tribe** <note>Original: "aiġi ḟine"</note> or of anyone at all, but only for her own household; that is, she shall not be responsible for hospitality here and there at the end of the land; that is, there shall be no tax or maintenance burden upon her, nor shall she provide food for the youths of the territory or the fortress, but only the specific payments required by law. 

**On the designated roads**; that is, she shall not be hindered on or upon the road without her half-share, and without the duties of warding off and attacking. **They are made free by the tribe**; that is, their right to join the land of the tribe is affirmed in that manner. **Because it is a female-inheritance that remains**; that is, under the grace which is the inheritance for which the land is rightfully recovered afterward, regarding giving it all to her with the duties of warding off and attacking, or giving her half-share without those duties; or under the grace which is the inheritance for which the land is rightfully recovered from her after her time; that is, there was a security given to them for its recovery.

**It is perceived by the observation of those who perform the entry.** There are **three ten-day periods** <note>Original: "teora deaċma-ḋaiḃ," periods of ten days used as legal waiting times in Irish law</note> of law, if it be a short time in which it is contested; from a **unit of value** <note>Original: "cumal," originally meaning a female slave, but used as a standard unit of currency or land-value</note> up to thirty, with the nine-fold observation of the entry, even if it be double the amount of land.

**Two horses in hand at the border of the single property** <note>Footnote 2: "Leaṫ aen realḃa" refers to the ritual act of bringing horses to the edge of the land to claim possession</note>, with **worthy witnesses** <note>Original: "ḟiaḋnaiġe indruic"</note>, and the law is brought to her for her right, if it be **family inheritance** <note>Original: "ḟeineċar," land held under the common tribal law of the Féni</note>. 

If it be not family inheritance, perform the entry after a delay upon the tenth day, with **four horses** driven to the border of the property with **two worthy witnesses**; the share of the contract is divided; three days are required by law if it be family inheritance. 

If it be not family inheritance, perform the entry after a delay on the next tenth day, with **eight horses** driven to the tribal property, with **three worthy witnesses** from the grades of the Féni. The share of the contract is divided. It is the beginning of the legal decision between them, if it be family inheritance. If it be not family inheritance—

**Taken possession of**; that is, she established the boundaries, or they placed pillar-stones there. **She was a woman of two lineages**; that is, I hold or insist that she was descended from two races, her father being of the **Ulstermen** <note>original: "Ulta," the people of the northern province of Ulaid</note>, and her mother of the **Féni of Tara** <note>original: "Feini of Teamhair." The Féni were the free, land-owning class governed by the common laws of Ireland, and Tara was the symbolic high seat of Irish kingship</note>. **Entitled to the land**; that is, she was directly entitled to the land which she loved, or which was dear to her; that is, she was justly entitled to the land which she cherished. **That it should not be after the custom of servants**; that is, that she should not, according to the traditional knowledge, be bound to perform the military services of **attack and defence** <note>original: "oc fuba ocus oc ruba," a standard legal phrase for the military duties of a landowner</note> for the entire territory. There shall be neither rent nor maintenance burden upon her, nor shall she provide meals for the guests of the territory nor of the **fortified residence** <term>Dun: a royal or noble fort</term>, but every such tax is removed from her. **Or dispossessed persons**; that is, she was not removed from the land without receiving one-half of it without being obliged to perform the military services of attack and defence. **She was freed by her tribe**; that is, she was released from the true obligations of the lands of the tribe in that manner. **Because female possession reverts**; that is, because it is a type of property where the land is to be eventually restored to the male line. This is why she was given the whole of it without the obligation of military service, or half of it without military service; because it is property which must **revert** <note>original: "revert"</note> from her after a set term; that is, there was a legal guarantee for restoring it.

# 20. Of Taking Lawful Possession.

<margin>
OF TAKING
LAWFUL
POSSESSION.
</margin>
**Taking lawful possession**; that is, a payment of value [established] with grass, with food, with fire <note>original: "tein," signifying the establishment of a hearth</note>, with residence, and with the tending of cattle; except for the common land of the first contract, or the casting out from land which is a sanctuary <note>original: "nemead," land belonging to the church or a privileged class that was exempt from common legal entry</note>. It is through this [form of] entry that every possession is established among the **Féni** <note>original: "feine," the free, land-owning classes of early Ireland</note>.

**The enclosure of the land to be entered**, in which one thing is acknowledged as value—namely, goods; it is paid, if it be with lowing cattle, a **cumal** <term>Cumal: a standard unit of value in early Irish law, originally worth one female slave or three cows</term> is guaranteed for it. Unless the land is under the legal possession of another, without commonality or kinship, the ownership of the cattle is transferred.

---

**Doighin, that you may know**; that is, her son; Nin said to Doighin, "so that you may know, or that there may be with you the beautiful or pleasant knowledge of taking possession according to the **Fénechas** <note>the traditional body of Irish law</note>." Nin said this here to Doighin, the son of the wise Ulsterman. **In three periods of ten days**, that is, the law of taking possession is within the three periods of ten days, or it is after the three periods of ten days that it is required of him to bring his whole herd into it. **If it be with satisfaction**, that is, if his own status is equal, or if he is consulted by the wise, it is in this way he shall act. **From the value of a cumal**, that is, when there is property of mine from the land worth a *cumal* up to the portion which is thirty *cumals*, and whether that be of a known person or an unknown person; that is, whether it be land of one *cumal* or land of thirty *cumals*, it is the same single procedure that is here for entry. **But one procedure**, that is, it is a portion according to the beautiful or pleasant knowledge of the law of taking possession. **Though it be double the land he completes**, that is, though it be double what he completes throughout its length, it is in that way it shall be.

**Two horses in hand**; that is, two horses led by hand as far as the half-boundary of the land, and let there be no <unclear>interruption of his presence</unclear> there, and let there be a witnessing of the grass being consumed immediately around the land; that is, the half-grass of the possession, or in the portion [of the possession] of the half-ridge, for the consumption of the grass only. The "full-grass," however, is the possession where a man consumes both grass and corn; a "half-wounding" [partial claim], however, is the possession when nothing is consumed but grass or corn only. **Half-arable**; that is, between the ditch and the plowing. **Witnessing of the breach**; that is, witnessing the breach of his kinship-land, so that it was legally he entered into the land. **Five for the law, if the law-tract be yours**; that is, if there be a deviation from the law of the **Féne**—

OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.

...[if it] be not the **Fénechas** <note>original: "Feinechus," the traditional common law of Ireland</note>, lawful possession is granted; its value is to be offered with sheds, cows, food, habitation, and the presence of cattle, except in the case of the land of **Conn of the Hundred Contracts** <note>original: "Conn Cetcorach," a legendary High King; here referring to a specific legal precedent or territory</note>, or land devoted to the support of a residence belonging to a **Nemed**-person <note>original: "Nemeadh," a person of privileged status, such as a cleric, poet, or lord, whose land had special protections</note>. 

<margin>
By means of.
</margin>
It is through this kind of entry that all land is seized by the **Féni** <note>original: "Feini," the free-born class of land-owning farmers</note>.

In an entry upon land that is fenced, the property value does not increase equally in **séts** <note>original: "seds," a unit of value typically worth half a cow</note>; it is decided that if he takes possession with cattle, a **cumal** <term>Cumal: a standard unit of value, originally equal to a female slave or three cows</term> is the amount mentioned. Unless it is a case of lawful possession in land without a chief and without a tribe, the cows that are brought onto the land are forfeited.

> **Doighin, do you know?** <note>This begins a traditional teaching dialogue between a father and son</note>—that is, her son; Nin said to Doighin, "that you may know, or that you may have pleasant or delightful knowledge of taking lawful possession according to the **Fénechas**." Nin said this to Doighin, who was the son of a wise man of the **Ulstermen** <note>original: "Ulta"</note>. **In thrice ten days**, that is, in three periods of ten days, the legal right of possession is to be granted, or it is after these thirty days that he is required to bring all his cattle there. **If you consult wisdom**, that is, if you consult your own wisdom or confer with wise men, this is how you will act. **From land of one "cumal,"** that is, as I am treating of land ranging in value from one **cumal** to thirty **cumals**; and this is a case of "certainty for uncertainty," meaning whether it is land worth one **cumal** or thirty, the custom for the entry is the same. It is one custom; the law of possession is the same according to this pleasant knowledge. **Though the length of the "foirge"-measure should be doubled** <note>original: "foirge," a specific linear measurement of land</note>, that is, even if the **foirge**-measure is doubled throughout, the law remains the same.
>
> **Two horses in hand**, that is, he is to have two horses held by the bridles in his hand until he reaches the border of the land. It is not permitted to unharness them there; if they are unharnessed immediately upon the land, there is a fine of five **séts**, which is half the "freedom" of the land. Alternatively, the old land is considered "half free" if only its grass is eaten, but it is "fully free" if both its grass and corn are consumed; the land is half free if only the grass or the corn alone is eaten. **Border**, that is, the area between the boundary mound and the tilled soil. **Worthy witness**, that is, a pure witness to see that he entered the land lawfully. **That his legal right be granted to him, if there be Fénechas**, that is, if the usage of the law [is followed].

# 24 CONCERNING LAWFUL POSSESSION.

<margin>OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.</margin> Two types of taking possession are recognized here. This pertains to a **Nemed** <term>Nemed: a person of high social or legal status, such as a noble, cleric, or master-poet</term>, that is, it concerns the land from which rent is due to a **Nemed**, such as the lands of Tir Mugain or Rot Comain. <gloss>1</gloss> It is through this **entry** <term>tellach: the formal, ritualized legal act of entering onto land to claim ownership</term>, that is, through this method of taking possession, that all land is recovered into which cattle are brought to take possession according to the **Fénechas** <note>original: "fenechais," the traditional common law of ancient Ireland</note>.

Fences of the land, that is, taking possession of the land where there are fences. It is not the same increase of wealth for anyone to take possession of land with fences <gloss>2</gloss> and in land without fences. That is, I do not consider it the same increase of wealth for the owner of the land regarding the payment for taking possession of the land with a fence around it versus one without a fence, but rather more is given when there is a fence around it; or, I do not consider it the same increase for the man who is brought to take possession whether he brings horses with shoes <gloss>3</gloss> or without horses with shoes, but more is given when he has horses with shoes. If it be with cattle, that is, if it is with the cattle that the "cow-entry" <note>The ritual of taking possession involved bringing specific animals (horses or cows) onto the property in stages.</note> is performed for taking possession. A **cumal** <term>cumal: a standard unit of value, usually worth three cows, but here specifically valued at six cows</term> of six cows is the compensation for it; that is, a **cumal** of six cows is fixed for taking possession of land without a contract <note>original: "cunn"</note> and without kinship <note>original: "coibne"</note>. Unless it be under a claim of previous ownership; that is, unless it is said that it was his own land that he had taken possession of, it is in that case this applies. Without a contract, that is, without a binding agreement. Without kinship, that is, without being related by blood or legal ties—namely, the "holy and the stiff" <note>A legal metaphor for different types of kin or legal relationships.</note>. Forfeiture of the cattle brought, that is, the forfeiture of the cattle brought in the unlawful taking of possession, in addition to the **cumal** mentioned before.

->That is, this is a **cumal** of six cows, and it is the same whether it is taking possession of land with contract and kinship, or even taking possession of land without contract and kinship; or otherwise, it is a **cumal** of six cows for taking possession of land without contract and kinship, and a **cumal** of three cows in the other type of taking possession.<-

If it be over a full fence for the high-ranking classes, and it is land without contract or kinship, there is a **cumal** and forfeiture of the numbered cattle. If it be over a half fence, it is three-quarters of a **cumal** and three-quarters of the numbered cattle. If there is no fence at all, it is half a **cumal** and half the numbered cattle. A numbered fine only for the low-ranking classes, as we have said, and a half **cumal** if it be by the **Cáin** law <note>The "Cáin" refers to a higher level of statutory law, often ecclesiastical or provincial, as opposed to the local "Fénechas."</note>. If it be land with contract and kinship, there is forfeiture of the numbered cattle plus a **cumal** for entering over a full fence, three-quarters for a half fence, and half for no fence at all; and this is the same for both low-ranking and high-ranking classes.

If it be through ignorance that he did not know it was land with a contract, a half-fine is due from him, or the same as for land with a contract.

***

<gloss>1</gloss> Which belongs to a **Nemed** person. The reading in another manuscript is "or the rent of a **Nemed**, that is, land from which it is due."
<gloss>2</gloss> With fences around it. The phrase "crui ime" may also mean "a fence which is a paling."
<gloss>3</gloss> Of horses. The word "ech" was not translated by the scholar Dr. O'Donovan: it is here rendered "horses," its meaning in modern Irish, a meaning also found frequently in the Brehon Laws. That horses were required for taking possession in some cases is evident from this and several other passages in the present tract.

<margin>

...such as Dun Araill <note>An ancient place-name associated with legal precedents</note>, for it is persons that are brought to take possession of it. This pertains to a **Nemed**-person <term>Nemed: a person of high social or legal status, such as a noble, cleric, or master-poet</term>, that is, the land through which the rent of the **Nemed**-person is truly secured to him, such as Tir Mughain or Rot Admairi. It is by means of this **entry** <term>tellach: the formal, ritualized legal act of entering onto land to claim ownership</term>, that is, by this form of taking possession, that every land is taken possession of into which cattle are brought to legalize the possession according to the **Fénechas** <term>Fénechas: the traditional customary law of ancient Ireland</term>.

<margin>Before us. <note>original: "Ir. Befor us"</note></margin>
Land which has **fences**, that is, an entry made upon land that is enclosed by fences. The **increase of wealth** is not equal; that is, the property increase (or penalty) is not the same for one who has made entry into land with fences as it is for land without fences. I do not consider the value to be the same regarding the increase of wealth to the owner of the land—specifically in the payment of **seds** <term>sed: a unit of value, often equivalent to a young heifer</term> to him—for taking lawful possession of land with fences around it versus land without fences; more is given for land with fences. Furthermore, I do not deem the increase to be the same for a man who brings the means of taking possession using horses as for one who does so without horses, but the value is higher when he uses horses. If it be with **kine**, that is, if he enters with cows to perform the ritual of taking lawful possession. A **cumal** <term>cumal: a high unit of value, originally representing a female slave but later equal to three or six cows</term> is mentioned—specifically, a **cumal** worth six cows is mentioned as the fine for taking possession of land that lacks a chief or a tribe alliance. Unless it be in a **lawful possession**, that is, if the claimant asserts it is his own land that he has entered, this rule applies. **Without a chief**, meaning without a chief belonging to the same tribe. **Without a tribe**, meaning without a legal agreement, such as one overseen by saints and just men. The cows which are brought for the entry are forfeited—that is, the cattle used as an unlawful means of taking possession are seized, along with the six-cow **cumal** fine mentioned before.

<margin>With. <note>original: "Ir. With"</note></margin>
<margin>Without. <note>original: "Ir. Without"</note></margin>
That is, this is a **cumal** of the value of six cows, and this is equally given as the **fine** for taking possession of land which **has** a chief and a tribe, or for taking possession of land which **has not** a chief and a tribe; or, according to other authorities, it is a **cumal** of the value of six cows for taking possession of land without a chief and tribe, and a **cumal** worth only three cows for the other type of possession.

<margin>For the nobles. <note>original: "Ir. For the nobles"</note></margin>
<margin>For. <note>original: "Ir. For"</note></margin>
If the **nobles** have entered over a full fence, and it is land which does not have a chief and a tribe, **the fine** is one **cumal** and forfeiture of the stock used for entry. If they have entered over a half-fence, the fine is three-quarters of a **cumal** and three-fourths of the stock. If **they have entered on land which has no fence at all**, the fine is half a **cumal** and half the stock. For **plebeians** <note>commoners or those of lower legal standing</note>, only the stock is to be divided in the same proportions, and half a **cumal** is the **fine if the case falls under Cáin-law** <term>Cáin: statutory or proclamatory law, often carrying stricter penalties than customary law</term>. If it be land that has a chief and a tribe, the penalty is forfeiture of the stock along with a **cumal** fine if the entrance was over a full fence, three-quarters of a **cumal** if over a half-fence, and one-half if there was no fence at all; this applies equally to both plebeians and nobles.

If it was unknown to the person **who entered** that the land did not have a chief, only half the fine is paid by him, or the same rate as if the land had a chief.

Another form: If it be land held with a contract and with relationship <note>Kinship ties between the claimant and the occupier</note>, if there be cattle [or fences]¹, the penalty is one **cumal** <term>cumal: a standard unit of value in ancient Ireland, originally the value of a female slave, later equated to three milk-cows</term>; if there be not, it is half a **cumal**, and that is common between the low-born and the high-born. # 27 Concerning Taking Lawful Possession.

<margin>
OF TAKING

<margin>
a Irish: "With"
</margin>
Another version—If it be land that has<sup>a</sup> a chief and a tribe <note>Meaning land held within a recognized social structure of kinship and lordship</note>, and if there are cattle <note>The term often implies land that is "stocked" or properly fenced</note>, the fine is one **cumal** <term>cumal: a primary unit of value in ancient Ireland, equivalent to three milk-cows</term>; if there be not cattle, the fine is a half **cumal**, and this applies equally to both the commoner and the noble. Should he seize in one day a lawful number of people, horses, and cows, they are all forfeited up to the value of a **cumal**, provided there are cattle on the land.

If there be not cattle, the fine is half a **cumal**. If he brings cows and horses, and the value is less than one **cumal**, the forfeiture of the livestock is the "mercy" of the case <note>A legal leniency where only the specific animals used in the trespass are seized</note>, if there be cattle; if there be not, the penalty is half-forfeiture of the stock plus a full **cumal** in the severity of the law, if there be cattle. If there be not cattle, the penalty is half a **cumal**.

<margin>
b Irish: "Without"
</margin>
In the case of land that has not<sup>b</sup> a chief and a tribe <note>Referring to "unclaimed" or lawless land, or land where the occupier has no kin-group to defend the title</note>, if there be cattle, the penalty for a noble is a **cumal**-fine and the forfeiture of his stock; if there be not cattle, it is a half **cumal** and the forfeiture of half the stock. If the entry was made by commoners with stock, it is a full forfeiture of the stock. If there be not cattle, it is forfeiture of one-half the stock.

### Unless it be into lawful land.

That is, unless he acts on the assumption that the land is his own when he brings his requirements for taking possession of land that has not<sup>b</sup> a chief and a tribe, both in **Cain-law** <term>Cain-law: universal or statutory law, often applying to all of Ireland</term> and in **Urradhus-law** <term>Urradhus-law: local customary law or the law of a specific territory</term>, i.e., unless he seizes land by force only.

> *In the case of land that has not a chief and a tribe, the kine <note>cattle</note> which are brought thither are forfeited.²*

That is, land which has not a head of a tribe—meaning well-wishers of the tribe—meaning land without relatives, inhabited by fierce and lawless people. The penalty is the forfeiture of the cattle brought to take unlawful possession, together with the **cumal** mentioned before, whether the claimants be commoners or nobles. That is, all the cattle are forfeited. When it is land without a chief or a tribe, the penalty is the forfeiture of the stock and three **seds** <term>sed: a unit of value, usually half a cumal or the value of a heifer</term> as compensation for the grass consumed. 

According to others, it is three **seds** only when three days are not allowed after it is proven that the land is not the claimant’s, and the penalty for theft is the cause of this; but when the penalty is both forfeiture of cattle and the three **seds**, there was a perfect fence then; if, however, there was only a half-fence, the penalty is forfeiture of one-half of the stock.

# OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.

<margin>OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.</margin>
...with his cattle, and the neighbors say that the law of the land is that a judgment be given for him to enter into a third of the land. A cow, a heifer, and a yearling heifer <note>original: *dairtais* — a young heifer of about two years</note> are what they pay as the value of the grazing of the land; and they are cast out after three days, and his crime <note>meaning the legal liability or fine</note> follows him; and this applies if it is land of kin-relationship <note>original: *coibne*</note> to him, for it is likely that law is law; if it be land without kin-relationship, however, it is forfeiture of the counted stock, as we have said.

There are three types of road-men: a road-man seeking his property, a road-man pressing hard for his property, and a king’s road-man; and the reason he is called the man of the king’s road is because his portion of the road-feast is with him, and because of his commonality. When <term>distraint <note>original: *athgabail* — the legal seizure of property to compel someone to fulfill a legal obligation</note></term> is sought to be taken from the road-men—excepting the king—a notice of five days is required for the road-man of chieftain rank, and a notice of one day for the road-man of commoner rank, as we said above <note>original: *ut supra diximus*</note>.

When the law requires forfeiture of the counted stock from everyone else, it is only three <term>valuables <note>original: *seoit* — standard units of value, often young cows</note></term> from the road-men. This is the "severity" of the law; the "mercy," however, is that he pays whichever is less: the forfeiture of the counted stock or the three valuables, so that only one is taken from him. Or, three valuables are taken from the road-men, and forfeiture of the counted stock from everyone else for taking possession as far as a third of the holding.

<margin>O'Donovan MS 419.</margin> [The road-man is safe <note>legally exempt from certain penalties</note> though he goes to a third of the holding in land of "sense" and kin-relationship, even if he does not give notice, because there is no land to support him during the time of notice; three valuables are charged against him if he goes further, or if he stays there past three days after legal notice was given to him. And this applies to land after a refusal, and it is half-fine if there be no cattle.]

his cattle, and his neighbors say the land is his, and judges tell him to go as far as one-third of the land. He shall pay a cow, a <term>three-year-old heifer <note>original: *samhaise*</note></term>, and a <term>yearling heifer <note>original: *dartaigh*</note></term> as the price for grazing the land; and he shall be ejected after three days if he fails to establish his claim. This applies to land to which he thinks he has a <term>hereditary right <note>original: *coibhne* — a right to the land by descent through kinship</note></term>, for he believes it is his; but if it be land to which he has no hereditary right, the penalty is the <term>forfeiture of his stock <note>meaning the loss of the cattle used to make the legal entry onto the land</note></term>, as we have stated previously.

There are three *sorts* of <term>road-men <note>original: *raitech* — a person traveling the roads, often a claimant or a person of a specific legal status</note></term>: a road-man who falls into failure, a road-man who deserts in the face of failure, and the king as a road-man. The reason that the king is called a "road-man" is because he owns a share of the <term>waifs <note>unclaimed goods or property found on the road</note></term> found on his road, and also because of his generosity. When <term>distress <note>the legal seizure of property to settle a debt</note></term> is involved, it is considered appropriate to take from the road-men—except for the king. A notice of two days is served on a road-man of the <term>chieftain grade</term>, and a notice of one day on a road-man of the <term>commoner grade <note>original: *Feini*</note></term>, <note>original: *ut supra diximus* — as we have said above</note>.

When the law requires the forfeiture of stock from *all others*, the road-men are required to pay only three <term>valuables <note>original: *séds* — standard units of value, often young cows</note></term>. This represents the "severity" of the case; however, the "leniency" of the law is that he shall pay whichever is less: the forfeiture of the stock or the three valuables. Or, *according to other authorities*, three valuables *are due* from the road-men, while forfeiture of the stock is required from *all others* who have come to take possession of up to a third of the land.

<margin>
*a* Irish: *With.*
</margin>
It is legally safe for the road-man even if he enters as far as a third of the land in a territory that has a chief and a tribe, even if he has not given formal notice. This is because the land is not supporting him during the notice period. However, he faces a fine of three valuables if he goes further, or if he remains there for more than three days after satisfying the legal requirements. *This rule applies when he crosses over a fence; if there is no fence, the fine is reduced to one-half of the three valuables.*

<margin>
*b* Irish: *Without.*
</margin>
If it is land that does *not* have a chief and a tribe, he incurs the forfeiture of his stock just like everyone else. Or, *according to others*, the penalty is calculated proportionally: the ratio of the three valuables to the <term>unit of value <note>original: *cumhal* — a standard ancient Irish unit of value, originally equivalent to a bondmaid, later valued at three cows</note></term> is the same as the ratio of his stock to the stock of *all others*. Or, *according to others, where stock is forfeited by everyone else, only three valuables are recovered from the road-man*. This is the "severity" of the case, but its "clemency" is that he pays whichever is less—the forfeiture of stock or the three valuables—for entering one-third of the land, while forfeiture of the stock remains the penalty for all others.

# OF LAWFUL ENTRY LONG-CONTINUED.

One does not sue for copper, nor silver, nor gold, except from a noble; one does not sue for the cattle of Cinnia <note>original: *buar ba Cinnia* — referring to a legendary figure said to have first brought cows to Ireland</note> from a person who has no cows; one does not sue for land from a wanderer, unless he has a foundation of possession; one does not sue for clothing from one who is naked, unless it increases his raiment; it is a "preparation without fruit" <note>original: *grethe cen toradh* — a legal metaphor for a futile or hollow action</note> which causes the destruction of judgment. It is the estimate that pledges the capability of everyone.

**One does not sue**, i.e., you should not sue for the silver, or the gold, or the copper except from the noble, for it is likely that they have it, or it is easier for them to obtain it. **One does not sue for cattle**, i.e., you should not sue for cattle like the cattle which Cinnia the merchant brought over <note>original: *taris* — across the sea</note> from a person who has no cows, or who would not be able to find them easily. **One does not sue for land**, i.e., you should not sue for land from one who is wandering from his place of residence, unless land is established by him, or unless he has land as a foundation. **From a wanderer**, i.e., from a lawless wayfarer. **One does not sue for clothing**, i.e., you should not sue for clothing from a person who is naked, unless he has clothing to cover him. **Unless it increases his raiment**, i.e., unless clothing is added to him promptly. **It is a preparation without fruit**, i.e., it is a thing that is according to the reason or the sense of the judgments; just as the appearance of a "blind nut" <note>original: *cnu caeich* — an empty nut shell</note> is without fruit inside it, so it is a void thing to do those acts. **It is the estimate that pledges**, i.e., it is the thing that has been estimated to be pledged by everyone according to what he is able to give in a pledge, the thing which he will have; i.e., it is what the <term>Brehon</term> <note>a judge in the ancient Irish legal system</note> estimates as the capability of the pledge for everyone.

...i.e., whether by knowledge or by ignorance; i.e., knowledge on the part of the plaintiff, and knowledge on the part of the surety, or ignorance on the part of the plaintiff that they [the goods] were not in the possession or in the places that were promised there, then the pledge is void. Estimation of ignorance on the part of the plaintiff and knowledge on the part of the surety, ...is paid for or lent.

Every debt for which a person gives a pledge which is not in his possession, or which is not likely to be obtained, the fine is according to what he promised; i.e., when it is not in the possession of the debtor.]
