<page-num>37</page-num>
# OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.

<margin>OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.</margin>

> **You shall not bind anyone to pay in copper, or silver, or gold, except a chieftain; you shall not bind anyone to pay in cattle like those of Cinnia, who does not have cattle; you shall not bind anyone to pay in land who is a wanderer, unless he possesses land; you shall not bind a naked person to pay in clothes, unless he has garments; to adjudicate in this manner is like a nut without fruit. The promises of all should be adjusted to their ability.**

**You shall not bind**, that is, you shall not impose the *payment* of silver, or gold, or copper, except upon the noble, for it is with him they are likely to be, or it is he that is likely to obtain them. **You shall not bind**, etc., **cattle**, that is, you shall not impose the *payment* of cattle like the cattle which Cinnia the merchant <note>Cinnia is a legendary figure in Irish legal tradition, often identified as a merchant who brought specific breeds of cattle to Ireland across the sea.</note> used to bring across with him, upon a person who does not have cattle, or who cannot easily procure them. **You shall not bind land**, that is, you shall not fix *payment* in land upon a person who is moving from place to place, unless it is found that he has land, or unless he has land to support him. **Who is wandering**, that is, upon a wanderer. **You shall not bind clothes**, that is, you shall not bind *payment* in garments upon the man who is bare naked, unless he has clothes to relieve him. **Unless he has got raiment**, that is, unless he finds clothes quickly. **It is as a nut without fruit**, that is, it is a thing which is according to the wisdom of judgments; as the shell of the "blind nut" <note>original: *cnú chaoch* — a nut that appears whole but is empty or rotted inside</note> without fruit is profitless, it is likewise profitless to do these things. **The promises should be adjusted**, that is, the thing by which the promises of all are to be estimated is the thing by which he is kept to his promise, which is the property he actually has; that is, the <term>Brehon</term> <note>A traditional Gaelic judge and arbiter of the law.</note> estimates every one's promise by his power to *fulfill* it.

If by his knowledge, or by his ignorance—that is, *if* the plaintiff has knowledge, and the surety has knowledge, or the plaintiff does not have knowledge that the <term>seds</term> <note>Units of value, typically items of moveable property or livestock.</note> which he promised on the occasion were not in his possession—it is settled upon the security of "<term>arra-goods</term> for <term>anarra-goods</term>." <note>Arra-goods refer to the specific items promised or those of a similar category; Anarra-goods are different types of items given as a substitute, such as a cup being given instead of a cow.</note> If the plaintiff be ignorant, and the surety has knowledge of *the fact*, the thing which is pledged is paid.

That is, *every* debt which a man promises when he is in a wealthy condition, or when he thinks he will obtain the payment from another; if a necessity should arise, or if it should be afterwards taken from him, it is then the case falls under the rule of "substituting one type of goods for another."

In every case of debt which a person promises when he is not in a wealthy condition, or which he does not expect to obtain, the <term>eric-fine</term> <note>A payment made in compensation for an offense or breach of contract.</note> is as a "blind nut" to him; for it is of no profit to him who breaks the agreement. It is the same with a person who binds upon another a thing which he does not possess.

<summary>This page establishes the principle of "judgment according to ability," arguing that legal penalties must be realistic based on a person's social class and current assets. It introduces the rules for "arra" and "anarra" (equivalent and non-equivalent goods) to handle debt repayment when the specific items promised are no longer available.</summary>

<term>fuidir</term>-tenants <note>A class of semi-free tenants who settled on a lord's land.</note> and <term>gormacs</term> <note>original: "gormic"; often referring to sister's sons or those who support their elderly kin.</note>. for just as they partition the inheritance, so shall they pay for the crime. **If it be from the entry** <note>original: "Maḋ don tellach"</note>, that is, if it be after the abandonment of the <term>geilfine</term>’s possession of their land, it is then that it is partitioned—the land—among the three tribes. **Except a fourth for the <term>innfine</term>** <note>original: "Aċt ceathruiṁe do finḃfine"</note>, that is, there is nothing for the <term>innfine</term> except a fourth of the <term>geilfine</term>'s inheritance, which is the sixteenth part. **From the twelve laws** <note>original: "O reċt vec"</note>, that is, from the twelve tribal laws onward, it is then they are separated, so that they are not a "tribe of the heritage" from that point out, but a "people of the heritage." **A <term>fuidir</term>-tenant does not bear liability for a kinsman’s crime**, that is, the branch of... that is, the <term>fodaer</term>, the natural unfree person, does not bear the crime of his relative. **Unless there are five households benefiting** <note>original: "Muna cuic treaḃa toirḃeanaḃar"</note>, that is, unless he has five households for his support, namely the "five-house-hundred" <note>original: "cuic raiṫ ceṭaċ"</note>, and unless they are under one lord. **If there be five complete households**, that is, if five households of every <term>rath</term>-steward of the "five-house-hundred" are completed; if there be five men of them and a hundred cattle from every man, every inheritance and crime shall be as that of a freeman <note>original: "urraiḋ"</note>, since they have the "five-house-hundred" and are under one lord; A mother's land, etc., that is, the land where the claim is valued based on the mother’s wealth; this wealth belongs to the person who enters into the contract. Her sons from the days of her public testament—that is, her sons shall own her share of the land from the day she openly made her will; meaning, they shall own it from the day of her death. "Hand" and "thigh" land <note>original: "cruhb" and "sliasta" – property acquired through personal labor or through marriage</note> is divided here just as the crime was divided previously. This refers to a female heir <note>original: "bancomarba"</note>, and her tribe is not required to restore property to her if the tribal land is closer in female succession to the mother of the son than to the father; in that case, the tribe claims it by their right of partition, as it is her duty to bring her tribal property back to the tribe.

<margin>
From the Irish *Of*.
</margin>

**But half of it is returned,** that is, the half belonging to the original owner of the land is restored to his tribe. The reason the word "but" is used here is because this is tribal land, whereas "hand" and "thigh" land were mentioned previously. The logic of "but" is that no part of the father’s own possessed land is returned, but his proper ancestral land is indeed returned. **The other half,** meaning the other portion according to a true judgment, or according to the true judges. **Her own offspring shall divide it,** meaning it is partitioned among the "seed of her flesh"—her children. This refers to the son of a secondary wife <note>original: "adaltrach" – a woman in a recognized but secondary marriage contract</note> and the tribe; the land is divided into two equal parts between them. **The tribe by just partition,** meaning the tribe comes to divide it according to the law. In this partition, the tribe gives land worth fourteen <term>cumhals</term> <note>A "cumhal" was a standard unit of value, originally equal to a female slave, used here to measure land value</note> to the daughter of the highest-ranking <term>bo-aire</term> <note>A "cattle-lord," a prosperous free farmer</note>. **There is no claim by right of relationship,** meaning no claim arises from kinship according to what is legal. **Except the proper land of a bo-aire,** meaning except for the land of the bo-aire chief; specifically, half of a father's land goes to his daughter after he dies, exempt from the duties of hosting <note>military service</note>, rent, or providing formal hospitality. In this instance, a land worth twenty-eight <term>cumhals</term> had been held by a bo-aire chief of the highest rank. **Fourteen cumhals, etc.,** meaning the amount was settled at fourteen cumhals, which is the land used by a middle or lower-ranking bo-aire to provide for her. **Half the father's land passes to the daughter after the father's death;** this is without the obligations of military attack or defense. **Land given up for a road, and concerning which there are obligations,** meaning land designated for a roadway, which involves two duties: an obligation on the tribe to demand its return, and an obligation on the woman to surrender it.

That is, land <note>Land: This commentary is found as a note on the lower margin of column 2, page 9, of the manuscript E. 3. 5.</note> which is designated for a road must be restored. The obligation falls on the person who does not receive it for the livestock of the <term>fuidhir</term> <note>A tenant or stranger who does not have full rights within the tribe</note>; that person pays half of the <term>honor-price</term> <note>The legal value of a person's status</note> to one party, half to the person who gives the land, and one-third to the person to whom it is given. Honor-price is paid to the person who gives it, except for their specific time. The force of "but" here is that he does not return the father's land which he currently occupies, but he returns his own proper land; or rather, their true land is restored to the tribe. The "but" signifies that this is tribal land, and we were previously discussing "hand" and "thigh" land.

# OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.

<margin>
**OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.**
</margin>

## The children of the person to whom it is given, except for a resident—that is, his birth and his being given away cannot be achieved outside; or he who takes land as payment or for maintenance—that is, land stolen from a lord or from a church. He carries it into the tribal land <note>original: "in-ur-r-o"</note>, unless the female heir <note>term: "bancomarba" (a woman who inherits her father's land when there are no sons)</note> enters into a contract with the tribe <note>term: "fine" (the extended family group sharing land rights)</note>; the tribe takes it if they do not enter into a contract with them. This is a false claim <note>original: "imaebur"</note> for which half-compensation <note>term: "leithdire" (a fine paid at half the standard rate)</note> is paid.

**For which half-compensation is paid,**—that is, it is the payment made for the horse that reaches the person with the appropriate honor-price <note>term: "eneclainn" (the legal value of a person's status)</note>—that is, half of his land; the other half is for his restoration.

## What is the "false claim" <note>original: "smaebur"</note> mentioned here? That is, a false claim by the daughter and a false claim by the tribe. The law <note>original: "dliged"</note> says: it is a false claim by the tribe to demand restoration from the daughter when there is no son left after the father, and it is a false claim by the daughter to say the restoration belongs to the tribe.

## Safety of the overlook <note>original: "slan fairsge" – a legal term for when a neighbor watches a trespass or land use without objecting</note>, a journey of succession, grazing of land, accompanying protection. No compensation is paid after a year has passed, but it brings payment for use; for no injury that is fully healed with time is a matter for a lawsuit according to the Irish Law <note>term: "Feineachus" (the traditional laws of Ireland)</note>.

**Safety of the overlook,**—that is, the safety of restoration of the grass of the land from the person who is truly observing the farm without proper correction, so that he remains silent without making a claim until the mystery of the land grows upon its grass. **Grazing of land,**—that is, the grazing of its interior with the permission of the neighbor on his land—that is, for two or three intervals between your tenants. **No compensation is paid,**—that is, no great fine is paid after a year has truly passed while being present throughout the year without a claim, until the mystery of the land grows upon that man mentioned. **But it brings payment for use,**—that is, but the man who gives for payment according to a beautiful or pleasant contract; for even if someone remains present during the payment without a claim until the mystery grows upon its grass, the payment he is owed for it is not the less. **Because no injury,**—that is, because no lawsuit regarding grass that is fully healed with the growth of time or the lack of a claim is denied, so that it is not a proper lawsuit according to the Irish Law—that is, between a wound and grass, nothing is paid as restoration except the compensation for the wound and the fine.

That is the obligation from which the <term>half-compensation fine (leith-dire)</term> is paid.

This half-compensation fine is paid—that is, it is from this that half the portion of the land which comes to her as honor-price is paid (meaning half her land); the other half comes from her movable property.

What obligation is mentioned here? It refers to an obligation placed on the daughter and an obligation on the tribe. What the law says is: "let there be an obligation on the tribe regarding the restoration of land to the daughter when there is no son after the death of the father, and an obligation on the daughter to restore that land again to the tribe <note>likely if she dies without heirs or her line ends</note>."

In the <term>Farm-laws (Bruighrechta)</term> <note>original: "Bruighrechta"; laws governing fences, grazing, and neighboring farmers</note>, it is considered guiltless to look upon cattle grazing on the jointly-fenced land of a co-occupant. No payment shall be made after a year has passed, except according to the custom of hire; for every "wound" <note>legal term for damage to land or property</note> that is settled by arbitrators is not to be re-litigated under the <term>customary law of the free people (Feinechus)</term> <note>original: "Feinechus"</note>.

**It is guiltless to look on,**—that is, restitution for the grass of the land does not need to be made by the person who is actually watching the land, and for whom it is not his place to correct the situation, if the land remains unclaimed until the grass grows back on top. **Grazing on a farm,**—that is, they graze the top of the grass on the land while the neighbor is aware of it (for two or three nights unprofitably) on your partner's land. **Nothing shall be paid,**—that is, the <term>restitution fine (eric)</term> <note>original: "eric"</note> shall not be paid for it after the owner has been aware of it for a year without making a claim, until the grass grows back. **But after the custom of hire,**^2—that is, regarding the grass which he lets for hire without claiming it until it grows back, he is still entitled to have his hire paid to him. **For every wound,**—that is, for every damage to grass that is repaired by arbitration, it cannot be further sued for; the prefix "de" is a negative <note>original: "de"; a Latin/Old Irish linguistic note</note>, meaning there is no further claim for it according to the Feinechus-law^3—that is, regarding^b the "wound" and the grass, compensation is not paid, but rather the **compensation fine (dire)** for the damage 
<margin>b Irish: *Between.*</margin>
and the **penalty fine (smacht)** <note>original: "smacht"; a fixed fine for specific infractions</note>.

**Honor-price:** one-fourth for land and "dead" chattels <note>non-living property like tools or furniture</note>, half of that for land alone, so that one-half of this is given to her (the sixteenth part). Or, indeed, it is a balance struck between land and dead chattels, or one-sixteenth for either, unless they are made equal through arbitration.

***

^2 **But after the custom of hire.** In document C. 859, the following note is given:—"But after the manner of hire. The custom of this is: whatever is contracted is enforced; but if no contract has been made, no payment is made. Thus it is with trespasses in the case of co-occupancy: unless they are claimed within a year of the trespass, they shall not be enforced."

^3 **Feinechus-law.** That is, whatever is submitted to arbitration and decided must be considered finally settled. There can be no further appeal to the^4 **Feinechus-law.**

# OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.

<margin>
**OF TAKING**
**LAWFUL**
**POSSESSION.**
---
</margin>

.i. <note>original: ".i."; an abbreviation for "id est" or "that is to say"</note> As for the wounds <note>original: "na cneḋa"</note>, if they have not been healed to health, and no legal necessity was involved, restitution <note>original: "aiṫgin"; the return of an equivalent value</note> is not paid, but only the <term>body-fine (eric)</term> <note>original: "colann eiric"; the standard compensation for physical injury or death</note>.

If a man has been negligent in not making a claim against another freeman in his place, the right to restitution <note>original: "aiṫġina"</note> is voided, and the <term>smacht-fine</term> <note>original: "smaċta"; a fine for minor offenses or breach of contract</note> is forfeited in that case; the compensation for the trespass passes away from the person through lapse of time, and it is then that the right to restitution falls away from a person through their own neglect.

.i. What is meant here is a person who was aware of a neighbor's trespass against him, but through neglect, he failed to sue his man; [the case] may be mediated, but restitution is not paid, and that is the one instance where a person's neglect causes them to forfeit restitution, and <term>sick-maintenance (othrus)</term> <note>original: "oṫrus"; the legal obligation to provide medical care and food to an injured party</note> is not paid in the case of such neglect.

The peace of every ancient law is the comparison <note>or "adjustment"</note> of every territory. When every territory is without comparison <note>meaning a state of legal disorder or lack of local arbitration</note>, it is then that every "headless" <note>original: "díġeand"; a case without a clear legal head or local judge</note> case is brought to the King.

"The peace of every ancient law," that is, the streams of every ancient law, or every distinction of them that reached each other, or every ancient law compared to one another, or every law according to the elders. "When it is without comparison," that is, when there is no judge for the local community or for the claimant. "It is then that every headless case is brought to the King;" that is, it is then that every "headless" case—without a leader or a prior judgment—is brought toward the King, because it is with him that finality <note>original: "tairċeċtaċ"</note> is likely to be found. "Headless" <note>original: "Díġeand"</note>, that is, the good deciders of a contest.

He is no King who has no hostages in shackles, to whom "tribute-rods" <note>original: "cíṫ-ṡlaṫa"; symbols of authority and the payment of dues</note> are not given, and to whom the fines of the law are not paid. When the King receives these duties, it is then that the King's <term>honor-price (dire)</term> <note>original: "díre"; the legal value of the King's status</note> is assigned to him, provided he is without falsehood, without betrayal, and without unjust expulsion of his people.

"He is no King," that is, he is not to be called a King unless he has hostages for the fulfillment of his kingship or his <term>base-tenancy (céillsine)</term>. "To whom tribute-rods are not given," that is, the dues of base-tenancy, or food-rents. "Fines of the law," that is, the <term>smacht-fine</term> of the law. "When the King receives," that is, when he receives the subjection or the grip we mentioned before. "It is then that the honor-price is assigned," that is, it is then the King's full <term>honor-price (eneclann)</term> is paid, through these duties—namely, hostages, tribute, and fines. "Without falsehood," that is, in his judgment, or regarding false witness, or regarding his unjust expulsion [of subjects].

That is to say, regarding the wounds, indeed, unless a claim is made for them before they have healed—and assuming no unavoidable necessity prevented the claim—no compensation is paid except for the <term>body-fine (eric)</term> <note>original: "eric"; the standard compensation for physical injury or death</note> alone.

If a person has neglected to sue for the loss of grass <note>referring to grazing trespass by a neighbor's livestock</note> until new grass has grown in its place, the right to compensation is forfeited, though the <term>penalty-fine (smacht)</term> <note>original: "smacht"; a fixed fine for minor offenses or breach of contract</note> for that item must still be repaid; the compensation for the damage becomes obsolete to the person, and in this case, the right to compensation <margin>Irish: falls from</margin> a person through their own neglect.

This is the only instance in which compensation is forfeited by a person through their own neglect, and <term>sick-maintenance</term> <note>original: "othrus"; the legal obligation of an injurer to provide medical care and food to the injured party</note> is not paid due to the neglect.

## Constant is every old law of every territory of covenants. When any territory is uncovenanted, it is then every disputed case is brought before the king.

"Constant is every old law," that is, perpetual is every ancient arrangement and every decision that follows one another, or every old law shared between territories, or every law according to the ancestors. "When uncovenanted," meaning when either the defendant or the plaintiff does not have a <term>Brehon</term> <note>original: "Brehon"; a professional class of jurists and judges in early Ireland</note>. It is then that every disputed case is brought before the king; that is, every disputed case of crime and judgment is brought before him, for it is with the king that the solution to every difficulty is most likely to be found. "Disputed case" refers to the specific matter brought forward to be settled.

Irish: Without.
</margin>

## He is not a king who has not hostages in fetters, to whom the rent of a king is not given, to whom the fines of law are not paid. But when the king gets these submissions, it is then the <term>honor-price (dire)</term> <note>original: "dire"; the legal value or status-price of a person, which determined their rights and the fines due to them</note> of a king is paid, provided he is <margin>Irish: without</margin> falsehood, from the betrayal of his nobles, and from unworthy conduct toward his people.

"He is not a king," meaning he is not to be titled a king unless he holds hostages to ensure the security of his kingship or his tenants' loyalty. "To whom the rent of a king is not given" refers to the rent paid under <term>base-tenant (daer-stock)</term> <note>original: "daer-stock"; a form of tenancy where the tenant receives livestock from a lord in exchange for labor and a portion of produce</note> agreements, such as malt. "Fines of law" refers to the <term>penalty-fine (smacht)</term> of the law. "When the king gets" means when he receives the submission or allegiance mentioned previously. It is then that the <term>honor-price (dire)</term> is paid; that is, the king's full honor-price is completely paid to him once these submissions—namely hostages, rent, and penalty-fines—are secured. "Free from falsehood" refers to the king's integrity regarding judgments passed, false witness borne, or general impropriety.

# OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.

<margin>
**OF TAKING**
**LAWFUL**
**POSSESSION.**
</margin>

Without deceit <note>original: "eaḃḃnat"</note>, that is, without the concealment of wounds; and it is not lawful to conceal wounds. Without an immediate outcry—concerning the falsehood of his law, or concerning wounding or theft upon his tribes; for if he did not possess these <note>referring to the qualities of justice and protection</note>, he would not be entitled to the full <term>honor-price (eneclann)</term> <note>original: "eneclaṉṉ"; the value of a person's legal status</note> of a king.

There are seven witnesses which attest to the falsehood of every king: plundering a <term>synod</term> <note>original: "ṡenaḋ"; an ecclesiastical council or church assembly</note> within its precinct; acting without truth and without law; the neglect of a protector, unless it be for the sake of justice; defeat in battle; famine during his reign; milkless water <note>a sign of a barren land where cows produce no milk</note>; the destruction of the mast <note>original: "meaſa"; the crop of acorns and nuts in the forest, vital for feeding livestock</note>; and the failure of grain. These are the seven "living candles" <note>original: "mbeocaíndle"</note> that expose the falsehood of every king.

There are seven witnesses, that is, there are seven laws like witnesses that prove the falsehood of every man who is a king. Plundering a synod, that is, the synod of the Church being turned away from its sanctuary. Without truth, that is, regarding the debts of the guilty, which is without justice. Without law, that is, regarding the debts of the innocent being imposed upon them. The neglect of a protector, that is, in an unlawful manner. Unless it be for justice, that is, unless there is an exception, and I have an exception here: if it be for the sake of legal fulfillment for him, it is not an unlawful neglect. Defeat in battle, that is, when his numbers are not equal to the enemy's, he loses half of the <term>honor-price</term> of a chariot-chief. Famine, that is, to be without food, or for hunger to exist during his reign. Milkless water, that is, water without milk, or the wateriness of the milk. Destruction of the mast, that is, after it has been produced, it is destroyed. Failure of grain, that is, a blight upon the seeds or crops, or a smallness of the grain being present. These are the "living candles," that is, these laws mentioned above are like living candles which manifest or reveal the falsehood of every person who is a king.

There are three falsehoods that are most grievous to God upon every territory: the addition of a false binding; the attestation of false witness; and a false judgment given for a reward.

Three falsehoods, that is, three specific lies that are the worst for God to find upon the tribes. The addition of a false binding, that is, receiving a payment for acting as a false <term>surety</term> <note>original: "naḋma"; a person who guarantees a contract</note>, and it is not lawful to receive payment even for true suretyship—that is, a fee for the guarantee when it does not exist. Grievous to God, that is, to be punished by God. The attestation of false witness, that is, the perjury that is sworn. A false judgment for a reward <note>original: "ġuḃreaṫ ar ḟoċraıc"</note>, that is, the false decisions delivered by him for the sake of receiving wealth or payment; and it is not lawful to deliver such judgments even if they were given for free.

<margin>

**LAWFUL**
**POSSESSION.**

...done by him. **From betrayal, that is,** without betraying the nobles; and it is no more lawful for him to betray the <term>plebeians (aithech-thuatha)</term> <note>the commoners or tenant farmers</note>. **From unworthy conduct, that is,** regarding a false decision of his law, or regarding wounding or robbing his own people; for if he had *been guilty* of any of these, he shall not be entitled to the full <term>honor-price (eneclann)</term> <note>original: "eneclann"; the legal value of a person's status</note> of a king.

There are seven proofs which attest to the falsehood of every king: to turn a <term>synod</term> <note>original: "ṡenaḋ"; an ecclesiastical council or church assembly</note> out of their noble <term>lis-fort</term> <note>original: "lios"; a circular earthen enclosure or sanctuary</note>; to be without truth and without law; <term>neglect of protection (dide aire)</term>, unless the demands of the parties were beyond what is right; defeat in battle; famine <note>original: "gorta"</note> during his reign; the dryness of cows; the blight of fruit; and the scarcity of grain. These are the "seven live candles" <note>original: "mbeocaíndle"</note> which expose the falsehood of every king.

There are seven witnesses, that is, there are seven things that act as witnesses to prove the falsehood of every king. **To turn a synod out,** that is, to turn the council of the church out of their noble enclosure <note>their place of assembly or sanctuary</note>. **Without truth,** that is, regarding certain fines—acting without justice. **Without law,** that is, regarding the granting of uncertain debts. **"Neglect of protection" (Dide-aire),** that is, acting unlawfully. **Unless, etc., beyond right,** that is, "unless" is used here to mean "but"; I make an exception here—if it is after he has already offered a legal settlement, it is not then unlawful for him to refuse further demands. **Defeat in battle,** that is, being defeated by an equal number on a lawful battlefield; half of his honor-price is taken away because of it. **Famine,** that is, to be without wealth, meaning that famine should occur during his reign. **Dryness of cows,** that is, failure—to be without milk or the destruction of the milk supply. **Blight of fruit,** that is, after its appearance, it is *afterwards* destroyed *while still in the bud*. **Scarcity of grain,** that is, the disappearance of the corn, its vanishing, or only a small quantity of grain being in existence. **These are the seven live candles,** that is, these things above are the seven signs, like living candles, which expose or display the falsehood of any man who is a king to everyone.

There are three falsehoods which God most avenges upon every territory: additional gain by a false contract; a decision based on false witness; and a false judgment *given for a fee* <note>original: "ar log"; a bribe or payment</note>.

There are indeed three falsehoods for which God takes the worst vengeance upon the lands. **Additional gain by a false contract,** that is, to receive an extra reward for a false contract when it is not lawful to receive it even for a true contract—for instance, getting a reward by claiming there is a covenant where there is none. **Which God avenges,** that is, for which God pours down His vengeance. **Decision by false witness,** that is, to approve of or accept false testimony. **False judgment for hire,** that is, false judgments being passed by him in exchange for payment or hire, when it is not lawful to pass them even if done for free.

# OF THE PERMANENT LAWFUL POSSESSION.

<margin>
**Of taking**
**Lawful**
**Possession.**
</margin>

There are four bonds which do not hold, even though they should be attempted: a servant against his lord; a son against his father; a monk against his abbot; a <term>person without legal standing</term> <note>original: "ulaċ"; often referring to a "silent person" or one whose testimony is not recognized</note> against another, if he be alone. For a lord, a kindred, and a church dissolve every <term>favorable contract</term> <note>original: "roċar"; a contract of equal or advantageous value</note> and every <term>unfavorable contract</term> <note>original: "noċar"; a fraudulent or disadvantageous contract</note> which is made by their members, unless it was commanded; for these are the three bonds of litigation which are bound in Irish law <note>original: "la feine"</note>: a contract made by the members of a church, a contract made by the servants of a lord, and a contract made by the <term>helpless members</term> <note>original: "faenleaġaċaiḃ"; literally "those lying on their backs," meaning dependents or those without full legal capacity</note> of a kindred. For a lord, a kindred, and a church annul every contract that is not consented to; for it is required of them that the contracts be not void, for if they themselves were to void a contract, it is then that they do not annul the contracts of their members.

---

For it is difficult in the jurisprudence of contracts in Irish law to determine "strong contracts." For strong contracts in Irish law are: one made by a man regarding his prohibition, and another regarding his command; for it is of this it is said: "The command or the prohibition of the wealthy man is what decides the doubtful dispute."

**There are four bonds,** that is, there are four who make a binding, and they are not held valid even though they were entreated into them, that is, a contract made by members in the absence of their heads; the heads dissolve those contracts unless they have a desire for them, that is, it is thus, or it refers to the <term>fine</term> paid here even if the restitution is not paid. **Even though they should be attempted,** that is, even if they were completed by them. **A servant against his lord,** that is, the lord voids it if he wishes. **A son against his father,** that is, the same here. **A monk against his abbot,** that is, until their heads pay for it, for it is the duty of the member to perform every service for the head who takes responsibility for him until they receive their counter-services. **A person without legal standing against another,** that is, because he voids it; that is, a person who is without witnesses, even if he be in a field, it is thus he shall be. **For it dissolves,** that is, it would not be a matter of wonder if there were no recovery from them, for it dissolves every contract they make. **Every favorable contract,** that is, a contract of equal value. **Every unfavorable contract,** that is, an unfair dealing. **Placed upon their members,** that is, which are placed upon their subordinates, upon their members; even though the heads did not dissolve them or void the contracts that were made with themselves. **Except what was commanded,** that is, except that which...

**Lawful**
**Possession.**

There are four agreements which are not binding even if the parties are legally pursued: that of a servant with his lord; of a son with his father; of a monk with his abbot; and of a <term>person without legal standing</term> <note>original: "ulach"; likely referring to someone whose testimony is not recognized, such as a "silent person" or one without property</note> with another, if they are alone. These are the three defective agreements mentioned in <term>Irish Law</term> <note>original: "Feini"; refers to the ancient legal system and the free classes of Ireland</note>: an agreement made by a subject of the church, an agreement made by a servant of a chief, and an agreement made by fugitives from a tribe. For the chief, the tribe, and the church may annul every agreement of this kind to which they did not consent. They are required to be vigilant regarding these agreements, because if they are negligent, they lose the right to annul the agreements of their subjects.

In the judgment of agreements within Irish Law, the agreements of three specific groups are difficult to resolve. The <term>binding agreements</term> <note>original: "ternal"; likely "eternal" or "strong" contracts</note> in Irish Law are those where one man commands the agreement and another forbids it; for the authority to command belongs to the one who has not forbidden what he has heard.

There are four agreements—meaning there are four types of persons who make agreements—against whom legal proceedings cannot be successfully maintained even if they are sued. These are: agreements made with subjects in the absence of their chiefs. The chiefs may dissolve these agreements unless they gave their consent to the making of them. In such cases, a <term>disciplinary fine</term> <note>original: "smacht"; a fixed fine for a specific offense under Brehon law</note> is paid, even if full compensation is not. 

**Though they are proceeded against**, meaning though they are sued in court. **A servant with his chief**, meaning the chief may reject the deal if he wishes. **A son with his father**, meaning <note>original: "sic oc"; Latin "sic hoc," meaning "it is thus"</note> it is the same. **A monk with his abbot**, meaning until he has paid for his offenses; for it is difficult for a subject to serve a chief who takes property from him until he receives something in return. **A person without legal standing**, because he will simply deny the whole matter; an "ulach" who lacks a witness—even if they are out in the open—will have his agreement treated this way. **Will rescind**, meaning it is no surprise they cannot be forced into these deals, for the superiors rescind every contract the subjects make. **Every good contract**, meaning every contract of full and fair value. **Every bad contract**, meaning fraudulent ones. **Which are made with their subjects**, meaning those placed upon their dependents; for if they can dissolve contracts made with others, they can certainly deny those made with themselves. **Except what they themselves order**, meaning...

They should make these agreements themselves with another person, for it is not possible to rescind them except as they have made their own contract. For these are the <term>three covenants</term> <note>original: "teora naidmann"</note> that are found in the <term>Irish Law</term> <note>original: "fenechas"; the ancient legal system of the Gaelic people</note> to be defective, and it is a loss of their profit from the one who makes them. These are: a contract made against the property of the **church** (that is, in its absence or without authority); a contract regarding the **services of a lord** (that is, making a contract with the people who are in service to the lord); and a contract regarding **fugitives** (that is, a contract made by those who have been cast out or have wandered away from the **tribe** <note>original: "fine"; the extended family or kin-group</note>).

For the lord, the church, and the tribe may challenge every contract that is not pleasing to its members. The reason for this is as we have said before: there are three covenants to be refused. This applies to those who are in a state of "great friendship" <note>likely referring to a specific legal status of alliance</note>; the one who sold his share of it, it is forfeited from him; and the one who did not sell it, it is not forfeited from him. For it is required of them that they should not be "clinging" or "neglectful" when it comes to recovering unlawful contracts made by their members. They must not be slow to recover them after the contract is truly made. For if they were "decayed" (that is, if they were biased or negligent without taking action against the contracts), then we do not turn back—meaning, the contracts made by the members cannot be overturned if there was such negligence.

For it is among these things that judgment is most difficult regarding contracts according to the Irish Law. It concerns the "portion of three" (that is, the portion of three people or three groups). One of them <gloss>at the command of doing it</gloss> <note>original: "dia forngaire"</note> <gloss>at the prohibition of not doing it</gloss> <note>original: "anncursaire"; see translator's note below</note>. For there is a command for those things; for it is to those people that it applies, whether to a person or to things, to command its doing unless a prohibition is made against its doing.

There are three covenants in Irish Law which nothing can reach or invalidate: a reduction of the **honor-price** <note>original: "log eneach"; the legal value of a person's status</note> of a freeman, or a bond that goes upon someone when a proclamation is discovered; a bond for the settlement of **theft** <note>original: "gaide"</note> with a thief though he did not steal it himself; and an excessive **bride-price** <note>original: "coibche"</note> given to a woman. For there are two types of "excessive" contracts in Irish Law: a woman to whom a bride-price is given and she is bonded to it, and a man who gives a great bride-price for a <term>noblewoman</term> <note>original: "baidrig"</note> from whom he does not legally separate. For these are...

These are:
1.  **The covenant with a subject of a church:** that is, an agreement made in the absence of the church authorities.
2.  **The covenant of a servitor of a chief:** that is, a contract made with those people who are performing service for a lord.
3.  **A covenant with fugitives from a tribe:** that is, a contract made with individuals who have fled from their <term>kin-group</term> <note>original: "fine"; the extended family unit that held collective legal responsibility</note>.

For the lord, the church, and the tribe may annul every contract with which their subjects are not satisfied. The logic here is as we stated before: there are three defective covenants. This also refers to a shared asset <note>original: "sed"; likely referring to a *sét*, a unit of value such as a heifer, held in common</note> owned by many persons; the person who sold their share of it forfeits it, but as for the person who did not sell it, it is not forfeited by them. 

For they are bound—that is, it is required of them that they not be remiss or negligent in setting aside the unlawful contracts which their subjects make. Specifically, they must not be slow in setting them aside once they have gained knowledge of the contracts. Because if they should be negligent—that is, if they should be remiss and fail to challenge the covenants—then they cannot annul them. It is in that case that they cannot abrogate or set aside the contracts their subjects made by opposing them later.

For they are difficult—that is, these are among the most difficult matters in the judgment of contracts according to the <term>Irish Law</term>. These are the **ternary covenants**—that is, the contracts involving three persons or three parties. One man commands it—that is, he commands that it be done and forbids it not being done. For from him comes the command—that is, from that principle is derived the rule that it is the same for a person to command an action as it is to forbid its omission.

3.  Giving an excessively large wedding gift to an **unstable person** <note>original: "eachlach"; usually a messenger or person of low/unstable status</note>.

# ON THE TAKING OF LAWFUL POSSESSION.

<margin>
**Of taking lawful possession.**
</margin>

A price of full value is paid for it. "Every heart," <note>original: "craide"; here used metaphorically for a person's intent or a binding contract</note> that is, every contract that brings forth the full fulfillment of its joint-duty in gift and covenant. He is entitled to a "sound heart," that is, he is entitled to the preservation of his contract as is the will of the **Brehon** <note>a traditional Gaelic judge and legal scholar</note>, or as the Brehon shall decide according to his will. "Except when it is forbidden," that is, when property is given to one who knows it is "proclaimed," <note>publicly declared illegal or outlawed</note> that is, an agreement of theft with a thief. Or "great power," that is, excessive force at any time against a layman, for that person is not lawful, and nothing is obtained by "force," <note>original: "ar eicin"</note> that is, by violence; or that which is bought in a "bad market," <note>original: "mbecluag"; a transaction lacking legal transparency or proper witnesses</note> that is, a contract that should be made truly and with security, or alternatively, a contract made by a sub-member of a family without authority.

There are three agreements which are "unbound" by the **Feini** <note>the ancient free classes of Ireland governed by these laws</note> against the will of the parties: a woman who is given with a **bride-price** <note>original: "coibche"; the payment given to a woman's family or the woman herself upon marriage</note> when her father is acting unlawfully; if it is through the neglect of the father, for the father alone owns that bride-price; a contract made apart from his kin-group which ought to be with them; or a contract of "tillage" <note>likely referring to land use agreements</note> made apart from the family who holds the rights. For these are the agreements that are unbound by the parties as they are not lawful to be bound.

There are three prohibitions, that is, three sacred prohibitions which are mentioned in the ancient law. "Unbinding," that is, denying them, so that neither the sureties nor the parties are bound by those who have taken charge, that is, though they be made to be restored. "A woman to whom a bride-price is given," that is, unless they are of equal status, or unless it is a "lawful heart," <note>a valid and fair marriage agreement</note> within the kinship. "If it be through neglect," that is, if it be for the sake of the father's own hidden gain that this is done. "For the father alone," that is, the father is entitled to that bride-price, and the woman is "lawful" to the one to whom she is given.

<margin>
O’D. 426. <note>Refers to the O’Donovan transcripts of the Irish Laws.</note>
</margin>

That is: If the daughter knows that the disposal of her bride-price was made for the sake of the father’s hidden gain, whatever portion the father was entitled to from the bride-price is added to the woman's own portion or shares, until there is a complete bride-price there; and even if the woman commits an illegal act regarding the bride-price or a portion of it, the father does not pay any of it; if, however, the daughter did not know it was done for the sake of hidden gain, she is "clear," <note>legally exempt from penalty</note> and the person who made the "tillage" <note>the arrangement or contract</note> pays for it.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of valid and invalid contracts within the Gaelic legal system. # OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION. 61

<margin>
**OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.**
</margin>

Every property—that is, every property which is insecure regarding her full marriage-gift <note>The "dower" or "bride-price" provided at the time of marriage</note> by contract and covenant—is entitled, etc., to be made secure. This means her property is entitled to be protected according to the decision of the **Brehon** <note>original: "Breitheamh"; a traditional Gaelic judge and legal expert</note>, or as the **Brehon** shall rule regarding it. Exceptions include cases of poverty or prohibition—that is, *concerning the act of giving*. For example, an agreement made with someone who is aware of a public proclamation <note>A legal notice declaring certain goods or people to be outside the protection of the law</note>, such as a contract involving stolen property made with a thief. Other exceptions include a "lack of power," such as giving an excessive marriage-gift to a harlot, for that is an unlawful agreement and nothing makes it binding; or agreements made through violence, or the "barrier" of a man who purchases something for far less than its value. A valid contract requires the agreement of two sane persons acting with full knowledge and legal warranty; or, according to other legal opinions, it refers to a contract made with those under one's authority.

There are three covenants entered into by the **Feini** <note>The ancient free classes of Ireland who were subject to these laws</note> which the parties who have claims <note>original: "feiceam"; a term that can mean a creditor, a debtor, or a legal advocate. See footnote 2 below.</note> may dissolve:
1. That of a woman to whom a marriage-gift is given if it is concealed from her father. (If it is hidden from the father, this marriage-gift is due to the father alone).
2. A covenant which is made without the *knowledge* of the chief of a tribe, who ought to be *present* with them.
3. A contract of adoption which is made without the knowledge of the tribe being petitioned.

For these are the "bad covenants" which the parties having claims may dissolve, and which are not considered binding.

There are three covenants—that is, three specific types of agreements—which are "fastened" or made permanent, as mentioned in the **Fenechus-law** <note>The body of traditional Irish customary law</note>. To "dissolve" them involves the prefix "di," which acts as a negative. This means the sureties do not bind the parties for whom they have entered into security, even if it is cast upon them as a reproach. Regarding "a woman to whom a marriage-gift is given," this applies unless she is of equal family status, or unless it is a legally recognized marriage-gift, even if she is of equal status. "If concealed" means if the act was done specifically for the purpose of defrauding the father. "It is to the father alone" signifies that the marriage-gift belongs entirely to the father, and the woman's right to it is forfeited because of the person who gave it.

If the daughter is aware that the agreement for her marriage-gift was made specifically to defraud her father, then whatever portion of that gift the father is entitled to must be paid to him in **seds** <note>original: "seóit"; units of value in the Brehon system, often represented by cattle or specific luxury items</note> out of the woman's own lawful property until the full gift is restored. Furthermore, even if the woman commits a crime for which her marriage-gift (or a part of it) would normally be liable to pay a fine, the father is not required to pay any part of it. However, if the daughter did not know the contract was intended to defraud her father, she is considered guiltless, and the person who initiated the marriage contract shall be the one to pay.

</note>

-># Concerning Lawful Possession.<-

<margin>
**OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION.**
</margin>

A contract entered into without the head of the tribe¹, <gloss>that is, the contract made without the person who is the perfection of the tribe, namely, the chief of the **Gelfine** <note>The 'Gelfine' was the most immediate family circle in Brehon law, consisting of the father and his closest male descendants.</note>.</gloss> It is more proper for him to be involved, <gloss>that is, it is more fitting that the contract be made with his participation.</gloss> The contract of a "reared son" <gloss>that is, the contract entered into regarding a son who is being supported by the tribe, and not out of a duty of maintenance by the **Gelfine**.</gloss> Without the "waiting tribe" <gloss>that is, without the kin-group that is waiting to pay for his liabilities.</gloss> For these are the "unbinding bonds," <gloss>since these are the covenants that are being nullified;</gloss> and they are denied <gloss>so that the sureties and the debtors for whom they have stood as security are not bound by them.</gloss> They are not proper, <gloss>that is, it is not right to bind them.</gloss>

## Half of every first marriage-gift <note>original: "coibche"; the bride-price or gift given at marriage</note> of every woman belongs to her tribal head, if it be after the death of her father, if he has paid for her liabilities; a third for the second, a fourth for the third marriage-gift. If she be a woman who moves frequently <note>A woman who changes husbands often</note> for a lawful reason from that position, they are shared in proportions of the fine; for there is a share of the marriage-gift of every woman for her tribal head, just as there is a share in the "unbinding" of it. It is upon this foundation that the judgments of the professional poet and the unlearned poet <note>original: "duain" and "ambuain"</note> are settled according to the law of the **Feini** <note>The free legal class of ancient Ireland</note>.

Half of every first marriage-gift, <gloss>that is, this is not taken until it is the legal property of the woman.</gloss> The reason a smaller portion is taken from the woman as she more frequently leaves her husbands is so that the frequency of her being abandoned may be lessened. To her tribal head, <gloss>that is, to the person who is the perfection of the tribe.</gloss>

<gloss>That is: If the father is not living, she receives half the fosterage fee from the tribal head, or half the "fosterage-return" <note>original: "iarraid"</note> with her, and a binding agreement with her kin-group, and a third of the **Tinol**² <note>original: "tinol"; a collection of wedding gifts from friends and relatives</note> with her for every man she shall go to; and though she may be bound many times to one man, she is only entitled to a third of the marriage-collection one time³.</gloss> If, however, the father is living, she receives half the "fosterage-return" or half the fosterage fee from the father, and a binding agreement with her kin-group; and a third of the marriage-collection with her for every man she goes to, and so forth; as it is in the **Judgments of Inadvertence**⁴ <note>original: "Bretha Eidgeadh"; a legal text concerning accidental injuries and certain marriage laws</note>.

---

¹ <note>**To the head of the tribe.**—The Irish gloss may also mean, ‘to the most perfect person who is of the tribe.’</note>
² <note>**‘Tinol’—marriage collection.**—‘Tinol’ was the collection of gifts which the relatives and friends presented to the woman on her marriage. (See volume 2, page 346, note 3).</note>
³ <note>**But once.** That is, if she was divorced and afterwards married to the same man. In other legal manuscripts, it is added that it is lawful to marry her to the seventh person; beyond that, she is considered a ‘vulture of a battlefield’ <note>original: "gatbul baidbe"; a derogatory term for a woman who has had an excessive number of husbands</note>.</note>
⁴ <note>**Judgments of ‘Eidgeadh.’** See volume 3, pages 88-97.</note>

# OF TAKING LAWFUL POSSESSION. 63

<margin>
**ON THE LAWFUL TAKING OF POSSESSION.**
</margin>

A contract which is made without the *knowledge* of the chief of a tribe, <gloss>that is, the contract which is made without the *knowledge* of the head of the tribe, namely, the chief of the **immediate family group** <note>original: "geilfine"; the smallest and most senior unit of the Irish kin-group</note>.</gloss> Who ought to be with them, <gloss>that is, it is right that he should be present at the making of it.</gloss> A contract of adoption, <gloss>that is, a covenant which is made with the adopted son of the tribe, and it is not intended for his future support to come from the **immediate family's** share of land.</gloss> Unknown to the petitioning tribe, <gloss>that is, without the knowledge of the kin-group that is responsible for the *payment* of his legal liabilities or crimes.</gloss> For these are the "bad covenants," etc., <gloss>that is, for these are the covenants which, having been made, are dissolved again;</gloss> and 'de' is a negative, <gloss>that is, the sureties do not bind the debtors for whom they enter into security.</gloss> Which are not binding, <gloss>that is, it is not right to make them permanent.</gloss>

*Half of each first marriage gift <note>original: "coibche"; the gift given by a husband to his wife's family or to the wife herself</note> of every woman is due to the head of her tribe, if she is married after the death of her father, provided it was the chief who had sustained and paid for the costs of her crimes; one-third of the second marriage gift is due, and one-fourth of the third. If she leaves that marriage out of necessity, the gift shall be distributed according to the arrangements of the **Law-abiding Irish** <note>original: "Feini"; refers to the free classes of ancient Ireland and their legal system</note>; for a share of the marriage gift of every woman is due to the head of her tribe, just as he has his share in the **legal gains** <note>original: "abad"; here referring to the fines or profits the tribe receives from the activities of an unattached woman or harlot</note> of a harlot. It is by these rules that the legal standing of every proper and improper woman is known among the **Law-abiding Irish**.*

Half of each first marriage gift, <gloss>that is, this portion is not given until it is lawfully due to the woman.</gloss> The reason that a smaller portion is taken from the woman if she has been put away or divorced frequently is because the amount of her livestock and wealth has been reduced. To the head of her tribe, <gloss>that is, to the leader of the kin-group.</gloss>

<margin>
a Irish: *With her.*
b Irish: *From.*
c Irish: *And.*
</margin>

If the father is no longer living, half the *price* of her fosterage <note>The fee paid for the upbringing and education of a child by foster parents</note> is paid by the chief of the tribe; or, according to other legal opinions, *she shall bring* <margin>a</margin> one-half of the fosterage price into a marriage with a man of the same tribe, and one-third of the **marriage collection** <note>original: "tinol"; the collection of goods or cattle brought by the woman into the marriage</note> is given to every man to whom she goes; and however many times she may have been contracted to one man, it is required by law that she should bring the third of the **marriage collection** with her *only once*. But if the father is still living, her half fosterage-price, or half the *expense* of her fosterage, is paid by <margin>b</margin> the father, in the event of <margin>c</margin> marriage with a man of equal social rank; and one-third of the **marriage collection** is brought by her to every man to whom she goes, etc., as it is *set forth in the **Book of Aicill** <note>original: "Eidgedh"; one of the principal texts of the Brehon Laws, dealing largely with civil liabilities and torts</note>.*

**If after the death of her father,** <gloss>that is, it is the one who is next of kin who is in that position.</gloss> **If it be he who has paid for her crimes,** <gloss>that is, if it be the head of the tribe <term>taigi fine</term> <note>The "householder of the tribe," acting as a legal guardian</note> who sustains the costs of her liabilities.</gloss> **A third of the second** <note>original: "taniroe," likely a scribal variation of "tanaiste"</note>, <gloss>that is, regarding the second marriage-gift <term>coibche</term> <note>The gift given by a husband to the wife’s family or the wife herself</note>; a legal term for a woman's union made without tribal consent</note> when she goes to him by force, whether it be a "madness" of the air <note>referring to mental instability</note> or a "madness" that does not...; and the distribution of her honor-price <term>eneclann</term> <note>The fine paid to compensate for an individual's loss of status or injury</note> is according to the nature of the marriage-gift in her other blood-liabilities. **His share,** <gloss>that is, what has been assigned to him.</gloss> **It is upon this that the permanent and non-permanent judgments of lawful women, and the non-permanent judgments of unlawful women, are reached.** **Permanent,** <gloss>that is, good, i.e., pure women.</gloss> **Non-permanent,** <gloss>that is, bad, i.e., women of ill-repute.</gloss>

**If after the death of her father,** <gloss>that is, in the case of the person who is next in line for the position of chief.</gloss> **If it be he that had sustained his crimes,** <gloss>that is, if it is the head of the tribe who bears the weight of the legal liabilities for his family members.</gloss> **One-third of the second,** <gloss>that is, regarding the second marriage-gift <term>coibche</term><note>A gift or payment made by a husband to a wife or her family; its distribution changed depending on whether it was the first or subsequent marriage.</note>. In the case of the second marriage-gift, her father—if he were still living—would have received two-thirds of it;</gloss> and a brother receives less than a father because he is considered less responsible for directing the girl’s affairs regarding the third of her <term>tinol</term> <note>original: "tinol"; a collection of goods or cattle brought together for a marriage</note>—the marriage-collection—if her own property has been lost. 

**If she goes away of necessity,** <gloss>that is, due to death;</gloss> **or is divorced;** <gloss>the legal uncertainty here is that if she separates from her husband without a valid necessity, it shall not deprive the male relative of the portion of the marriage-gift he would normally receive.</gloss> **From that out,** <gloss>that is, as I am discussing this specific case involving a separation by necessity.</gloss> **It shall be distributed,** <gloss>that is, the property is fairly divided according to the regulations of the traditional law <term>fenechas</term> <note>The ancient common law of Ireland</note> as it passes to the nearest kin-group.</gloss> 

**For a share of the nuptial present,** <gloss>that is, there is a portion of the marriage-gift of every woman due to the head of her tribe.</gloss> This applies even in the case of a <term>lewd woman</term> <note>In this legal context, women in informal or socially unrecognized unions</note> who is visited despite legal warnings. From this principle is derived the custom that the tribal head has a right to a share in twenty-one specific cases. This is his legal right in the case of a woman living outside formal marriage—whether she is one who accepts payment or one who does not—for even if she is taken by force, her **honor-price** <note>The "status-price" or value of a person in society used to determine legal settlements</note> is divided by the tribal head among her other relatives. 

**His share,** <gloss>that is, his portion of the <term>smacht</term>-fine <note>A fixed penalty or fine for minor offenses or breaches of contract</note>.</gloss> **It is by this are known,** <gloss>that is, it is through these rules that the legal judgments for both "good" and "bad" women are determined—distinguishing between those in lawful and unlawful unions.</gloss> **Proper,** <gloss>meaning the legal status of "good" women in recognized marriages.</gloss> **Improper,** <gloss>meaning the legal status of "bad" women in unrecognized or irregular unions.</gloss>

# THE <term>JUDGMENTS OF CO-TENANCY<note>original: breatha comaithcesa; this refers to the early Irish legal code governing the interactions between "co-tenants" or neighboring farmers who shared boundaries or common land.</note></term> HERE.

<margin>
**JUDGMENTS OF CO-TENANCY.**
---
</margin>

Why is it called <term>co-tenancy<note>original: comaithces; the relationship between neighbors regarding shared land.</note></term>? It is from "equal practice," because it is an equally practiced custom for each to discuss <term>fines<note>original: smacta; specifically fixed penalties for minor legal infractions.</note></term> and <term>trespass<note>original: cáiche; the legal term for damage caused by wandering livestock.</note></term> with the other; otherwise, it is co-tenancy because it is equally undertaken by a <term>nobleman<note>original: aire; a man of rank in the Irish social hierarchy.</note></term> toward a <term>commoner<note>original: aithech; a tenant or peasant farmer.</note></term>, and by an <term>erenagh<note>original: airchinnech; the steward or hereditary warden of church lands.</note></term> toward a <term>herdsman<note>original: bachlach; literally a "staff-bearer," referring to a lower-status laborer.</note></term>.

<gloss>The judgments of co-tenancy: i.e., this is the legal judgment that is given concerning co-tenancy, or concerning common residence, or regarding the "equal practice"—that is, the common custom.</gloss>
<gloss>Why is it called co-tenancy? i.e., why is the common residence so named or described? It is from "equal practice." Because the custom of each of them toward the other is equally the same. Fines: i.e., the [measured] penalties. Trespass: i.e., the debt of a person for trespass—that is, if the co-tenancy is not carried out according to the law. Alternatively, it is co-tenancy: i.e., another type of common residence. Because it is equally taken: i.e., because the same amount or an equal share is required from a nobleman of the lordly grades to be undertaken with a man of the commoner grades, and for an erenagh of the church to undertake it with a herdsman in the church [lands].</gloss>

Question—from where does co-tenancy grow? From <term>joint inheritance<note>original: ail comarbus; refers to the division of land among heirs which necessitates the creation of shared boundaries.</note></term>. What form does it take? Joint heirs first divide their portions and their estates, and each fences against the other, and each gives a <term>pledge<note>original: diguin; here meaning a guarantee or security for the fulfillment of mutual obligations.</note></term> to the other.

<gloss>Question—from where does co-tenancy grow? i.e., I ask from whence the common residence increases. From joint inheritance: i.e., from the pleasant inheritance of land. What form does it take? i.e., what is the manner of its course? Joint heirs: i.e., the guardians of the inheritance fairly divide the land for the first time—at the first instance I tell or relate of it. Their portions: i.e., the newly-acquired land. Their estates: i.e., the land of the father and grandfather. Each fences against the other: i.e., protecting against each other. Each gives a pledge: i.e., a pledge of three <term>screpalls<note>original: scrapall; a unit of value in early Ireland, based on the weight of a silver coin.</note></term> for the fulfillment of the co-tenancy; [it is called "di-guin" or "no-wounding"] so that no trespass of each other's cattle reaches the other.</gloss>

---

1 **<term>Erenagh<note>original: Airchinnech</note></term>.**—The steward of the church lands, or the ecclesiastical holder of the church lands. He was a layman, but had <term>the first tonsure<note>original: primam tonsuram; a ritual shaving of the head marking one as under the jurisdiction of the Church.</note></term>.

# THE JUDGMENTS OF CO-TENANCY HERE.

<margin>
**JUDGMENTS OF CO-TENANCY.**
</margin>

Why is <term>co-tenancy<note>original: comaithces; the legal framework governing neighbors who share boundaries or common lands.</note></term> so called? It is from "equal practice" (<term>cumagnais<note>derived from 'cuma' (equal) and 'gnás' (custom or practice).</note></term>), because the customs are equally good for all to reciprocally levy <term>fines<note>original: smacht; specific fixed penalties for minor legal infractions, often related to livestock.</note></term> and <term>penalties<note>original: cáiche; trespass fines.</note></term>; or, otherwise, it is called co-tenancy because it affects the <term>noble<note>original: aire; a man of rank or a chief.</note></term> equally with the <term>commoner<note>original: aithech; a tenant or peasant farmer.</note></term>, and the <term>erenagh<note>original: airchinnech; the hereditary warden or steward of church lands.</note></term> the same as the shepherd.

The <term>judgments of co-tenancy<note>original: breatha comaithcesa.</note></term>: that is, these are the legal decisions that are passed concerning lands held in common, or concerning the shared residence, or concerning the "equal practice"—that is, the common usage or the common custom *of holding land*.

**Why is co-tenancy so called?** That is, why is the holding of land in common so named or described? **Equal practice,** that is, the common usage. **Because the customs are equally good for all,** meaning because the usage is equally good (<term>commaith<note>the linguistic root of 'comaithces'.</note></term>) for everyone in their dealings with one another. **Fines,** that is, the "sacks" <note>This likely refers to payments made in grain or produce as a penalty.</note>. **Penalties,** that is, the fine for "man-trespass"—which are imposed unless the laws of co-tenancy are lawfully observed. **Or, otherwise it is co-tenancy,** which is another reason why it is so called: it is a common holding. **Because it affects, etc.,** meaning for the reason that it applies in an equal degree or in the same proportion; the noble of the lordly grade and the noble of the <term>lay-farmer<note>original: Feini; the class of free, land-owning farmers who were the backbone of early Irish society.</note></term> grade are bound to accept it, just as the steward of the church is to accept it the same as a shepherd in the church.

Question—Whence does co-tenancy arise? It arises from several heirs. In what manner does this happen? The heirs, in the first place, partition their shares and their possessions, and each of them guards against the other, and each of them gives a pledge of indemnification to the other.

**Question—Whence does co-tenancy arise?** That is, I ask how this common custom begins. **From several heirs,** meaning from the noble heirs *who are increasing in number on the family land*. **In what manner is this?** That is, in what way does it occur? **The heirs partition,** meaning the landholders fairly divide the land in the first place—the details of which I shall tell. **Their shares,** that is, their <term>inherited land<note>original: dibadh; property left by a deceased person, often partitioned among male heirs.</note></term>. **Their possessions,** meaning the lands belonging to the father or the grandfather. **Each of them guards against the other,** meaning each person is protected from the actions of the neighbor. **Each of them gives a pledge of indemnification,** that is, a pledge of two <term>screpalls<note>original: screpall; a unit of value, traditionally the weight of twenty-four grains of wheat in silver.</note></term> to observe the *law* of co-tenancy. This is "indemnification" because it ensures that the fine for any injury done by the cattle of one neighbor would not fall upon the other. <note>The original manuscript appears to have an error or missing text at this point regarding the distribution of these fines.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the legal concept of "co-tenancy" (comaithces), explaining that it is a system of mutual rights and fines that applies equally to all social classes, from nobles to commoners. It establishes that co-tenancy begins when family lands are partitioned among multiple heirs, who must then provide pledges to respect each other's boundaries and property.</summary>

<keywords>co-tenancy, Brehon Law, land partition, social hierarchy, fines, inheritance, erenagh, commoners, early Irish legal system</keywords>
